items.title: OTel tracing overhead cliffs at c=50 on TP=2 deployments — level/flush tuning has no effect
items.author: wangxf1987
items.body_excerpt:
## Title

OTel trace overhead benchmark on a production-style K8s deployment (TP=2, 2 replicas): throughput loss of 20-33% at c>=50, trace level and flush threshold have negligible effect

## Summary

We benchmarked `--enable-trace` overhead on a production-shaped K8s deployment (RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, not docker-compose), Qwen3.6-27B-CHO on sglang v0.5.18, TP=2 per replica x 2 replicas (4 GPUs total, not an exclusive full node). This complements the larger-scale results already discussed elsewhere for TP=8 exclusive-node setups, and shows the overhead shape is very different at smaller TP.

Full report (charts + tables): attached PDF (`report-en.pdf`). Raw data (`result.csv`, GPU/CPU logs) available on request.

## Environment

- sglang `v0.5.18` (community image), `SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC=1`
- Deployment: K8s RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, TP=2 per replica, 2 replicas, 4x H20 GPUs
- Trace path: sglang engine -> local OTel Agent (DaemonSet, node-local endpoint) -> Gateway -> backend, i.e. a two-hop agent-gw architecture, not a direct hardcoded Gateway connection
- 4 configs compared:
  | Group | trace level | async | flush threshold |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | G1 baseline | disabled | - | - |
  | G2 | 2 | 1 | default |
  | G3 | 3 | 1 | default |
  | G4 | 2 | 1 | 50 |
- Load generator: fixed-prompt benchmark client, concurrency swept across 1/10/50/100/200, 3 repeats per level (median)

## Findings

1. **Overhead is mild at low concurrency (c<=10)**: ttft_p99 +6~71%, throughput loss only 3~4%.
2. **c=50 is a clear inflection point**: ttft_p99 jumps 4.6x (172ms -> 965ms) going from G1 to G2 — roughly equivalent to the G1 baseline's own c=100 latency level being pulled forward to c=50. In other words, enabling trace shifts the whole latency-saturation curve left by one concurrency tier.
3. **From c>=50 onward, throughput loss is stable at 20~33%**, and grows with concurrency (-20.3% at c=50, up to -33.1% at c=200).
4. **Trace level 2 -> 3 produced no measurable incremental overhead** at c>=10 (all deltas within noise, ±2%).
5. **`SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC_FLUSH_THRESHOLD=50` vs. default also produced no measurable benefit** at c>=50 (within ±16%, mostly ±2%; one anomalous +132.9% ttft_p99 spike at c=10 looked like a transient one-off, not reproduced at other levels).
6. **Root cause for (4) and (5): CPU was never the bottleneck in this setup.** Host CPU utilization on the GPU node stayed at 2~3% across all 4 groups (vs. GPU sm% rising from 14.8% baseline to 16~19% with trace enabled). Both trace-level and flush-threshold tuning target CPU-side span processing cost — with only 2 TP ranks, span volume is low enough that CPU headroom is never exhausted, so those knobs have nothing to bite on at this scale.
7. This is a **much smaller overhead** than what we see at TP=8 on an exclusive full node (throughput loss there was 75~79%, itl_p99 spiking ~28x, with CPU pegged at 99% — happy to share that data too if useful). The magnitude gap tracks roughly linearly with TP rank count, since span generation scales with the number of ranks, and the TP=8 test used synchronous export while this one used async by default.

## Why we're filing this

- The community advice we've seen elsewhere ("lower `SGLANG_TRACE_LEVEL` to reduce overhead", "tune the async flush threshold") holds at high TP / high CPU pressure, but **doesn't transfer to smaller TP configs** — those knobs are simply inert until CPU saturates. Worth calling out in docs/guidance so users at TP<=2-4 don't spend time tuning a lever with no effect.
- The **c=50 inflection point** (throughput loss going from ~4% to ~20% within one concurrency step) suggests there may be a queueing/lock-contention effect on the trace export path that kicks in once concurrent in-flight spans cross some threshold, rather than a smooth linear cost per request. Might be worth profiling `trace_async.py`'s buffer/flush path under concurrent load to see if there's a lock or queue that serializes once request volume rises (in our TP=8 investigation, we found `trace_req_finish()`/`abort()` and `__getstate__` all trigger unconditional flushes regardless of the configured threshold, and `trace_req_start()`'s `tracer.start_span()` + `propagate.inject()` calls are synchronous OTel API calls on the request path — happy to dig further if maintainers think that's a productive direction).
- Production guidance: for small/mid TP deployments (TP<=2-4), default trace config (level=2, async on) is fine as-is. For TP=8-class deployments, overhead is materially higher and level-tuning is the effective lever — but this should probably be stated explicitly since it's not obvious from the trace docs which regime a given deployment falls into.

## Attachments

- `report-en.pdf` — full benchmark report with charts (ttft_p99 / itl_p99 / e2e_p50 / throughput vs. concurrency, delta% overview, GPU/CPU resource usage)
[Uploading report-en.pdf…]()

items.title: [Bug] Hybrid-SWA + radix cache: admission livelock when the SWA prefix lock pins a finished request's untrimmed last chunk
items.author: bill-h-lin
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

With a hybrid-SWA model, the radix cache on and a tight SWA pool, the scheduler can stop admitting a request forever: 1 waiting, 0 running, GPU idle, no log line. We hit it on MiMo-V2.6-Flash (sliding window 128, page size 1) and traced it to `SWAComponent.acquire_component_lock` pinning a whole tree node that holds a finished request's untrimmed last chunk of SWA, instead of one window.

**Sequence** (`--chunked-prefill-size 8192`, `--swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.06448` → SWA pool 8,451, `--context-length 131072`, `--max-running-requests 1`, overlap scheduler on):

1. A 32,768-token request with `max_new_tokens=1` (it finishes at its first token).
2. A request with the same 32,768 tokens, a different next token, then 4,999 more (37,768 in all).

Request 2 matches 32,768 cached tokens, needs 5,001 SWA slots and never runs. `/v1/loads` stayed at 1 waiting, 0 running for 43 minutes. The same sequence runs fine with `--chunked-prefill-size 4096` or with a 16,643-token SWA pool.

### Root cause (line numbers on `main` @ 6624999385)

1. Under the overlap scheduler, a request that finishes at its first token still gets one decode step prepared before its prefill result is processed: `alloc_for_decode` (`allocation.py:587`) commits one more token, and `release_kv_cache` → `insert_req(req, up_to=req.owned_kv_len())` keys `(origin_input_ids + output_ids)[:kv_committed_len]`. So it is cached with 32,769 tokens, its output token included.
2. `cleanup_after_caching_req` (`swa.py:1011`, the `not is_finished` guard at `:1023`) frees out-of-window SWA only for unfinished requests. So the request's final 8,192-token chunk keeps its SWA live. In the tree that is a node `[24,576, 32,641)` holding 8,065 live SWA slots, then the 128-token window leaf that `_maybe_split_leaf_for_swa_lock` (`swa.py:555`) capped "so locking it pins only one window".
3. Request 2 diverges at position 32,768, so its match splits the window leaf into 127 + 1. `acquire_component_lock` (`swa.py:811`) pins whole nodes until it has covered 128 tokens: the 127-token node, then the whole 8,065-token parent. **8,192 slots pinned** for a 128-token window.
4. `SWAPrefillBudget.check_prefill` (`prefill_budget.py:213`) sees 5,001 needed and 259 available. Since 5,001 fits an empty pool, it is not a permanent shortfall ("Transient pressure waits"), so the request waits for running requests to free slots. None exist.

The bound: only an untrimmed final chunk holds more than about one window of live SWA, so the lock over-pins by at most one chunk, while a request needs at most one chunk + 1. A pool of 2 × chunk + window + slack therefore always leaves enough (by 258 slots here), and one of chunk + window + slack, as above, can deadlock whenever a request reuses the path of one that finished at its first token (`max_tokens=1`, an immediate EOS or stop) and diverges inside its last window.

### Reproduction

- End to end: on a GPU (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell) with SGLang at 542a043, reproduced with the sequence above. That build carries local changes (an MoE expert-offload tier, and #41263's chunked-prefill SWA free order); none of them changes the radix tree, the SWA lock or `check_prefill` (#41263 only moves when a chunked request's out-of-window SWA is freed).
- On CPU, on the same build: the same four steps, with the scheduler's own `UnifiedRadixCache`, SWA allocator and `PrefillAdder` plus the orphan decode step, give 259 / 5,001 available / needed (not admitted) at chunk 8,192 / pool 8,451, and admit at chunk 4,096 (4,355 / 4,097) and at pool 16,643 (8,451 / 5,001).
- On `main`: the unit test in the linked PR builds a live parent + capped window leaf, matches a key that diverges on the last page and locks it; the lock pins the whole parent. Links 1, 2 and 4 are unchanged in the code on `main`; we have not run the end-to-end sequence on `main`.

### Proposed fix

In the lock walk, split a live, unlocked device-SWA node that is longer than what the window still needs, so only the in-window tail is pinned (the same idea as the leaf cap, applied to whatever node the walk reaches). PR: #41580.

Related: #27210 caps compute locks by splitting the lock's endpoint node. It does not cover this case: at page size 1 the match ends inside the capped leaf, the endpoint is shorter than a window, and the over-pin comes from its parent. #32379 fixed a different SWA admission livelock (decode headroom double-counted for cached resumes).

### Environment

SGLang 542a043 (end to end) and `main` 6624999385 (unit test), CUDA 13.0, torch cu130, one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm120), `--tp-size 1`, radix cache on, overlap scheduler on.

items.title: [Bug] GLM-5.3-Flash on SM120: fa4 attention backend crashes at CUDA-graph capture (hybrid extend reshape) — triton is the only working backend
items.author: Lei-010
items.body_excerpt:
# GLM-5.3-Flash on SM120 (RTX PRO 6000): attention backend matrix — fa4 crashes on hybrid extend, triton is the only working path

## Environment

- 8× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (SM120, 96 GB each), driver/CUDA as stock
- SGLang `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.20` docker image (built 2026-09-18)
- Model: `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` (official FP8 weights, TP8)
- Draft (for spec decoding legs): `incoai/GLM-5.3-Flash-DFlash2` (DFlash2DraftModel, sha256-verified)
- `--trust-remote-code`, `--context-length 131072`, `--mem-fraction-static 0.85`

## Summary

We systematically tested every attention backend that boots for Glm5Next on SM120. **Only `triton` works.** Both `flashinfer`-default (trtllm-gen fmha — already tracked in #40558) and `fa4` crash during engine init / CUDA-graph capture. The fa4 failure is a distinct bug: a shape reshape error in `forward_extend` that also reproduces **without** speculative decoding, i.e. it is not DFlash2-specific.

## Backend matrix (all TP8)

| Config | Result |
|---|---|
| default (trtllm-gen fmha) | ❌ `TllmGenFmhaRunner ... Unsupported architecture` (see #40558) |
| `--attention-backend fa4` + DFLASH | ❌ see below |
| `--attention-backend fa4`, no spec | ❌ same error — **reproduces without spec decoding** |
| `--prefill-attention-backend fa4 --attention-backend triton` + DFLASH | ❌ same error at decode capture |
| `--attention-backend triton` + DFLASH | ✅ healthy, accept len 2.73–3.90 |
| `--attention-backend triton`, no spec | ✅ healthy |

## fa4 failure signature

```python
RuntimeError: shape '[-1, 64, 8, 0]' is invalid for input of size 753975296
```

Stack (abridged):

```
sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/decode_cuda_graph_runner.py, line 464, in __init__ → self.capture()
  ... capture_one_shape → self.backend.capture_one
sglang/srt/layers/radix_attention.py, line 290, in forward
sglang/srt/layers/attention/hybrid_linear_attn_backend.py, line 1327, in forward → 1276, forward_extend
sglang/srt/layers/attention/flashattention_backend.py, line 1704, in forward_extend
RuntimeError: shape '[-1, 64, 8, 0]' is invalid for input of size 753975296
```

Observations:

1. The failing view has a trailing **0** dimension — with Glm5Next's hybrid layout (KDA linear-attention layers interleaved with full-attention layers) the fa4 `forward_extend` path receives a zero-length draft/extend token axis and `reshape` fails instead of short-circuiting.
2. `flash_attention_v4_sm120` (selected automatically when `device_capability[0] == 12`) handles decode `flash_attn_with_kvcache`, but the extend path reshaping assumes a non-empty second batch axis.
3. Repro is deterministic across ≥3 containers; failure occurs at first CUDA-graph capture (bs=48, ~90 s after weights load).

## Reproducer

```bash
docker run --gpus all --network host --ipc host \
  -v /path/GLM-5.3-Flash:/model:ro \
  --entrypoint python3 lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.20 \
  -m sglang.launch_server --model /model --tp 8 --trust-remote-code \
  --attention-backend fa4 --port 8000 --mem-fraction-static 0.85
# → RuntimeError: shape '[-1, 64, 8, 0]' is invalid ... at decode graph capture
```

## Working config (for anyone blocked on this)

```bash
... --attention-backend triton [--speculative-algorithm DFLASH --speculative-draft-model-path /draft]
```

With `triton`, GLM-5.3-Flash FP8 TP8 serves fine on SM120, and DFLASH spec decoding reaches accept len ~3.3 (block_size 8). Note prefill throughput with triton is low (~140 tok/s on an 8K prompt, single stream), which is why a working fa4/flashinfer path on SM120 matters.

Happy to provide full logs if useful.

[by Claude Code]

This issue tracks **flaky tests** and **recurring CI infrastructure failures** seen in NVIDIA `PR Test Base` / `PR Test Extra` runs while babysitting PRs with the `/sglang-pr-babysit` Claude Code workflow. items.title: [Bug] `--enable-symm-mem`: the 4 GiB symmetric-memory pool and NCCL buffers are not taken out of `--mem-fraction-static`, so the server runs out of memory after start-up
items.author: bvolpato
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [ ] The bug persists in the latest version. (Reproduced on v0.5.20 only. Main has the same memory accounting by code reading, see below. We ran a main nightly, `nightly-dev-20261011-d32d8fa0`, on TP8 with `--enable-symm-mem` only at `--mem-fraction-static 0.88`, where it works. We did not run main with the failing settings.)
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

With `--enable-symm-mem`, SGLang preallocates a 4 GiB symmetric-memory pool, and NCCL runs with cuMem and NVLS enabled and allocates its own buffers. The memory sizing does not take these allocations into account. They must fit in the memory that `--mem-fraction-static` leaves outside the static pool, together with activations and CUDA graphs. A configuration that runs without the flag can run out of CUDA memory after the server starts when the flag is on.

What we saw on SGLang v0.5.20 with GLM 5.3 Flash (a fine-tune) on 8x B200, MTP EAGLE (4 steps, top-k 1, 5 draft tokens, rejection sampling), CUDA graphs on and `--mem-fraction-static 0.90`:

1. TP8 with the default 4 GiB pool passed every step benchmark, which runs without start-up warmups. With `--warmups prefill_shapes`, the server ran out of CUDA memory in the warmup at 4K to 8K tokens:

   ```
   CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 910.00 MiB. GPU 7 has a total capacity of 178.35 GiB of which 804.62 MiB is free. Including non-PyTorch memory, this process has 177.55 GiB memory in use. Of the allocated memory 171.27 GiB is allocated by PyTorch, with 4.10 GiB allocated in private pools (e.g., CUDA Graphs), and 493.20 MiB is reserved by PyTorch but unallocated.
   ```

2. TP8 with `SGLANG_SYMM_MEM_PREALLOC_GB_SIZE=1` passed the `prefill_shapes` warmup. It then failed at the first verify broadcast with an NCCL CUDA error, as TP4 did (item 4). A smaller prealloc alone did not leave enough memory on TP8.
3. TP8 with the default 4 GiB pool and `--mem-fraction-static 0.88` passes all warmups and serves. The KV cache has 11.47M tokens instead of 11.90M at 0.90.
4. TP4 with the default 4 GiB pool reported ready, then crashed at the first verify broadcast of the first request. Excerpt of the log (only matching lines, in order):

   ```
   1420:[2026-10-11 07:17:52 TP0] Pre-allocating symmetric memory pool with 4 GiB
   1445:[2026-10-11 07:17:59 TP0] FABRIC handle export failed on rank 0; falling back to POSIX fd transport: cuMemExportToShareableHandle(FABRIC): <CUresult.CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE: 1>
   1556:[2026-10-11 07:18:28 TP3] Scheduler hit an exception: Traceback (most recent call last):
   1578:  File "/opt/t2/ov-s4symm/sglang/srt/speculative/eagle_worker_v2.py", line 1353, in forward_batch_generation
   1581:  File "/opt/t2/ov-s4symm/sglang/srt/speculative/eagle_worker_v2.py", line 1671, in verify
   1584:  File "/opt/t2/ov-s4symm/sglang/srt/speculative/eagle_worker_common.py", line 592, in run_eagle_verify
   1587:  File "/opt/t2/ov-s4symm/sglang/srt/speculative/eagle_utils.py", line 959, in eagle_sample
   1589:  File "/opt/t2/ov-s4symm/sglang/srt/distributed/parallel_state.py", line 1482, in broadcast
   1597:torch.distributed.DistBackendError: NCCL error in: /__w/pytorch/pytorch/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/NCCLUtils.cpp:92, unhandled cuda error (run with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO for details), NCCL version 2.30.7
   1598:ncclUnhandledCudaError: Call to CUDA function failed.
   1599:Last error:
   1600:Cuda failure 2 'out of memory'
   ```

5. TP4 with `SGLANG_SYMM_MEM_PREALLOC_GB_SIZE=1` starts and serves.

Code reading of main (`c0584cf9af`). v0.5.20 has the same code:

- `python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/memory_hook.py` lines 351 to 356: when `--enable-symm-mem` is set and `SGLANG_SYMM_MEM_PREALLOC_GB_SIZE` is not set, the prealloc size becomes 4 GiB. `mem_fraction_static` does not change.
- `python/sglang/srt/model_executor/model_runner_components/cuda_graph_setup.py` line 437: `finalize_cuda_graph_capture` calls `prealloc_symmetric_memory_pool` after CUDA graph capture, so after the KV pool is sized.
- `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/kv_cache_configurator.py` line 2674: the KV budget is the free memory minus `pre_model_load_memory * (1 - mem_fraction_static)`. Nothing in this path or in the default `mem_fraction_static` heuristic reads `enable_symm_mem` or the prealloc size.
- `python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/overrides.py` line 1756: `post_capture_kv_sizing_planned` returns `False` for MLA models such as GLM 5.3 Flash, so the KV pool is not resized after the prealloc.
- `python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/engine.py` lines 1864 to 1873: the flag sets `NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=1` and `NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=1`. NCCL then allocates its own buffers, and these also come from the memory outside the static pool.

Possible fixes, for discussion:

- When `--enable-symm-mem` is set, take the prealloc size (and an estimate of the NCCL buffers) out of the KV budget or out of the default `mem_fraction_static`.
- At least log a warning that tells users to lower `--mem-fraction-static` by about the prealloc size, and fail at start-up with a clear message instead of at the first verify broadcast.

Related:

- #36943 (open): all TP schedulers can deadlock in `ncclCommWindowRegister` when the symmetric-memory pool grows at runtime. A smaller `SGLANG_SYMM_MEM_PREALLOC_GB_SIZE` avoids the out-of-memory error here, but it can make runtime growth of the pool, and with it that deadlock, more likely. A lower `--mem-fraction-static` with the default pool avoids this.
- #34230 (open): with symmetric memory, speculative decoding, TP > 1 and CUDA graphs, ranks can register different windows. Our setup has this combination. We did not test

items.title: [Performance]: FlashInfer NVFP4 KV cache causal prefill is ~1.7-1.8x slower than FP8 on SM120
items.author: lemonade1997
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On NVIDIA consumer Blackwell (SM120), FlashInfer attention with an NVFP4 KV cache shows a significant causal prefill regression compared with an FP8 KV cache.

In a matched profiler segment with the same 48 causal paged-prefill kernel calls, the NVFP4 path took about **145.8 ms**, while the FP8 path took about **84.0 ms**. This makes NVFP4 prefill approximately **1.74x slower** (about 1.7-1.8x across measurements).

The profiler indicates that the current SM120 path uses BF16 Q with packed NVFP4 KV:

```text
NVFP4:
BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel<
  ...,
  __nv_bfloat16,      # Q
  __nv_fp4x2_e2m1,    # KV
  __nv_bfloat16,      # output
  ...
>

FP8:
BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel<
  ...,
  __nv_bfloat16,      # Q
  __nv_fp8_e4m3,      # KV
  __nv_bfloat16,      # output
  ...
>
```

The regression appears to come from the existing SM120 NVFP4 software unpack/dequant path: packed FP4 KV values and their FP8 block scales must be unpacked, converted, and scaled before the BF16 QK/PV computation. Prefill is compute-heavy, so the KV bandwidth reduction does not compensate for this per-element conversion overhead.

### Environment

```text
GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell, compute capability 12.0 (SM120)
PyTorch: 2.10.0+cu129
CUDA: 12.9
FlashInfer: 0.6.15
Attention backend: FLASHINFER
KV cache layout: HND
Model dtype / Q dtype on this path: BF16
KV cache modes compared: nvfp4 and fp8_e4m3
```

The vLLM code includes the recently added NVFP4 KV cache path. The NVFP4 cache is represented as packed E2M1 data plus one FP8 block-scale value per 16 head-dimension elements.

### Kernel-level profile

A comparable trace segment was selected from each profile. Both segments contain exactly 48 causal prefill calls:

| Metric | NVFP4 KV | FP8 KV | NVFP4 / FP8 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Causal paged-prefill calls | 48 | 48 | 1.00x |
| Causal paged-prefill total | 145.81 ms | 84.03 ms | 1.74x |
| Mean per call | 3.04 ms | 1.75 ms | 1.74x |
| CUTLASS GEMM total in the same segment | 93.61 ms | 96.69 ms | 0.97x |
| All GPU kernels in the segment | 297.73 ms | 238.45 ms | 1.25x |

The similar CUTLASS GEMM time suggests that the model's weight/MoE kernels are not the primary source of this difference. Most of the additional GPU time is inside `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel`.

### Decode and KV append observations

The same profiles show that NVFP4 is beneficial for decode:

| Kernel | NVFP4 KV | FP8 KV |
|---|---:|---:|
| Single-token/decode paged attention | ~9.63 us/call | ~12.35 us/call |
| KV append/write | ~8.39 us/call | ~3.01 us/call |

NVFP4 decode is about 22% faster in this workload because decode is more bandwidth-bound. The NVFP4 append kernel is about 2.8x slower because it performs quantization, packing, block-scale generation, and slot mapping, but its cumulative cost is only around 7 ms and is not the end-to-end bottleneck.

### End-to-end capacity stress result

With 30 concurrent requests:

| KV dtype | Completed | Preemptions | Peak running | Peak cache | Wall time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NVFP4 | 30/30 | 0 | 30 | 68.6% | 102.3 s |
| FP8 | 30/30 | 6 | 24 | 97.6% | 65.4 s |

NVFP4 provides the expected capacity benefit and avoids preemption, but the causal-prefill regression dominates this particular workload.

### Expected behavior / proposal

On SM120, the packed NVFP4 KV representation matches the hardware block-scaled FP4 MMA layout well. An optimized path could:

1. quantize Q to per-16-block NVFP4 on the fly;
2. execute QK directly with SM120 block-scaled NVFP4 MMA;
3. avoid expanding K through the FP4 -> FP16/BF16 conversion chain before QK;
4. retain the existing dequantized P x V path where the V-scale axis does not match the MMA reduction axis.

This is similar to the A4Q approach demonstrated for SM120/SM121, where an opt-in FlashInfer kernel uses FP4 Q x FP4 K block-scaled MMA.

Would the vLLM maintainers be interested in tracking or integrating an optimized FlashInfer A4Q-style path for NVFP4 KV prefill on SM120? At minimum, it would be useful to document that the current NVFP4 KV path trades substantial prefill performance for capacity/decode benefits on this architecture.

### Additional notes

- The NVFP4 cache itself is correctly compact: packed FP4 data plus FP8 scales uses about 56.25% of FP8 KV storage, giving an expected capacity ratio of about 1.78x.
- The two profiler JSON files contain more than one non-contiguous capture interval, so the comparison above uses matched segments instead of comparing total trace file size or total event counts.
- Full profiler JSON files can be provided if useful.
- Related NVFP4 KV integration discussion: #49011 and #32220.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Searched existing and past issues for NVFP4/FP4 KV prefill performance and unpack/dequant regressions.

items.title: [Bug]: nvfp4 KV cache silently corrupt under token-major (BLNHC) KV-cache layout — writer/reader stride mismatch
items.author: OOsemka
items.body_excerpt:
> **Disclosure:** this report was drafted with the assistance of an AI agent; the root-cause analysis, the repro, and the environment details below were verified by hand on the machine described in the Environment section.


## Environment

```
vLLM 0.30.0 (vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0)
Python 3.12.3, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130 (CUDA 13.0)
GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell (SM120), 2x, TP2 + EP
Model: nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 (Qwen4Exp/QSA sparse-attention path, modelopt-mixed)
Flags: --kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 --tensor-parallel-size 2 --enable-expert-parallel
Boot log: "Using BLNHC KV cache layout." (engine default)
```

## 🐛 Describe the bug

Running any model on the QSA path (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) with `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`
on v0.30.0 produces **incoherent output at every context length** — short prompts
included. It is silent: no exception, no crash, no Xid, no AER; the server stays up
and returns plausible-looking token streams. Deterministic sanity checks that a
healthy model answers trivially (arithmetic, capital-of-Japan, spell-a-word-backwards)
all fail, and ~253k-token needle retrieval finds 0 of N needles.

### Root cause

The stock C++ nvfp4 KV-cache **write** kernel
(`csrc/libtorch_stable/nvfp4_kv_cache_kernels.cu`,
`reshape_and_cache_nvfp4_dispatch`) derives head/token **data** strides and the
data|scale region split from **internal head-major (HND) formulas** after
detecting HND vs NHD from `stride(2) > stride(1)`. The standard **reader** helper
(`vllm/utils/torch_utils.py: nvfp4_split_data_scale`) instead scales the
*actual* tensor strides by `data_dim/full_dim`.

The two agree only for a head-major physical page. The engine's layout resolver
(`vllm/v1/attention/backends/utils.py: resolve_kv_cache_layout`) picks the first
entry of the backend's `supported_kv_cache_layouts()`; for the QSA backend that is
**BLNHC** (token-major: per-token rows of `2H` head slots × `full_dim` bytes, K/V
slots interleaved per token, each slot packing data+scale). Under that layout the
writer's internal formulas place head `h`, token `t`, and the scale region at
offsets that do not match where the reader looks → every K/V write (and its block
scales) lands in the wrong bytes, and the reader faithfully reads the garbage back.

The asymmetry that makes this easy to miss: a writer run against a contiguous or
head-major buffer (e.g. any test that builds `torch.zeros(...)` and passes
`[B, H, N, C]`) is self-consistent and passes. The token-major page is only ever
produced by the real allocator, so the bug is invisible to round-trip tests that
don't recreate the engine's physical layout.

### What we ruled out (this is not those)

- **QSA read kernel** (PR #54846): numerically correct. Round-trips at production
  geometry — multi-block block_table, multi-split/K + merge, multi-request,
  4096-row prefill chunks, top-k 2048 — match a bf16 reference on the
  dequantized cache to ≤6e-5.
- **MTP / speculative decoding**: garbage reproduced with MTP fully off.
- **Per-layer quant scales**: the modelopt-mixed checkpoint carries no per-layer
  K/V/q scale tensors; stock `set_default_quant_scales` leaves `_k_scale`/`_v_scale`
  = 1.0, matching all passing round-trips.

The failure is in the **write path / cache layout** — exactly where a
writer/reader stride mismatch lives.

### Evidence (writer→reader round-trip at production geometry B=2, N=5568, H=2, D=256)

| physical layout | K relerr | V relerr | verdict |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| token-major (BLNHC — engine default) | **1.4644** | **1.2185** | corrupt |
| head-major (BLHNC) | **0.0895** | **0.0895** | correct (pure nvfp4 rounding) |

0.0895 is the expected nvfp4 (E2M1 + E4M3 block scale) quantization error —
the same value a known-good round-trip produces. 1.46 / 1.22 means the
dequantized cache is unrelated to the input.

### Minimal reproduction

Self-contained script (one GPU, ~300 MB VRAM at production geometry; `REPRO_B`/
`REPRO_N` env vars shrink it on a busy box — the mismatch is a layout property,
not a size property):

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Stock nvfp4 KV writer vs reader under the two physical per-layer layouts
vLLM may resolve. Token-major (BLNHC, engine default for QSA) -> corrupt."""
import os, torch
from vllm.v1.attention.backends.fa_utils import reshape_and_cache_flash
from vllm.utils.torch_utils import nvfp4_split_data_scale

DEV = "cuda"
B = int(os.environ.get("REPRO_B", 2))
H, D = 2, 256
N = int(os.environ.get("REPRO_N", 5568))
HD, FD = 2 * H, D // 2 + D // 16      # K+V slots; nvfp4 full_dim = 144
PAGE, SD = HD * N * FD, D // 16
_E2M1 = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 6.0]

def _e4m3(bits):
    p = bits.to(torch.int32) & 0x7F
    e, m = (p >> 3) & 0x0F, p & 0x7
    v = torch.where(e == 0, m.float() / 512.0,
                    torch.pow(2.0, e.float() - 7.0) * (1.0 + m.float() / 8.0))
    return torch.where(p == 0, torch.zeros_like(v), v)

def _scale_coords(n, swizzled, dev):
    t, s = torch.arange(n, device=dev).view(-1, 1), torch.arange(SD, device=dev).view(1, -1)
    if not swizzled:
        return t.expand(n, SD), s.expand(n, SD)
    g = SD // 4
    return (t // 4) * 4 + (s // g), (s % g) * 4 + (t % 4)

def dequant_side(side, swizzled, device):
    data, scales = nvfp4_split_data_scale(side)
    data, scales = data.contiguous(), scales.view(torch.uint8)
    b, n, h, _ = data.shape
    table = torch.tensor(_E2M1 + [-v for v in _E2M1], dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
    nib = torch.stack((data & 0x0F, (data >> 4) & 0x0F), dim=-1)
    vals = table[nib.reshape(b, n, h, D).long()]
    ti, si = _scale_coords(n, swizzled, device)
    picked = scales[:, ti.reshape(-1), :, :].reshape(b, n, SD, h, SD)
    sel = si.view(1, n, SD, 1, 1).expand(b, n, SD, h, 1)
    picked = torch.gather(picked, 4, sel).squeeze(4).permute(0, 1, 3, 2)
    return (vals * _e4m3(picked).repeat_interleave(16, dim=3)).to(torch.bfloat16)

def relerr(a, b):
    a, b = a.to(torch.float64), b.to(torch.float64)
    return ((a - b).abs().mean() / b.abs().

items.title: [MP] Bound retrieve completion when a CUDA IPC event remains unsignaled
items.author: malaiwah
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`DeviceMessagingFuture.query()` can wait indefinitely after importing a CUDA IPC event if the event never becomes ready. The multiprocess vLLM connector has no deadline for this completion phase, so an affected request can remain in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` indefinitely and block scheduler progress.

## Code path

The future currently has three phases:

1. wait for the raw response/event handle;
2. import the IPC event;
3. poll `event.query()`.

Existing MQ timeout configuration bounds message transport, not phase 3. A synthetic future whose imported event always returns `False` from `query()` reproduces the unbounded wait.

## Safety constraint

A simple timeout followed by `finished_recving()`, invalidation, and recompute is unsafe for LMCache-driven zero-copy retrieval. The original H2D operation may still target the same paged-KV block IDs; releasing or reusing them before transfer terminality can allow late DMA to overwrite valid KV.

Transparent recovery therefore requires one of:

- cancel + positive terminal acknowledgement before block reuse;
- quarantine of timed-out block IDs until the event completes/cancellation is acknowledged; or
- a fail-stop policy that tears down the affected worker/context.

## Requested change

Please add a configurable MP retrieve-completion deadline (disabled by default for compatibility), plus:

- pending retrieve count and oldest pending age;
- timeout/failure counters labeled by phase (MQ response, IPC import, event completion);
- a safe timeout policy. An initial fail-stop policy is acceptable; transparent recompute must not release target blocks until terminality is established.

## Related but not equivalent

- vllm-project/vllm#49556: retrieve failures are not propagated/invalidated in the fallback connector
- LMCache#4419: ROCm deadlock while importing an IPC event
- LMCache#3336: AMD/HIP host-callback deadlock fix
- LMCache#2973: retrieve coordination improvements

Searches across open and closed LMCache/vLLM issues and PRs did not find an existing report matching an NVIDIA IPC event that remains imported but unsignaled indefinitely.

items.title: [Bug] SegmentTokenDatabase._fast_split_by_subtensor falls through its early-exit guard (missing `return`)
items.author: alooshxl
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

bug

**Describe the bug**

`SegmentTokenDatabase._fast_split_by_subtensor` (`lmcache/v1/token_database.py`, ~L470) guards two degenerate cases and then fails to exit. The method is a **generator**, so `yield tokens` only suspends — it does not return. As soon as the consumer asks for the next chunk, execution falls through into the sliding-window match that the guard was meant to skip:

```python
    def _fast_split_by_subtensor(self, tokens: torch.Tensor) -> Iterable[torch.Tensor]:
        """Match the `sep_tokens` with sliding windows"""

        if self.sep_len == 0 or len(tokens) < self.sep_len:
            yield tokens
            # <-- missing `return`: execution continues below

        # Unfold into sliding windows
        # shape: (num_tokens-sep_len+1, sep_len)
        windows = tokens.unfold(0, self.sep_len, 1)
        ...
```

This produces two distinct failures, one per guarded condition.

**1. `len(tokens) < self.sep_len` — raises `RuntimeError`**

`torch.Tensor.unfold(0, size, 1)` refuses to build a window wider than the tensor, so it trips its bounds check: `maximum size for tensor at dimension 0 is <len(tokens)> but size is <sep_len>`. The consumer receives the correct chunk from the first `yield`, then the generator blows up on the *next* `next()` — so the traceback surfaces at the iteration site (e.g. the `for start, end, key in self.token_database.process_tokens(...)` loops in `cache_engine.py`), not at the call that created it.

**2. `self.sep_len == 0` — silently shreds the input**

`unfold(0, 0, 1)` yields `len(tokens) + 1` zero-width windows. Comparing a zero-width window against the empty `sep_tokens` and reducing with `.all(dim=1)` is *vacuously true*, so **every** index registers as a separator match. For an 8-token input the generator emits 11 chunks instead of 1:

```
[whole input], [], [t0], [t1], [t2], [t3], [t4], [t5], [t6], [t7], []
```

Downstream, `process_tokens` turns each of those into its own cache key, so a single request is cached as one correct chunk plus ten junk chunks (including two zero-length ones, which `cache_engine` then allocates zero-token memory objects for).

`sep_len == 0` is reachable through configuration, not just in theory:

```python
self.sep_tokens = self.tokenizer.encode(config.blend_special_str)[1:]
```

The `[1:]` unconditionally drops the first token id — there is a `TODO (Jiayi)` immediately above it acknowledging that the leading-special-token assumption is a guess. Any tokenizer / `blend_special_str` pair that encodes to exactly one token leaves the separator empty, and the failure is silent.

**To Reproduce**

Both paths are reachable through the public `process_tokens` API on a blend-enabled engine:

```python
db = SegmentTokenDatabase(config, metadata)

# 1. input shorter than the separator (len(db.sep_tokens) == 3 here)
list(db.process_tokens(tokens=torch.tensor([7, 8])))
# RuntimeError: maximum size for tensor at dimension 0 is 2 but size is 3

# 2. empty separator (tokenizer encodes blend_special_str to a single token)
list(db.process_tokens(tokens=torch.arange(8)))
# 11 results instead of 1
```

The control flow itself needs no torch to demonstrate — a plain generator with the same shape keeps running past the early `yield`:

```python
>>> def g():
...     if True:
...         yield "early guard"     # no `return`
...     print("still executing!")
...     yield "fell through"
>>> list(g())
still executing!
['early guard', 'fell through']
```

**Expected behavior**

Both degenerate cases should yield the whole token tensor as one unsplit chunk and stop — which is clearly what the guard intends. The one-word fix is a `return` after the early `yield`.

**Additional context**

Separate, pre-existing observation while reading the same method (**not** part of this report's fix): when a separator sits at the very end of the input, the trailing `yield tokens[start:]` emits an empty tensor, which `process_tokens` turns into a zero-length `(start, end)` range with `start == end`. `cache_engine.store` then sizes a memory object from `end - start == 0`. Blend inputs normally end with content rather than a separator, so this looks latent rather than actively firing, and fixing it changes chunk-emission semantics — worth its own discussion.

items.title: [Bug] LocalDiskBackend leaks disk-space accounting on every external remove, eventually dropping all disk puts silently
items.author: alooshxl
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

bug

**Describe the bug**

`LocalDiskBackend` tracks how much of its disk budget is in use with
`self.current_cache_size`, but only its *internal* eviction loop ever decrements
that counter. Every other removal path shrinks `self.usage` and drops the entry
from `self.dict` while leaving `current_cache_size` untouched, so the counter
only ever grows. Once the accumulated phantom usage exceeds
`max_local_disk_size`, `submit_put_task` silently drops every subsequent disk
put — even though the disk is empty.

On `dev` (0373a573) `current_cache_size` has exactly four references, all in
`lmcache/v1/storage_backend/local_disk_backend.py`:

| Line | Code | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 175 | `self.current_cache_size = 0.0` | init |
| 346 | `while self.current_cache_size + required_size > self.max_cache_size:` | the capacity gate in `submit_put_task` |
| 358 | `self.current_cache_size -= self.dict[evict_key].size` | decrement — internal eviction only |
| 364 | `self.current_cache_size += required_size` | increment — every accepted put |

`remove()` (lines 252-286) pops the entry, decrements `self.usage`, unlinks the
file and updates the cache policy, but never touches `current_cache_size`:

```python
def remove(self, key: CacheEngineKey, force: bool = True) -> bool:
    lock_context = self.disk_lock if force else nullcontext()
    with lock_context:
        if not (meta := self.dict.pop(key, None)):
            return False
        path = meta.path
        size = meta.size
        self.usage -= size                                   # <-- usage shrinks
        self.stats_monitor.update_local_storage_usage(self.usage)
        os.remove(path)
        if force:
            self.cache_policy.update_on_force_evict(key)
    ...
    return True
```

The internal eviction loop gets away with this because it deducts the chunk
itself (line 358) before calling `self.batched_remove(evict_keys, force=False)`.
Every removal that originates *outside* the backend uses the default
`force=True` and is never accounted for.

**Trigger paths**

`StorageManager.remove` (`storage_manager.py:1069`) and
`StorageManager.batched_remove` (`storage_manager.py:1095`) both call into the
backend with the default `force=True`, so all of these leak:

- `LMCacheEngine.clear()` → `_clear()` → `storage_manager.remove(...)`
  (`cache_engine.py:1599`)
- `LMCacheEngine.move()` → `storage_manager.batched_remove(keys,
  locations=[old_position])` (`cache_engine.py:1313`) — moving a chunk off disk
  leaks the space it used to occupy
- `LMCacheEngine.compress()` / `decompress()` → `storage_manager.batched_remove(
  keys, locations=[location])` (`cache_engine.py:1472`, `:1533`)
- the remove-after-retrieve path used by the PD-disaggregation receiver role
  (`cache_engine.py:928` and `:1805`), when the disk backend is among
  `retrieve_locations`

**Consequence**

The drift is monotonic and never recovers within the process lifetime. Once
`current_cache_size` passes `max_local_disk_size`, the `while` loop in
`submit_put_task` asks the cache policy for eviction candidates, gets none back
(the dict really is empty, or holds far less than the counter claims), logs

```
No eviction candidates found. Disk space under pressure.
```

at WARNING level, and returns without storing anything. The disk tier then
degrades to a silent no-op for the rest of the process: puts stop landing, hit
rate collapses, and the only signal is a repeated warning that points at disk
pressure while the disk is in fact nearly empty. The reported `usage` metric
stays correct throughout, so monitoring shows an empty disk cache that refuses
to accept data.

**Expected behavior**

Removing a chunk should return its space to the budget, so that puts keep being
accepted for as long as the disk actually has room.

**Reproduction**

A standalone model of the four counter sites above (no torch required) makes the
drift visible. Chunk = 128 KiB, budget = 2.5 chunks:

```
A) store 2, remove both externally, store 1 more
   pre-fix: disk holds 0 chunk(s), usage=0 B, current_cache_size=262144 B, next put DROPPED
   fixed  : disk holds 1 chunk(s), usage=131072 B, current_cache_size=131072 B, next put ACCEPTED

B) repeated store/remove cycles on an empty disk
   pre-fix: first dropped put at cycle 2, current_cache_size=262144 B while usage=0 B
   fixed  : first dropped put at never, current_cache_size=0 B while usage=0 B
```

Scenario B is the important one: the disk is empty on every cycle
(`usage=0`), yet after two store/remove rounds the backend refuses all
further puts.

**Suggested fix**

Deduct the chunk in `remove()` when `force=True`, mirroring the existing
`if force:` guard that already distinguishes external removals from the
internal eviction path (which has already done the deduction itself).

**Related, not part of this report**

`submit_put_task` does not skip keys that are already in `self.dict` (unlike
`LocalCPUBackend`), so re-putting an existing key charges the budget twice while
`insert_key` only refreshes recency. That is a second, independent source of
upward drift and should be fixed separately.

items.title: [Bug][MP] CPU KV events withdraw a chunk while another L1 or salt copy is still live
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

The CPU KV events from #5307 can tell routers a prefix is gone while LMCache still has it in L1.

`KVEventModule` keys its records on `(model_name, chunk_hash)` and turns every `L1_KEYS_EVICTED` into a `BlockRemoved`. But one chunk hash can be live more than once:

- With several L1 managers (#5461), the same key can sit in two L1s, since there's no cross-L1 dedup. This happens on its own under memory pressure. A prefix overflows into the second L1, the first L1 evicts the head of it, the next request misses at chunk 0, and the connector stores the rest of the prefix again, this time into the first L1. The leftover copy in the second L1 is never read, so it's the first thing that L1 evicts.
- Two requests with the same tokens but different `cache_salt` get separate keys with the same chunk hash, because the hash only covers the tokens. This needs just one L1.

When any one of those copies is evicted, a `BlockRemoved` goes out. The worker side only keeps a set of announced hashes, so it forwards it, and nothing announces the surviving copy again. The router then thinks that worker has a shorter prefix than LMCache can actually serve, for as long as the other copy lives.

Nothing gets corrupted. It just costs cache-aware routing hits, which is what #5307 is for.

**To Reproduce**

With a real `StorageManager` (two DRAM L1s) and `KVEventModule` on the same event bus:

1. Fill the first L1, then store K. It overflows into the second L1.
2. Free space in the first L1 and store K again. It goes into the first L1, so both now hold K.
3. Evict K from either L1.

The records are `stored K, stored K, removed K`, and the other L1 still serves K. The salt case gives the same records with one L1, two salts and a single eviction.

**Expected behavior**

A chunk is announced when its first copy lands and withdrawn when its last copy is evicted.

**Additional context**

Seen on `dev` at e2a0c08c. Even with this fixed, salted hashes still won't line up with the router's own block hashes. That's the separate salted-hash follow-up listed in #5307.

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

items.title: Eval bug: UGM tokenizer ignores byte_fallback and emits UNK
items.author: lajosbencz
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
version: 0.4.0-dev (build 10809, commit 5266f24da7)
built with GNU 16.2.1 for Linux x86_64
```

Also reproduced on master at `b6b003d2c` 

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CPU, CUDA

### Hardware

AMD Ryzen 9900X

### Models

Only vocab:
- [google/mt5-small](https://huggingface.co/google/mt5-small) regression test target
- [picur/picur-tokenizer](https://huggingface.co/picur/picur-tokenizer) issue originally encountered with

Any SentencePiece Unigram vocab with `byte_fallback` surfaces the issue

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

_SentencePiece_ Unigram models trained with `byte_fallback` carry the 256 `<0x??>` tokens: `714 ▁this, 339 ▁is, 259 ▁, 243 <0xF0>, 162 <0x9F>, 169 <0xA6>, 156 <0x99>, 260 ., 297 c, 3758 pp`.
_llama.cpp_ on the other hand emits lossy `<UNK>`.
SPM tokenizer in _llama.cpp_ already handles the bytes fallback correctly, this is only a gap in UGM.

#### Steps:
1. `python3 convert_hf_to_gguf.py --vocab-only --outfile ggml-vocab-mt5-small.gguf mt5-small/`
2. `llama-tokenize -m ggml-vocab-mt5-small.gguf -p " this is 🦙.cpp"`

---

Creating this ticket as a required reference for a PR, I already have the possible fix on a branch.


### First Bad Commit

Present since the UGM tokenizer was first added.

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

```console
$ llama-tokenize -m ggml-vocab-mt5-small.gguf -p " this is 🦙.cpp"
   714 -> ' this'
   339 -> ' is'
   259 -> ' '
     2 -> '<unk>'
   260 -> '.'
   297 -> 'c'
  3758 -> 'pp'
```

</details>

items.title: SYCL on Arc B580: ternary weights and q4_0 KV attention on XMX (Bonsai 2 27B, 128K context in 12 GB)
items.author: Torchit1
items.body_excerpt:
I've been working on the SYCL backend for Intel Arc B580 (Xe2), mostly for PrismML's ternary Bonsai 2 27B, and wanted to share the results and a couple of findings in case they're useful to other SYCL work.

Branch: https://github.com/Torchit1/llama.cpp/tree/arc-b580 (guide: docs/bonsai-arc-b580.md)

What's in it:
- Ternary PTQ1_0 weights repacked to 2 bits at load and run on the int8 x int2 DPAS path (Intel's TernSYCL kernels), with round-to-nearest activation quantisation (KL divergence 0.00022 against reference logits).
- Decode and draft-verify attention (1-32 query tokens) straight from the q4_0 KV cache on XMX. Xe2's IGC provides `intel_sub_group_i8_i4_matrix_mad_k32`, which isn't in the public cl_intel_subgroup_matrix_multiply_accumulate list; the raw q4_0 bytes XOR 0x88888888 work as its B operand. It's exact on the B580.
- Full 1024-token prompt batches through oneDNN's int8 GEMM (about 10% faster long prompts).
- Memory changes so MTP drafting fits 128K context in 12 GB (q4_0 KV for the draft context, a smaller draft batch).
- The same attention kernel generalises to Gemma 4 12B (head 512, GQA 16), plus a q4_0 small-batch GEMM on XMX: Gemma 4 12B QAT with Google's assistant drafter goes from about 40 to 100 t/s on new code.

Results on a B580 at 128K context: about 90 t/s writing new code, 250-370 t/s on code edits, 42 t/s plain, 44 t/s with 115K tokens of history. Same card, model and flags against the SYCL support in PrismML's fork: prompt reading 207 vs 895 t/s, plain generation 21 vs 42, generation at 32K context 8 vs 36.

All the XMX paths are gated to Xe2 and fall back to the existing kernels elsewhere. One user report from an A770 (Alchemist): it runs on the fallback kernels but needed -b 256 -ub 256 to avoid a Level Zero ERROR_UNKNOWN, which may be worth a look on the mainline side too.

I'd be glad to help upstream any of the general pieces (the q4_0 KV attention in particular) if there's interest.

comments.author: catyans
comments.body:
Deterministic shadow-scheduler experiment (2026-07-13) to test the core enforcement hypothesis before touching Admission. This is simulation evidence only.

Environment: Lingjun H20 `lingjun-099`, Python 3.12.7 / NumPy, fixed seed 20260713. Model: 10,000 x 1 ms epochs, capacity 100 work units/epoch; foreground arrivals Poisson(40/epoch), background Poisson(90/epoch), foreground deadline 5 epochs. Compared a single unbiased FIFO against a work-conserving 60/40 class budget; unused foreground capacity was borrowed by background.

Results:

| mode | FG completed / arrived | FG miss | FG P99 wait | BG completed | utilization | final FG/BG backlog |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| FIFO | 307,991 / 400,150 | 99.829% | 2,286 epochs | 692,009 | 100% | 92,159 / 207,355 |
| budget | 400,150 / 400,150 | 0.000% | 0 epochs | 599,850 | 100% | 0 / 299,514 |

Conclusion: under sustained aggregate overload, explicit class budgets can protect feasible foreground demand while remaining work-conserving; the benefit is not higher total throughput (both are 100% utilized), but controlled allocation. The cost is explicit: background service fell by 92,159 units and its backlog grew, so aging/reclaim and overload policy are mandatory. This does not validate real TENT timing, hierarchical identity, byte-vs-request accounting or distributed guarantees. A code PR should begin in shadow-accounting mode and reproduce this comparison with tebench and real RDMA before enforcement is enabled.

# [Feature Request] Increase payload size limit for base64 images

## Problem
Sending 10MB JSON with base64-encoded images to SGLang server fails with "payload reached size limit".

```bash
curl -X POST http://server:58000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @base64.json
# Error: payload reached size limit
```

## Request
Add configuration option to increase payload size limit, such as:
- `--max-payload-size` flag
- Environment variable support

## Why needed
- Avoid setting up NFS/file servers for multi-machine image sharing
- Enable self-contained requests with multiple images
- Simplify deployment in distributed environments

## Current workaround
Store images in shared folder + use URLs (requires additional infrastructure setup)

items.title: [Bug] HiCache staged write-back: the 128 KiB batch path passes registered host VAs to cudaMemcpyBatchAsync and faults where CanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem == 0
items.author: Edwardssss
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

HiCache backup copies device KV into the host pool through the JIT kernel `python/sglang/kernels/jit/csrc/kvcacheio/staged_write_back.cuh`. The kernel has two D2H strategies and picks between them by copy granularity: per-page `cudaMemcpyAsync` for small copies, and one `cudaMemcpyBatchAsync` for `src_ptrs.size() * num_pages` descriptors once `first_page_bytes = page_size * src_stride(0) * item_size >= kLargeCopyThresholdBytes` (128 KiB, defined at `:106`, branch at `:154`, call at `:170`, call sites `:274` MLA and `:279` MHA).

For the batch call the kernel passes **the raw host virtual addresses** of the host pool as the destination pointers (`dst_ptrs[t].data_ptr() + dst_indices[...] * stride * elem`). On a platform where `cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem` is **0** — i.e. registered host memory is
*not* accessible at the same virtual address on the device — those addresses are not valid device-space addresses, and the copy fails with an **asynchronous `cudaErrorIllegalAddress`**. The fallback path in the same kernel uses `cudaMemcpyAsync` over the *same* addresses and works,
because that API translates host pointers for you.

**Minimal demonstration.** One program, one descriptor, 128 KiB; only the destination form varies:

| `dst` passed to `cudaMemcpyBatchAsync` | submission | sync | bytes |
|---|---|---|---|
| host VA of `mmap()` + `cudaHostRegister()` — **what the kernel does today** | `no error` | **`an illegal memory access was encountered`** | not copied |
| `cudaHostGetDevicePointer()` alias of the *same* buffer | `no error` | `no error` | correct |
| `cudaHostAlloc()` buffer | `no error` | `no error` | correct |
| host VA of plain pageable `mmap()` (never registered) | `no error` | `no error` | correct |
| per-copy `cudaMemcpyAsync()` into the registered buffer | — | `no error` | correct |

Observed on the machine described under *Environment*:

```
$ ./repro_host_va_vs_alias va
cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem = 0
mode=va      dst=0x72be8c02b000
  submission -> no error
  sync       -> an illegal memory access was encountered
  host[0]    = 0x00 (expected 0x11)

$ ./repro_host_va_vs_alias alias
cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem = 0
host VA = 0x74371c101000, device alias = 0x204c00000 (same=NO)
mode=alias   dst=0x204c00000
  submission -> no error
  sync       -> no error
  host[0]    = 0x11 (expected 0x11)
```

The same holds at the kernel's real geometry (2 host tensors x 4 pages = 8 descriptors, 128 KiB each): host VAs -> illegal memory access; the two aliases -> success with `k=0x11`, `v=0x22` verified at both the first and the last byte of both buffers.

 `cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem` is documented as "Device can access host registered memory at the same virtual address as the CPU". On this machine it is `0`, and it is consistent with what the runtime reports for the two host-memory flavors:

```
mmap + cudaHostRegister : host VA 0x74371c101000 != device alias 0x204c00000   (same = NO)
cudaHostAlloc          : host VA == device alias                              (same = YES)
```

On typical native Linux x86_64 with UVA the attribute is `1`, so a host VA *is* a valid device address and the raw-address usage happens to be correct. That is consistent with #21631's benchmark (~48 GiB/s through this same API) and with the absence of earlier reports. Note that
sglang already encodes this exact concept for ROCm — `_resolve_device_accessible_ptr_fn()` in `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/pool_host/common.py` documents that "on HIP they differ" and `get_device_accessible_ptr` exists to translate; the batch destination is the one place where the translation is not applied.

The two conditions are the default combination in production: the default host pool is `mmap`-backed and registered (`ALLOC_MEMORY_FUNCS` defaults to `alloc_with_host_register`, which calls `cudart.cudaHostRegister(ptr, size, 0)`, on buffers from `HostTensorAllocator.allocate -> alloc_mmap`; only `npu`/`musa` use `alloc_with_pin_memory`), and essentially any real checkpoint exceeds 128 KiB per page (e.g. `page_size=64`, 32 layers, 8 KV heads x 128 dim, bf16 -> 4 MiB). So the batch path is the *default* path, and whether a deployment survives depends on a device attribute that differs by platform/driver — including WSL2, which is where I hit it.

The batch call returns `cudaSuccess`; the error is asynchronous and sticky, so it is only observed at the next synchronization point. In our runs the first symptom was a stream query inside the HiCache ready-count logic:

```
torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered
  unified_radix_cache.py:3069 _count_ready_acks -> torch/cuda/streams.py query()
  reached via _produce_buffer_l3 -> _buffer_backup_and_wait -> _pump_hicache_until
           -> check_hicache_events -> _sync_hicache_ready_counts
```

The frame in that traceback is not the faulting call, and under `retry()` the test retries until the budget is exhausted, so it presents as a flaky test rather than a broken D2H.

End-to-end confirmation at the sglang level (same test, same geometry, only the host pool backing changed):

| configuration (`test_buffer_only_load_back_drops_on_sibling_published_span`, page_size=32, num_layers=16) | result |
|---|---|
| default: host pool = `mmap` + `cudaHostRegister` | **FAIL** — illegal memory access |
| host pool = `cudaHostAlloc` (`torch.empty(..., pin_memory=True)`) | **PASS** |
| default, with `cudaMemcpyBatchAsync` forced

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Read the kernel on current main and the report holds exactly as written: the batch path builds every destination from `dst_ptrs[tensor_id].data_ptr()` (staged_write_back.cuh:147-150) and hands it to `cudaMemcpyBatchAsync` (:170), while the fallback `copy_page_first_pages_fallback` walks the same addresses through per-page `cudaMemcpyAsync` and works because that API translates host pointers. So the one place the device-accessibility translation is missing is the batch destination, matching your `cudaHostGetDevicePointer` control row.

On the fix shape, two kernel-local options, no wheel/op dependency either way:

1. Query `cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem` once (static cache) inside the batch helper and return false when it is 0. The caller then takes the existing fallback, which you already proved passes. Smallest possible diff, bulletproof, and the only cost is the batch fast path being unused on affected platforms.
2. Translate each batch destination through `cudaHostGetDevicePointer(..., 0)` and fall back to option 1's path if the alias call errors. Keeps the batch API on WSL2-class platforms at the price of a little more branching.

I would send option 1 as the safe default and mention 2 as a follow-up refinement; the per-page path is not the hot case on platforms where the attribute is 0 anyway.

One honest caveat: I do not have an attribute-0 platform (or any CUDA box) at hand, so my verification is code-level only and CI on UVA hardware can only prove no regression, not the fix itself. Your standalone repro is the right acceptance test for whoever lands it.

Happy to write the PR along these lines if you and the maintainers are good with the direction.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Sent #40571 with the option-1 shape from my earlier comment: the batch helper queries `cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem` per call and returns false (existing per-page fallback) whenever the device does not report support, or when the query itself errors. The alias-translation variant is noted in the PR as a possible follow-up refinement rather than part of this change.

Same caveat as before, repeated for honesty: I have no CUDA host here, so this is verified at code level only — CI plus your standalone repro are the real acceptance runs.

comments.author: Edwardssss
comments.body:
Thanks @he-yufeng — I worked through your reading line by line before replying, and it holds exactly as you wrote it:

- the destination is built from `dst_ptrs[tensor_id].data_ptr()` at `staged_write_back.cuh:147-150` and handed to the batch call at `:167-177`, while `copy_page_first_pages_fallback` (`:64-89`) walks the same addresses through `cudaMemcpyAsync` — checked in the file, not from memory;
- "no wheel/op dependency either way" also holds for the option-2 shape: the JIT-side `runtime.cuh` calls `cudaHostGetDevicePointer` directly rather than going through the AOT op, and the box behind this report has `sglang-kernel` 0.4.7, which has no `get_device_accessible_ptr` at all, yet the option-2 build runs.

You flagged that you have no CUDA host, so the part you could not run is the part I ran. I applied #40571 verbatim on top of `main` at `76f9213a41` and used the same configuration as in the report (`CacheConfig(page_size=32, num_layers=16)`, one subprocess per configuration, since an illegal access aborts the process):

| build | result |
| --- | --- |
| `main`, unpatched | FAIL — `err=2`, "an illegal memory access was encountered", exit 134 |
| `main` + #40571 applied as-is | PASS, exit 0 |
| #40233 (option 2) | PASS, exit 0 |

`cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem` is 0 on this machine, so in your build the gate returns false by construction and the existing fallback is what carries the run — exactly the outcome you predicted, and worth confirming on hardware given you flagged you had none.

Two observations, both about breadth rather than correctness:

1. The attribute query sits ahead of the `kLargeCopyThresholdBytes` check, so every staged write-back pays a `cudaDeviceGetAttribute` call — including copies that stay on the per-page path and platforms that were never affected. Your comment said "once (static cache)" while the PR body says per call; probably worth picking one and matching the other.
2. The attribute describes the device, not the memory. On an attribute-0 host it also retires the batch path for `cudaHostAlloc` / `pin_memory` pools, whose host VA is identity-mapped and was never the problem. That is the safe direction of error, just a wider brush than the defect needs.

On option 1 vs option 2, one piece of data you may not have had: option 2 is already implemented in #40233, so the "follow-up refinement" is code-complete rather than hypothetical. I put a temporary print in the batch helper to see which D2H path actually runs, and on this same attribute-0 box the batch call itself succeeds once the destination is the alias:

```
[probe] BATCH OK n=8 dst0=0x204e00000 host_va0=0x7cd2a813f000 alias_differs=1
```

So option 2 keeps the batch path on precisely the platforms where option 1 gives it up. Two smaller differences, stated plainly in both directions: the diff is 15 lines against 158; and #40233 carries a registered-host-pool regression test while #40571 has none — although, to be fair to your caveat, that test would pass on UVA CI with or without either fix, so it is a guard on affected hardware rather than a CI regression detector.

One clarification on your option 2, since it differs slightly from what #40233 does: for host memory that was never registered, `cudaHostGetDevicePointer` errors, and the helper there returns the host VA instead of falling back to per-page. That is deliberate — pageable host memory has no separate device address and the copy APIs expect the host VA, which is the combination that already worked in the report's table. Both behaviours are needed at one call site.

Suggestion for landing, maintainers' call and I am happy either way:

- if the smaller, assumption-free change is preferred, I will close #40233 and move its registered test into #40571, so the fallback path is at least covered by a test;
- if keeping the batch path on attribute-0 platforms is preferred, #40233 is ready, and #40571 folds in as an extra guard only if you want the belt-and-braces version —

items.title: RFC: Plugin Extension Points Needed for MetaX GPU Support
items.author: yangxin-mx
items.body_excerpt:
# Proposal: Generalize SGLang Hardware Plugin Interfaces for MetaX GPU Support

> Discussion draft based on a SGLang 0.5.19-derived codebase. The names below are proposed API shapes, not claims that they already exist on the latest `main` branch. If an equivalent upstream seam already exists, we would prefer to use or extend it. This is an umbrella discussion that can be split into smaller PRs.

SGLang already has useful foundations: hardware-platform entry points, `SRTPlatform.init_backend()`, an explicit OOT forward registry for fused ops, and MoE runner/fused-function registration. See the [plugin documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/hardware-platforms/plugin.mdx) and [expert-parallelism documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/advanced_features/expert_parallelism.mdx). When adapting another CUDA-compatible GPU, however, we still encounter framework call sites that select a built-in class, import a vendor implementation, or call a kernel through a module-level symbol before a platform plugin can participate.

Our goal is to make required hardware behavior expressible through platform methods and explicit, typed registries. We do **not** propose replacing module globals or monkey-patching framework functions. A missing optional platform implementation should preserve the current built-in behavior; a selected but unsupported implementation should fail with a clear capability error rather than silently run an incompatible kernel. The plugin owns its vendor kernels and package dependencies. The framework owns common algorithms, selection rules, lifecycle, and validation.

The Python snippets below illustrate **proposed interfaces and call sites, not complete, runnable code already present in the repository**. `ExampleGpuPlatform` and `vendor_ops` stand for any vendor plugin. Exact parameters should be settled against existing types and call paths in the corresponding PRs. Each section shows both where the framework would connect the extension point and how a plugin would use it.

## 1. JIT toolchain and cache identity

### Adaptation problem

In the 0.5.19-derived tree, JIT compilation derives the device compiler, architecture and flags through CUDA/ROCm-oriented paths in `kernels/jit/utils/compile/toolchain.py`. The build path (`ninja.py`) and cache path (`cache.py`) must agree on these values. A plugin cannot safely supply a different device compiler by changing only one path: the cache may reuse a binary built for another SDK or architecture.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Add an optional `SRTPlatform.get_jit_toolchain() -> JitToolchainSpec | None`. The immutable spec should include the host/device compilers, toolkit root, target architecture, include/link paths and flags, plus an explicit SDK/ABI cache identity.
- Resolve the spec lazily when compilation starts, and pass the **same resolved spec** to command generation and cache-key generation. `None` keeps the existing built-in toolchain logic.
- Let the vendor plugin package its AOT extensions itself. The common AOT setup need not import or name each vendor SDK.

On the framework side, add the optional method in `srt/platforms/interface.py` and have `kernels/jit/utils/compile/{toolchain,ninja,cache}.py` consume the same spec:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class JitToolchainSpec:
    host_compiler: str
    device_compiler: str
    toolkit_root: str
    target_arch: str
    device_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    include_dirs: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    link_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    cache_identity: str = ""  # SDK/ABI version

class SRTPlatform(DeviceMixin):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec | None:
        return None

def compile_extension(source, **kwargs):
    spec = resolve_jit_toolchain(get_platform().get_jit_toolchain())
    cache_key = make_cache_key(source, spec=spec, **kwargs)
    return build_with_ninja(source, spec=spec, cache_key=cache_key, **kwargs)
```

The plugin only describes its own SDK; it does not modify global `CUDA_HOME` or framework compiler symbols:

```python
class ExampleGpuPlatform(SRTPlatform):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec:
        return JitToolchainSpec(
            host_compiler="/opt/example/bin/c++",
            device_compiler="/opt/example/bin/device-cc",
            toolkit_root="/opt/example",
            target_arch="example-arch",
            cache_identity="example-sdk-1:abi-1",
        )
```

## 2. Device properties and per-operator Triton tuning

### Adaptation problem

Several launch paths infer hardware behavior from CUDA properties or NVIDIA/AMD architecture names, while `num_stages`, warps, tile sizes and shared-memory limits are selected locally. A plugin may expose a CUDA-compatible device but still need different launch parameters; pretending to be a particular SM is not a sound capability contract.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Expose a read-only `DeviceKernelProfile` through the active platform, with architecture identifier, warp size, maximum shared-memory bytes and relevant device capabilities.
- Add an optional `tune_triton_launch(op, shape, dtype, default) -> TritonLaunchConfig`. Each caller first computes its present default, then asks the active platform for a per-operator override and validates it before launch. There should be no global change to Triton's defaults.
- Start with launch sites where hardware differences actually affect correctness or feasibility (MoE, quantization and attention), keeping other paths unchanged.

The framework could define device facts in `srt/platforms/device_mixin.py`/`interface.py` and consume the policy immediately before each Triton launch, keeping hardware facts separate from per-operator tuning:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DeviceKernelProfile:
    arch: str
    warp_size: int
    max_shared_memory_bytes: int

@dataclass(frozen=

items.title: [Feature] Accept per-item precomputed media with explicit offsets and hashes
items.author: michaelfeil
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

An external frontend/encoder already knows each media item's expanded token span, embeddings, and content identity. It should be able to pass those items to SGLang without concatenating them and reconstructing their boundaries in the worker.

SGLang already represents per-item modality, offsets, and hashes, and `collect_mm_items_from_processor_output` reads that metadata. However, `_validate_one_modality` rejects more than one formatted item per modality. This blocks the per-item input shape below.

### Minimal reproducer

Checked against upstream `main` at `684fea8af3b11a5b51ec9966c02959a32ad3421c`; the same restriction exists at our pinned `7760d5264ac16b85392aefb1bf5c13ce38d9632e`.

```python
import torch
from sglang.srt.multimodal.processors.base_processor import BaseMultimodalProcessor

prompt = [7] + [99] * 5 + [8]
items = [
    {
        "format": "processor_output",
        "modality": "image",
        "precomputed_embeddings": torch.zeros(rows, 8),
        "offsets": [(start, start + rows - 1)],
        "hash": content_hash,
        "input_ids": prompt,
    }
    for start, rows, content_hash in [(1, 2, 101), (3, 3, 202)]
]
BaseMultimodalProcessor.validate_mm_data(image_data=items)
```

Actual: validation rejects the two formatted items. Expected: accept the two explicit, non-overlapping media spans, even though their placeholder tokens are adjacent and identical.

### Proposed scope

- Extend the existing precomputed/processor-output path to accept multiple explicit items per modality, while rejecting mixtures of raw and precomputed inputs.
- Preserve supplied offsets, hashes, embeddings, modality, and per-item position grids. Validate bounds, overlaps, and embedding-row counts with native helpers.
- Consume already-expanded input IDs without tokenizing, expanding, or running the vision encoder again.
- Ensure model-specific position handling uses grids from every item, rather than just the first processor-output dictionary.

This does not require a new cache-key format. Existing content-derived pad IDs can use the supplied item hashes. Concatenating items is an awkward workaround: adjacent identical placeholders do not retain their original item boundaries, and bundled identity reduces per-item prefix-cache reuse.

### Related resources

- [Current input validation and item collection](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/684fea8af3b11a5b51ec9966c02959a32ad3421c/python/sglang/srt/multimodal/processors/base_processor.py)
- [Existing item metadata and span validator](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/684fea8af3b11a5b51ec9966c02959a32ad3421c/python/sglang/srt/managers/schedule_batch.py)
- [Downstream integration](https://github.com/basetenlabs/baseten/pull/33470). The generic processor changes are candidates for an upstream PR; our adapter, router, and custom external-encoder processor are downstream-specific.

Validation so far is source inspection and isolated CPU checks; full serving/GPU validation is pending. A focused upstream PR should include regression tests in the existing CPU CI suite.
