items.title: [Bug]: `/metrics` (iteration-stats) route blocks the serve event loop — a 2 s Prometheus scrape inflates request latency 5–60× and cuts prefill throughput ~5× (4× RTX 5060 Ti TP4, Qwen3.5 hybrid-GDN NVFP4 27B, 1.3.0rc29)
items.author: sean640112
items.body_excerpt:
> **Update (2026-10-09): the root cause is not sm120.** The "fixed" per-request cost comes from the `/metrics` iteration-stats route blocking the serve event loop: a 2 s Prometheus scrape inflates request latency 5–60× and cuts prefill throughput ~5×. Controlled A/B, py-spy stacks and the Prometheus-side numbers are in the [follow-up comment](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/issues/19623#issuecomment-6076428189) below.

# ~6 s fixed per-request latency floor on sm120 (4× RTX 5060 Ti, TP4) with a Qwen3.5 hybrid-GDN 27B NVFP4 checkpoint

## Summary

On a 4× RTX 5060 Ti (sm120) box serving a **dense hybrid GDN + full-attention 27B** NVFP4 checkpoint with `trtllm-serve` (PyTorch backend, TP4), we measure a **~6 s per-request floor on time-to-first-token that is independent of prompt length**. A 212-token request takes **6.06 s** to first token (8.0 s total), and the floor persists at every length we tested (212 → 59,571 tokens). Requests are reproducible to ±5 ms across 12 measurements in 3 separate server starts.

The same hardware, same checkpoint, same prompt, same client, served by SGLang gives **0.26–0.30 s** for the identical request. `trtllm-serve` therefore looks ~20× slower on short requests, while its *marginal* prefill throughput is only ~2.6× lower (~2,143 tok/s vs ~5,600 tok/s).

We have ruled out MTP/spec-decode, scheduler policy, `max_seq_len`, chunked prefill, the CUDA caching allocator, and thinking-mode as causes (details below). We would like to know whether this per-request floor is **expected on sm120 for hybrid GDN models**, or a bug — and which knob/diagnostic we should look at next. We are happy to run any instrumentation you suggest.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | 4× NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, compute capability **12.0 (sm120)**, TP=4 |
| Driver | 610.57.04 |
| CUDA toolkit | 13.3 (`nvcc` 13.3, `CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-13.3`) |
| OS / Python | Linux, Python 3.12.11 (venv) |
| TensorRT-LLM | **1.3.0rc29.dev202609240000** (nightly from 2026-09-24; PyPI 1.2.1 does not contain `modeling_qwen3_5.py`, hence nightly) |
| torch | 2.14.0+cu132 |
| flashinfer-python | 0.6.18 |
| triton | 3.8.0 |
| nvidia-cutlass-dsl | 4.8.0.dev0 |
| tensorrt / tensorrt_cu13 | 10.14.1.48.post1 |
| MPI | OpenMPI 5.0.10 (`mpi4py` bootstrap path) |
| Model | `nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` — `architectures: ["Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration"]`, `model_type: qwen3_5`; 64 layers, hidden 5120, 24 Q heads, 4 KV heads |
| Quantization | ModelOpt `MIXED_PRECISION`: **FP8 per-tensor on 208 layers** (`block_size` absent) + **NVFP4 `group_size: 16` on 193 layers**, `kv_cache_quant_algo: null` |

Note on the attention backend: your hardware support matrix lists sm120 as supporting NVFP4 / MXFP4 / FP8 (per-tensor) / FP8 KV cache, which covers this checkpoint's formats — so the quantization scheme itself should be fully supported on sm120.

## How to reproduce

Server (the `mpirun -n 1` wrapper and `OMPI_MCA_*` are needed on this host because `import tensorrt_llm` otherwise blocks in the mpi4py `MPI.COMM_WORLD` initialization, and this host's own hostname resolves to loopback only):

```bash
export CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-13.3
export OMPI_MCA_btl_tcp_if_include=lo OMPI_MCA_oob_tcp_if_include=lo
mpirun -n 1 --oversubscribe trtllm-serve serve /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 1234 --tp_size 4 \
  --max_seq_len 140000 --max_batch_size 8 \
  --served_model_name qwen3.8-27b \
  --free_gpu_memory_fraction 0.80 \
  --extra_llm_api_options opts.yaml
```

`opts.yaml`:
```yaml
enable_chunked_prefill: true
max_num_tokens: 8192
speculative_config:
  decoding_type: MTP
  max_draft_len: 3
  speculative_model: /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4
```

Client — a minimal stdlib-only streaming client (this is the "probe" used for every number below; it measures the first chunk that carries `choices[0].text`/`delta.content`):

```python
import json, time, urllib.request
prompt = open("/path/to/corpus.txt").read()[:600]          # → 212 tokens
body = {"model": "qwen3.8-27b", "prompt": prompt, "max_tokens": 1, "temperature": 0, "stream": True}
req = urllib.request.Request("http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1/completions",
        data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
t0 = time.time(); ttft = None
with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=900) as r:
    for raw in r:
        s = raw.decode().strip()
        if not s.startswith("data: "): continue
        if s[6:] == "[DONE]": break
        d = json.loads(s[6:])
        ch = d.get("choices") or []
        if ch and ch[0].get("text"):
            ttft = time.time() - t0; break
print("TTFT", ttft)
```

## Measured results (same probe, same prompts, same box)

| prompt tokens | path | TRT-LLM stream TTFT | TRT-LLM non-stream total | SGLang stream TTFT | SGLang non-stream total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **212** | completions | **6.053–6.062 s** (n=5) | 7.995–8.035 s | **0.262 s** | 0.304 s |
| 222 | chat (medium template) | 12.11 – **22.21 s** (unstable across restarts) | 14.06 – 26.19 s | 0.268 s | — |
| 7,172 | completions | 10.10 s | 12.02 s | 0.243 s *cached* | 1.84 s *cached* |
| 12,131 | completions | 12.12 s | 14.06 s | — | — |
| 28,008 | completions | — | 20.13 s | — | 6.15 s *cached* |
| 59,571 | completions | — | 36.26 s | — | — |
| 65,032 | chat | 56.52 s | 56.45 s | — | — |

*("cached" = the SGLang side hit its radix prefix cache on the shared corpus prefix, so those cells are not a like-for-like prefill comparison.)*

Least-squares fit of the completions path (`total = C + N/R`, 5 points spanning 212 → 59,571 tokens):
**C = 8.10 s, R = 2,143 tok/s, R² = 0.9966** — i.e. a very large constant plus a modest rate term. (The streaming TTFT is ≈ 1.9 s lower at every point, i.e. TTFT ≈ 6.1 s + N/2143.)

For reference, an independent client (vLLM's `bench serve` against the same server) measured prefill throughput of **453 / 1,014 / 1,302 tok/s** at 8K / 32K / 64K with meanTTFT 16.15 / 29.28 / 46.44 s, i.e. the same

comments.author: LaelaZorana
comments.body:
Probe done, single GPU numbers below. This isolates the GDN prefill cost independent of the TP4, mpirun and NVFP4 27B variables.

Env is TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29, torch 2.14.0, single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell sm120. Model is Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B, qwen3_5, same hybrid GDN family, served via trtllm-serve at TP1.

Results, TTFT over 5 runs

With FlashInfer prefill on, the default, the 212 tok prompt with max_tokens 1 took 16.1 to 17.5 ms and the 4096 tok prompt took 49.6 to 53.9 ms. With FlashInfer prefill off, TLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_GDN_PREFILL=0, they took 17.8 to 19.1 ms and 49.9 to 52.5 ms.

Stream closes within 0.1 ms of TTFT, single token responses. FlashInfer is the default, see the server log.

Takeaways

On one card, GDN prefill is measured in milliseconds, nowhere near the 6.1 s floor. That floor comes from the TP4 path, the mpirun loopback setup, or something about the NVFP4 27B ckpt.

FlashInfer toggle moves latency only about 2 ms either way here.

Server log also flags an Autotuner cache miss, falling back, for nvfp4_gemm on shape 4 by 2560, which fits a small M shape, just FYI.

Next steps to nail down the 6.1 s

Serve the same 2B at TP4 on the same box, which shows if it is the TP4 path.

Short nsys capture around a single 212 tok request, where GPU busy vs. wall clock shows GDN kernels vs. gaps.

If the GPUs are idle for about 6 s, py-spy dump on rank 0 should show exactly where the wall clock goes.

comments.author: sean640112
comments.body:
**Follow-up: the per-request latency floor and the prefill throughput cap are both caused by scraping the `/metrics` route, not by sm120**

Thanks for the earlier guidance. Following it, we ran controlled A/Bs on the same binary and found that the "fixed per-request cost" comes from the **Prometheus scrape of `/metrics`**, and that it degrades more than first-token latency.

Setup: TRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29, sm120, 4× RTX 5060 Ti 16G, TP4, `Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (hybrid GDN), `mpirun -n 1 trtllm-serve ... --tp_size 4`.

**A. Short requests** (212-token prompt, reproducible ±5 ms)

| | engine on `127.0.0.1:1234` (Prometheus scrapes every 2 s) | same engine on `127.0.0.1:1235` (nothing scrapes it) |
|---|---|---|
| 212-token, non-stream | **7.74 / 8.07 / 8.07 s** | **0.137 / 0.137 / 0.178 s** |
| stream TTFT | **6.060 / 6.060 / 6.060 s** | **0.139 / 0.138 / 0.140 s** |

**B. Prefill throughput** (canonical `vllm bench serve`, `--dataset-name random`, 2 prompts, concurrency 1, output len 1)

| input len | scrape active | not scraped |
|---|---|---|
| 8,192 | 488 tok/s (Mean TTFT 14,996 ms) | **2,514 tok/s (2,911 ms)** |
| 32,768 | 1,081 tok/s (27,476 ms) | **2,386 tok/s (12,449 ms)** |
| 65,536 | 1,452 tok/s | **2,177 tok/s** |

So a 2-second monitoring scrape costs anywhere from ~5× to ~60× depending on the request shape.

Prometheus side (`job_name: llm`, `scrape_interval: 2s`, `scrape_timeout: 1500ms`, `metrics_path: /metrics`), its own `scrape_duration_seconds{job="llm"}`:

* with our TRT-LLM server up: every scrape **times out at 1.5003–1.5012 s** (`up=0`)
* with our SGLang server on the same port: 0.060–0.063 s (`up=1`)

Mechanism: the single serve event loop is blocked inside the `/metrics` handler, which awaits engine stats through a blocking RPC. py-spy from the frontend process shows the same stack at 0.6 s / 3 s / 6 s into a request:

```
get_iteration_stats (serve/openai_server.py) -> get_stats_async (llmapi/llm.py)
  -> aget_stats (executor/proxy.py) -> _call_sync (executor/rpc/rpc_client.py) -> Future.result()
```

TTFT ≈ 3 × 2.02 s and non-stream total ≈ 4 × 2.02 s — the scrape interval *is* the quantum. It also explains why the engine looked idle while requests were slow: GPUs at ~0% util, rank 0's executor parked in `queue.get()`, and the other ranks spinning in the per-iteration request-count broadcast — the request had not reached the engine yet.

Mitigations we tested:

1. **Not scraping the port** → full recovery (tables above).
2. `enable_iter_perf_stats: true` in the extra LLM API options → **short requests recovered** (0.184 s / TTFT 0.140 s) while Prometheus kept scraping every 2 s, **but prefill did not** (8K stayed at 488 tok/s vs 2,514 clean). So that flag is not a substitute for fixing the route.

The underlying hazard looks like the stats route awaiting a blocking RPC on the serve event loop (the source comment in that path mentions nvbug 6102381). Making `/metrics` non-blocking by default — or documenting that Prometheus should scrape `/prometheus/metrics` rather than the JSON stats route — would prevent a monitoring scrape from inflating latency and prefill cost by 5–60×.

Happy to share py-spy dumps, full server args, or run a patched build on this exact setup (4× sm120 consumer cards, TP4) if that helps.

Thanks again, @LaelaZorana — this was filed half expecting it to go unanswered, so your reply was a pleasant surprise, and it is what led us to run the A/B that found the real cause.

comments.author: Lewis-panda
comments.body:
I traced the stats/KV-event path in both RPC proxies on main `681cff123b96e0a8fd52d977366a62677de7ae08`. `aget_stats()` and `aget_kv_events()` call synchronous `.remote()` before returning their iterator; that path waits on `Future.result()`. Making the subsequent queue consumption asynchronous cannot avoid this earlier wait.

I have prepared a narrow fix: [patch on my fork](https://github.com/Lewis-panda/TensorRT-LLM/commit/f7c62625d5c8c7c4da79a83a9bba508264a4dae7). Each call returns an `IterationResult` subclass that starts the RPC on first consumption. Socket I/O stays on the client's existing private loop while the caller awaits the result without blocking. Fetch/done state belongs to each iterator, while unread records stay in the executor's shared queue: reading `A` from `[A, B]` and later fetching `[C]` retains `[B, C]`. Worker timeout forwarding and RPC-error handling are preserved; caller cancellation clears the pending client request without claiming server-side cancellation. Public signatures remain unchanged.

On the original production source, all **12** proxy/API/timeout regression cases fail because iterator construction already fetches. The patched source passes the full **52-case** new test file, including eight cases using the real HMAC/ZMQ RPC client/server to check caller-loop progress and cancellation cleanup. Changed-file pre-commit passes. Another **37 adjacent tests pass**: 24 existing RPC tests, nine protected LLM API checks, and four metrics-endpoint tests; two upstream tests retain their explicit flaky-test skips.

Tests import the actual checkout modules with official native wheel `1.4.0rc1.dev202610140007`, Python 3.12, PyTorch `2.14.0+cu132`, normal native initialization, and CUDA hidden. The wheel's native commit is 13 commits older than the Python base; intervening C++ changes are three CMake files. I have not measured serving throughput/latency or reproduced the report's 5–60× figures.

Would this RPC/iterator scope be approved for a PR under the contribution process? The tested implementation and signed-off commit are ready on the linked fork.

items.title: [Performance] XQA sm90 decode (head_dim 256, fp8 KV, page 16), batch 10 / 124K ctx: 18% of HBM peak, 66-block grid, 12.5% warp occupancy — 65% of the decode step
items.author: wenzhelee
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

Long-context, small-batch decode with **XQA** (`kernel_mha`, from `csrc/xqa/mha_sm90.cu`) runs at **18% of HBM peak** and accounts for **65% of the decode step** on an H20 (sm90). In the *same step on the same device*, a `deep_gemm` FP8 GEMM reaches 32%. The traced grid for `kernel_mha` is only **66 blocks for 78 SMs**, 1 block/SM (129.6 KiB smem) → ~12.5% warp occupancy, so we suspect a long serial KV chain rather than a bandwidth limit.

We may well be mis-configuring something (e.g. `page_size`), and we'd appreciate a pointer to the relevant knob or to the right kernel for this shape. Happy to run further experiments if useful.

### Environment

- vLLM `v0.30.0` (`vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0`), **flashinfer 0.6.18.post1**, torch 2.13.0+cu130 (CUDA 13.0)
- 2 × NVIDIA H20 (sm90, **78 SMs**, 97,871 MiB each), `--tensor-parallel-size 2`
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 — hybrid: **16 full-attention layers (4 KV heads, head_dim 256)** + 48 GDN (linear-attention) layers
- KV cache: **fp8 (e4m3)**, `--block-size 16` → `page_size = 16`, `--max-model-len 1000000`, MTP `num_speculative_tokens=2`
- Attention backend `FLASHINFER`; `--max-num-seqs 128`, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.88`
- Load: **10 concurrent requests**, 124,026-token prompts (94.6% prefix-cache hit, so prefill is negligible), 3000 decode tokens each, greedy
- The precompiled kernel that matches this run is exactly
  `xqa_input_bf16_kv_cache_e4m3_output_bf16_page_size_16_head_dim_256_head_group_ratio_2_use_sliding_window_False_use_spec_dec_False_spec_q_seq_len_1`
- For reference, swapping in `FLASH_ATTN` (FA3) made the *whole step* 1.8x slower (82.7 → 45.6 ms/step), i.e. XQA is already the better of the two available paths.

### Evidence

torch-profiler / CUPTI kernel events, one **42.2 s** steady-decode window = **955 engine steps** (steps derived from `spec_decode_num_drafts_total`), batch 10, 124K ctx. Per-step totals:

| kernel family | ms/step | share | grid | block | smem/block | bytes/step/card | effective BW |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`kernel_mha` (XQA)** | **27.51** | **64.9%** | — | — | — | KV 19.84 GB | **721 GB/s = 18.0% of 4.0 TB/s** |
| ↳ the dominant call | 26.78 | 63.2% | **[3, 2, 11] = 66 blocks** | [128,1,2] = 256 thr | 129.6 KiB | | |
| `deep_gemm::sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d_impl<…17408,5120…>` | 3.27 | 7.7% | [78,1,1] | [256,1,1] | 214.8 KiB | | |
| GEMM family (all deep_gemm/nvjet) | 10.51 | 24.8% | | | | weights 13.65 GB | **1,299 GB/s = 32.5%** |
| quant / copy / elementwise | 1.56 | 3.7% | | | | | |
| GDN (`gdn_decode_post_conv_mtp_kernel`) | 1.45 | 3.4% | [11,24,1] | [256,1,1] | 44.1 KiB | | |
| allreduce (`oneshotAllreduceFusionKernel`) | 1.18 | 2.8% | | | | | |
| **total** | **42.38** | 100% | | | | | |

`kernel_mha` is called **17 times per step** (16 full-attention layers + the MTP draft layer), 1552 µs per call.

Context control — same batch size, same everything, only ctx = 8K:

| | 124K | 8K |
|---|---|---|
| attention ms/step | **27.51** | **3.03** |
| GEMM family | 10.51 | 9.38 |
| GDN | 1.45 | 1.44 |
| allreduce | 1.18 | 1.09 |
| quant/copy | 1.56 | 1.44 |

**Every non-attention family is ctx-independent ( ±0.1 ms); the 25.9 ms step delta is 100% this kernel.** Fitting `t_attn ≈ 1.31 ms + 2.055e-4 ms × ctx` ⇒ marginal KV read bandwidth ≈ 758 GB/s. Impact on throughput: engine-peak 1716 tok/s at 8K ctx vs 696 tok/s at 124K with identical batch.

### Questions

1. For this variant, how is the KV/context split factor chosen (grid.z = 3 here → 3 × 2 KV heads × 11 requests)? With 124K ctx that leaves each block serially covering ~41K tokens of KV, which 66 blocks / 8 warps-per-SM apparently cannot hide. Is the split factor a build-time constant, or can it be increased?
2. Would a different `page_size` change the tiling/occupancy? The JIT cache already contains `page_size ∈ {16,32,64,128} × head_dim 256 × head_group_ratio 2`, so we plan to A/B `--block-size 32/64` next — if you already know the answer we'd rather not burn restart cycles.
3. Is there a recommended alternative decode kernel/flag for this shape on sm90 (**long context, small batch, GQA group ratio 2, fp8 KV, head_dim 256, page 16, MTP/spec-decode enabled**) that we should compare against — e.g. a non-XQA / non-tensor-core path?
4. Is the 18%-of-peak figure expected at these shapes, or is there a known config caveat (workspace buffer size, `VLLM_FLASHINFER_*`, autotune) we should check first?

### Repro sketch

```bash
vllm serve <Qwen3.8-27B-FP8> --tensor-parallel-size 2 --max-model-len 1000000 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 16 --max-num-seqs 128 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.88 \
  --attention-backend FLASHINFER --speculative-config '{"num_speculative_tokens":2,...}' \
  --profiler-config '{"profiler":"torch","torch_profiler_dir":"/tmp/vprof","torch_profiler_with_stack":false}'
# warm a shared 124K prompt prefix, then run 10 concurrent /v1/chat/completions with max_tokens=3000
curl -X POST localhost:8001/start_profile   # ~42 s of steady decode
curl -X POST localhost:8001/stop_profile    # note: this RPC can time out while the dump succeeds
# parse rank*.pt.trace.json.gz, sum "dur" per kernel where "cat": "kernel"
```

Kernel timing closure: the six families above sum to 42.38 ms/step, matching an independent measurement of 41.8 ms/step from `generation_tokens_total` / `spec_decode_num_drafts_total`, so nothing material is missing from the accounting.

items.title: `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla`: FP8 64-head persistent KeepsAb corrupts random 16-head tiles (NaN LSE)
items.author: kpham-sgl
items.body_excerpt:
`trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla(..., sparse_mla_top_k=2048, return_lse=True)` with FP8 Q/KV and **64 query heads** returns wrong output and NaN or wrong LSE on a handful of (row, 16-head tile) units once the batch has a few hundred rows and KV is short. The same inputs through two 32-head calls, through 128 heads, or in BF16 are correct.

Hits any sparse MLA decode/extend with 64 query heads per KV head in FP8: DeepSeek-V3.2 / GLM-5 at a TP that lands 64 heads on one rank, and context-parallel decode that gathers heads (sglang DSA DCP8 on GLM-5.3, sgl-project/sglang#43735). Extend batches of a few thousand rows fail on nearly every launch.

## Env

- NVIDIA B300 (SM103), 148 SMs. flashinfer-python / cubin / jit-cache **0.7.0.post1**, torch 2.14.1+cu130
- `0.7.1` and `main` use the same trtllm-gen artifact `2d6a5a029eefcc388ec0ceb87efb55d8bcce5c3c/fmha/trtllm-gen/` and the same `selectSparseMlaGenerationKernel`, so this is expected there too.

## Kernel

`FLASHINFER_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG`, 64 heads, FP8, KV length 64:

```
fmhaSm100fKernel_QkvE4m3OBfloat16HQk576HV512HVPerCta256PagedKvDenseStaticTokenSparseP1VarSeqQ64Kv128PersistentKeepsAbForGen
numCtasX = 1, numCtasY = 2, numCtasZ = <rows>
```

Clean controls select a different kernel: 32 heads → `...Q32Kv128PersistentSwapsAbForGen`; 128 heads → `...Q64Kv128Persistent2CtaKeepsAbForGen` (`clusterDimX=2`); BF16 → the `QkvBfloat16` build of this same Q64 KeepsAb kernel. KV length 2048 at small batch selects the non-persistent `...MultiCtasKvGmemSep...StaticKeepsAbForGen`.

Selection is `selectSparseMlaGenerationKernel` in `include/flashinfer/trtllm/fmha/fmhaKernels.cuh` (`numHeadsQ > 32` → KeepsMmaAb, tileSizeQ 64; 128 heads with batch > ~9 → 2CTA). Unchanged on main as of 2026-10-12.

## Repro

FP8, counter buffer passed, PDL off. One 64-head call against two 32-head calls on the same inputs.

```python
import math, torch, flashinfer, flashinfer.decode, flashinfer.utils
ROWS, LENGTH, HEADS, TOPK = 16384, 64, 64, 2048
SCALE = 1 / math.sqrt(192)
torch.manual_seed(981)
q = (torch.randn((ROWS, 1, HEADS, 576), device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) * 0.1).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn)
kv = (torch.randn((math.ceil(LENGTH / 64), 1, 64, 576), device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) * 0.1).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn)
indices = torch.full((ROWS, 1, TOPK), -1, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
indices[:, :, :LENGTH] = torch.arange(LENGTH, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
lengths = torch.full((ROWS,), LENGTH, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
workspace = torch.zeros(8 * HEADS * ROWS * 256 + (1 << 20) + (1536 << 20), dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
counter = torch.zeros(flashinfer.utils.get_trtllm_gen_multi_ctas_kv_counter_bytes(
    ROWS, HEADS, flashinfer.utils.get_device_sm_count(torch.device("cuda"))), dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")

def invoke(query):
    return flashinfer.decode.trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla(
        query=query, kv_cache=kv, workspace_buffer=workspace,
        qk_nope_head_dim=128, kv_lora_rank=512, qk_rope_head_dim=64,
        block_tables=indices, seq_lens=lengths, max_seq_len=LENGTH,
        sparse_mla_top_k=TOPK, bmm1_scale=SCALE, backend="trtllm-gen",
        return_lse=True, multi_ctas_kv_counter_buffer=counter, enable_pdl=False)

left, right = invoke(q[:, :, :32].contiguous()), invoke(q[:, :, 32:].contiguous())
ref = torch.cat((left[0], right[0]), dim=2).reshape(ROWS, HEADS, 512)
out, lse = invoke(q)
err = (out.reshape(ROWS, HEADS, 512).float() - ref.float()).abs()
print(float(err.nan_to_num(nan=math.inf).max()), int((err.amax(-1) > 0.02).sum()), float(lse.isnan().sum()))
```

```
16,384 rows: 10/10 launches fail
4,096: 3/5    1,024: 2/5    256: 0/5
KV length 2048 (16,384 rows): 0/5
```

The 32-head split matches a float32 PyTorch reference (max abs error ~1e-3 on sampled rows).

## Sweep

5–10 launches each, full float32 reference on every row.

| Variable | Clean | Fails |
|---|---|---|
| Heads (16k rows, KV 64) | 16, 32 (also 32 at 32k and 65,535 rows), 128 | 64 |
| Rows (64 heads, KV 64) | 256 | 384 (1/10), then 512 … 16,384 (10/10) |
| KV length (64 heads, 16k rows) | 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2047, 2048 | 1, 63, 64, 65 (5/5), 129, 130 (9–10/10) |
| Dtype | BF16 Q/KV | FP8 Q/KV |
| Sparse vs dense | `sparse_mla_top_k=0` | sparse |
| PDL, `max_seq_len=2048`, fresh workspace + counter, no counter buffer | no effect | |

Each failing launch has 1–7 bad rows. In a bad row exactly one aligned 16-head tile (heads 0–15, 16–31, 32–47, or 48–63) is wrong across all 512 V dims, and that tile's LSE is NaN or off by several units. Which rows and tiles change per launch. The bad output is not another row's result. The multi-CTA KV counter stays all-zero, so this is the single-CTA path.

KV lengths that are an exact multiple of 128 (one or two full tiles) are clean. A partial last tile with at most two tiles fails; a longer partial last tile (2047) is clean. Persistent scheduler + FP8 + a partially filled KV tile + a grid larger than the resident CTAs points at a pipeline or shared-memory reuse race in the persistent Q64 KeepsAb kernel.

items.title: [Bug] FP8 ragged prefill refcheck mismatch between trtllm-native and prims-ts on B200/GB300
items.author: yufeiwu-nv
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The official BatchPrefillWithRaggedKVCacheWrapper benchmark reports an FP8 output mismatch between trtllm-native and prims-ts on B200 and GB300. Both backends execute for this supported configuration, but their outputs fail the benchmark's current torch.isclose check (rtol=0.2, atol=0.01).

This reports a reproducible benchmark/backend-consistency failure. It does not establish which implementation is wrong or identify an introducing commit.

## Environment and supported configuration

- FlashInfer version printed by the benchmark: 0.7.2.
- Latest observed reproducing revisions: B200 f63b2e7; GB300 5f8c9ef. Their ragged benchmark source is byte-identical.
- Q/K/V: FP8 E4M3; output: BF16; causal dense ragged prefill.
- Q and KV heads: 16; QK head dimension: 192; V/output head dimension: 128.
- Batch sizes 1 and 4, each with Q/KV sequence length 2048 or 4096; seed 42; default CUDA-graph setting.
- deepseek-v4-pro_861b is a benchmark case label. These commands exercise synthetic dense attention, not an end-to-end model or sparse-MLA validation.

## Reproduction

From the public repository's benchmarks/ directory at an observed revision, with that revision's benchmark dependencies installed, run these exact commands on B200 or GB300:

```bash
python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine BatchPrefillWithRaggedKVCacheWrapper --backends trtllm-native prims-ts --batch_size 1 --s_qo 2048 --s_kv 2048 --num_qo_heads 16 --num_kv_heads 16 --head_dim_qk 192 --head_dim_vo 128 --causal --q_dtype fp8_e4m3 --kv_dtype fp8_e4m3 --out_dtype bfloat16 --refcheck --allow_output_mismatch --random_seed 42 -vv --generate_repro_command --case_tag deepseek-v4-pro_861b
```

```bash
python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine BatchPrefillWithRaggedKVCacheWrapper --backends trtllm-native prims-ts --batch_size 1 --s_qo 4096 --s_kv 4096 --num_qo_heads 16 --num_kv_heads 16 --head_dim_qk 192 --head_dim_vo 128 --causal --q_dtype fp8_e4m3 --kv_dtype fp8_e4m3 --out_dtype bfloat16 --refcheck --allow_output_mismatch --random_seed 42 -vv --generate_repro_command --case_tag deepseek-v4-pro_861b
```

```bash
python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine BatchPrefillWithRaggedKVCacheWrapper --backends trtllm-native prims-ts --batch_size 4 --s_qo 2048 --s_kv 2048 --num_qo_heads 16 --num_kv_heads 16 --head_dim_qk 192 --head_dim_vo 128 --causal --q_dtype fp8_e4m3 --kv_dtype fp8_e4m3 --out_dtype bfloat16 --refcheck --allow_output_mismatch --random_seed 42 -vv --generate_repro_command --case_tag deepseek-v4-pro_861b
```

```bash
python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine BatchPrefillWithRaggedKVCacheWrapper --backends trtllm-native prims-ts --batch_size 4 --s_qo 4096 --s_kv 4096 --num_qo_heads 16 --num_kv_heads 16 --head_dim_qk 192 --head_dim_vo 128 --causal --q_dtype fp8_e4m3 --kv_dtype fp8_e4m3 --out_dtype bfloat16 --refcheck --allow_output_mismatch --random_seed 42 -vv --generate_repro_command --case_tag deepseek-v4-pro_861b
```

The commands retain the original --allow_output_mismatch setting, so a mismatch does not stop timing. Without that option, the source raises on a mismatch; that modified command has not been rerun separately.

## Observed result

For batch size 1 and sequence length 2048 at the latest observed revisions:

```text
B200:
[ERROR] Output tensor mismatch between backends trtllm-native and prims-ts: 2211 / 4194304 (0.05%) elements are different

GB300:
[ERROR] Output tensor mismatch between backends trtllm-native and prims-ts: 2205 / 4194304 (0.05%) elements are different
```

The same primary signature appears for all four shapes on both GPUs: 88 completed benchmark executions across six B200 revisions and five GB300 revisions, with two repetitions for each shape/revision. These executions come from one CI pipeline; no independent paired rerun or causal bisect is claimed.

Immediately before every mismatch, prims-ts passes its eight sampled FP32 context-reference checks and CUDA-graph replay-reference checks. Those checks support investigation but do not establish complete-tensor ground truth or prove that trtllm-native is incorrect.

## Source attribution and expected behavior

Both backend configurations are accepted by the upstream benchmark's support checks. The dense ragged routine sets rtol=2e-1 and atol=1e-2 and calls is_close_stats, which uses torch.isclose elementwise. The counts represent values beyond that declared tolerance, rather than a request for bitwise agreement.

When FA2 is unavailable, the routine uses trtllm-native as its inter-backend comparison reference while independently checking sampled prims-ts outputs against FP32 attention. Reference priority alone does not establish implementation correctness.

Please investigate the backend discrepancy or the benchmark's FP8 comparison/reference contract. Supported backend results should satisfy the benchmark's declared validation criterion, or the benchmark should explain and validate a justified alternative criterion.

- [Ragged benchmark source](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/f63b2e7/benchmarks/routines/attention.py#L2397)
- [Elementwise comparison helper](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/f63b2e7/benchmarks/routines/flashinfer_benchmark_utils.py#L385)
- [B200 completed CI evidence](https://nv/flashinfer-ci/-/jobs/483764444)
- [GB300 completed CI evidence](https://nv/flashinfer-ci/-/jobs/483764439)

items.title: Should LMCacheMPConnector honor kv_transfer_config.kv_role — or is MP mode intentionally always-kv_both?
items.author: kezboard233
items.body_excerpt:
## Context

We run a production-shaped POC on 8×V100 (two vLLM TP4 instances of Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 sharing one LMCache MP server with a CPU L1 tier) and filed #5143 with a runtime-verified repro: an engine launched with `kv_role="kv_consumer"` still stores every request's KV into the shared L1 — a single 32K-token cold request produced `168 × "Stored 784"` lines (= full prefix × 4 TP ranks), and the only engine that received any request in that window was the `kv_consumer` one.

We later found #4665 (closed by its author without maintainer response) reporting the same mechanism from the CacheBlend angle: the single-process connector honors `kv_role` / `skip_save`, the MP connector honors neither. As of today's `dev`, `lmcache_mp_connector.py` still contains no occurrence of `kv_role` / `kv_consumer` / `kv_producer` / `force_skip_save`.

## The design question

Before we contribute a patch, we want to check intent: **is MP mode intentionally "every connected engine writes"?** Two readings:

1. **Contract gap** — vLLM makes `kv_role` mandatory, documents it as "Whether this vLLM instance produces, consumes KV cache, or both", and exposes `is_kv_producer` / `is_kv_consumer` for connectors to branch on; LMCache's own single-process adapter honors it (`force_skip_save` in `vllm_v1_adapter.py`). Under this reading we'd gladly contribute a small PR that skips store-metadata generation when `is_kv_consumer` (mirroring the single-process gate), so warm-then-read-only fleets and PD-style topologies become possible on the MP path.

2. **Intentional always-kv_both** — the MP tier is a shared scratch space where every connected engine contributes. Under this reading we'd instead ask for the intent to be documented, plus ideally a one-line warning at connector init when `kv_role != "kv_both"`, so users aren't misled (we only noticed via instrumented counter evidence ourselves).

Happy to do either — a steer from maintainers decides which.

(Impact context: no correctness issue — stored content is identical — but a consumer-role engine burns D2H bandwidth and shared-L1 capacity; a 32K prefix on our model is ≈8.6 GB across 4 ranks.)

items.title: moe_cute_util.cuh: util_convert_type returns a tensor that points at a local array
items.author: BwL1289
items.body_excerpt:
In `cpp/tensorrt_llm/cutlass_extensions/include/cutlass_extensions/gemm/kernel/moe_cute_util.cuh`:

```cpp
auto frag = convert_op(*reinterpret_cast<cutlass::Array<From_type, numel> const*>(tensor.data()));
return cute::make_tensor(cute::make_rmem_ptr<To_type>(&frag), tensor.layout());
```

The returned tensor is a view of `frag`, a local of `util_convert_type`. `frag` is gone once the function returns, so
reading the result is undefined behaviour. Both routines in `fused_moe_kernel_routine.cuh` read it
(`util_convert_type<...>(accum)`, then the copy to shared memory).

With nvcc this happens to work. With clang (device code at -O3, sm_121a) the conversion and the SwiGLU that feed it are
removed, ptxas then removes the MMAs whose results are no longer used, and the kernel stores registers nothing wrote.
SASS counts (HMMA / LDSM / F2FP / FMUL) for the bf16 32x128x64 SwiGLU instantiation of
`fused_moe::run_global<Fused_Moe_Kernel_sm80<...>>`:

- nvcc (NVIDIA's flashinfer-jit-cache 0.7.0+cu130 wheel): 96 / 64 / 12 / 72
- clang: 64 / 40 / 0 / 48
- clang with the change below: 96 / 64 / 12 / 72

A bf16 or fp16 MoE call through this kernel (DeepSeek-V2-Lite shapes, 256 and 8192 tokens) then gets every row wrong
(NaN or values up to 1e37), and the output changes from call to call. With the change, the output matches the nvcc build
to every printed digit (max abs error against a float32 reference: 1.6e-05 for bf16 at 256 tokens, as with nvcc).

Suggested change, which returns a fragment that owns its registers (same layout, same element order):

```cpp
static_assert(cute::cosize_v<Layout> == numel, "util_convert_type: the fragment must be contiguous");
auto frag = convert_op(*reinterpret_cast<cutlass::Array<From_type, numel> const*>(tensor.data()));
auto out = cute::make_tensor<To_type>(tensor.layout());
CUTLASS_PRAGMA_UNROLL
for (int i = 0; i < numel; ++i) {
  out.data()[i] = frag[i];
}
return out;
```

To see the lifetime problem without a GPU: compile the function against small stand-ins for the CuTe/CUTLASS types it
uses, read the returned tensor after the call, and run it under AddressSanitizer with
`ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1`. The current code is reported as a stack-use-after-return; the change
above is not.

FlashInfer's own `include/flashinfer/attention/hopper/utils.cuh` (`convert_type`) has the same pattern.

items.title: [Bug] calculate_nvfp4_global_scale returns wrong per-token scales for hidden sizes above 8192 that are not multiples of 8192
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM 1.2.1 wheel, torch 2.9.1+cu130, A100 80GB PCIe (driver 610.57).
- The kernel is unchanged on main `b031dbe`: `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/quantization.cu` and `cpp/tensorrt_llm/common/reduceKernelUtils.cuh`.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

`torch.ops.trtllm.calculate_nvfp4_global_scale(x, None)` on a bf16 `x` of shape `[m, n]` should return `448 * 6 / max|x[i]|` for each token. When the hidden size is above 8192 and not a multiple of 8192, many tokens get a wrong scale once a CTA handles more than one token (for a 2-D input, `m` above the SM count).

A minimal script:

```python
import torch
import tensorrt_llm  # registers torch.ops.trtllm

m = 512
torch.manual_seed(0)
rows = torch.arange(m)
amp = 2.0 ** ((rows * 5) % 11 - 3) * (1 + (rows * 3 % 8) / 8)  # per-token maximum
for n in (12288, 8192):
    x = (torch.rand(m, n) - 0.5) * amp[:, None]
    x[rows, torch.randint(n, (m,))] = amp
    x = x.bfloat16().cuda()
    ref = 2688.0 / x.double().abs().amax(1, keepdim=True)
    got = torch.ops.trtllm.calculate_nvfp4_global_scale(x, None)
    bad = ((got.double() - ref).abs() > 1e-4 + 2e-6 * ref.abs()).sum().item()
    print(f"n={n}: {bad} of {m} tokens have a wrong global scale")
```

On an A100 (SXM4 80GB) it printed:

```
n=12288: 309 of 512 tokens have a wrong global scale
n=8192: 0 of 512 tokens have a wrong global scale
```

Results with the 1.2.1 wheel:
- each call was checked in full against a float64 reference;
- a call counts as wrong if any token's scale is non-finite or off by more than 1e-4 + 2e-6 · |ref|.

| x shape (bf16) | wrong calls | wrong tokens in sampled calls |
|---|---|---|
| [512, 12288] | 914302 / 914302 | 301–318 of 512 |
| [256, 28672] | 920766 / 920766 | 101–114 of 256 |
| [512, 8192] | 0 / 924832 | |
| [1024, 4096] | 0 / 914518 | |

For example, in the first call at [512, 12288], token 3 got 28.0 instead of 42.0.

### Expected behavior

Each token's global scale is `2688 / max|x[i]|`, for any `n` the operator accepts. The launcher checks only `n % 256 == 0`.

### actual behavior

In `computePerTokenGlobalScaleForFP4QuantizationKernel` (`quantization.cu:351–374`), `getMaxAbs` calls `blockReduceMaxV2`, which contains a `__syncthreads()`, inside the per-thread loop:

```cpp
for (int vecIdx = threadIdx.x; vecIdx < n / ElemsPerVec; vecIdx += blockDim.x)
{
    float4 vec = reinterpret_cast<float4 const*>(input + tokenIdx * n)[vecIdx];
    float maxAbsVal = getMaxAbs<T>(vec);   // blockReduceMaxV2 -> __syncthreads()
    perTokenMaxAbsVal = cuda_max(perTokenMaxAbsVal, maxAbsVal);
}
```

The launcher uses `blockDim.x = min(n / 8, 1024)`. When `n / 8` is above 1024 and not a multiple of it, threads with `threadIdx.x < (n / 8) % 1024` run one more iteration per token than the others. CUDA requires a `__syncthreads()` in conditional code to be reached by all threads of the block, and here it is not.

The warps with fewer iterations run ahead. Each barrier instance then joins warp 0's reduction of one token with the other warps' reductions of later tokens handled by the same CTA. After those warps exit, it joins with the values they left in shared memory. The reduced maximum mixes tokens. In a standalone copy of the kernel, run without Compute Sanitizer, every wrong value matched the one predicted from this pairing.

A second, smaller problem: `blockReduceMaxV2` has no barrier between warp 0's read of `shared[lane]` (`reduceKernelUtils.cuh:281`) and the next call's write of `shared[wid]` (line 269). On the standalone copy, Compute Sanitizer racecheck reports hazards between these two lines at every shape we tested, including `n` = 4096 and 8192. Under racecheck or synccheck, those two shapes also returned wrong scales (one launch each), though they were correct in every plain run.

### additional notes

Suggested fix: reduce once per token, after the loop, followed by a barrier.

```diff
@@ -343,7 +343,6 @@ __device__ float getMaxAbs(float4& vec)
     {
         absMaxVal = static_cast<float>(cuda_max(absMaxVec.x, absMaxVec.y));
     }
-    tensorrt_llm::common::blockReduceMaxV2<float, 1>(&absMaxVal);
     return absMaxVal;
 }
 
@@ -365,6 +364,11 @@ __global__ void computePerTokenGlobalScaleForFP4QuantizationKernel(
             float maxAbsVal = getMaxAbs<T>(vec);
             perTokenMaxAbsVal = cuda_max(perTokenMaxAbsVal, maxAbsVal);
         }
+        // Reduce once per token, outside the per-thread loop: threads make different numbers of loop iterations
+        // when n / ElemsPerVec is not a multiple of blockDim.x.
+        tensorrt_llm::common::blockReduceMaxV2<float, 1>(&perTokenMaxAbsVal);
+        // blockReduceMaxV2's shared slots are rewritten by the next token's reduction.
+        __syncthreads();
         float globalScaleVal = 448.f * 6.f / perTokenMaxAbsVal;
         if (threadIdx.x == 0)
         {
```

A standalone copy of the kernel with the equivalent change gave no wrong scales on A100 and A40, and is clean under racecheck and synccheck.

**Reach.** Callers in the tree:
- the opt-in NVFP4 low-precision MoE combine in `nccl_ep.py:460` (`use_low_precision_moe_combine`, default off). It requires NVFP4 and a hidden size that is a multiple of 512, so sizes such as 10240 or 12288 can reach it. Its input is `[ep_size, max_tokens_per_rank, hidden]`, so a CTA handles several tokens once a rank receives more than SMs / `ep_size` tokens;
- `deep_ep_low_latency.py:386`, which runs this combine only for hidden sizes 4096, 6144 and 7168, and is not affected;

items.title: flashMLA utils.h: convert_type returns a tensor that points at a local array
items.author: peter941221
items.body_excerpt:
In `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/flashMLA/utils.h` (line 277-286):

```cpp
auto frag = convert_op(*reinterpret_cast<cutlass::Array<From_type, numel> const*>(tensor.data()));
return make_tensor(make_rmem_ptr<To_type>(&frag), tensor.layout());
```

Same defect as #19943. `make_rmem_ptr` on a raw pointer is the identity, so the returned tensor is a view of `frag`, a local of `convert_type`; reading the result after the call is undefined behaviour. Both live call sites are in `flash_fwd_mla_kernel.h`:

- line 271 (store epilogue): `Tensor rO = flash::convert_type<ElementO>(tOrO);`, then `retile_S` and `cute::copy` read through the pointer; `tOrO` is the `partition_fragment_C` accumulator.
- line 817 (splitkv combine kernel): `Tensor rO = flash::convert_type<Element>(tOrO);`, then `cute::copy(rO, gO)` reads it.

`convert_type_out` in the same file takes the output by reference and is fine; its comment already notes that the output can be wrong when the result is allocated and returned inside the helper, so the returning variant looks like a known hazard that was not fixed.

With nvcc the read returns stale values (registers/local memory), so it is silent in practice; it is still the same lifetime bug that was fixed in `cutlass_extensions` by #20017.

Reproduction without a GPU: compile the function verbatim in a host translation unit, read the returned tensor after the call, run under AddressSanitizer with `ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1`. The current code is reported as a stack-use-after-return pointing at `frag` inside the `convert_type` frame. Returning `make_tensor<To_type>(tensor.layout())` (an owning ArrayEngine) with the elements copied in is clean. The contiguity the HACK comment assumes can be enforced with `static_assert(cosize_v<Layout> == numel, ...)`, which holds for both real instantiations: the `partition_fragment_C` layout has cosize 128 == size 128, and the combine kernel's `make_tensor<ElementAccum>(shape(...))` layout has cosize 4 == size 4.

This helper is a copy of FlashInfer's `include/flashinfer/attention/hopper/utils.cuh` (`convert_type`), which still has the same pattern at line 153.

items.title: torch._inductor.runtime.cache_dir_utils.cache_dir() raises a raw, unguarded PermissionError/OSError when the cache directory is unwritable, surfacing at torch._dynamo import time
items.author: miggle711
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch/_inductor/runtime/cache_dir_utils.py`'s `cache_dir()` calls `os.makedirs(cache_dir, exist_ok=True)` with no error handling. When the target directory can't be created or written to (disk quota exceeded, permission denied, read-only filesystem), this raises a raw `PermissionError`/`OSError` with no context about what failed or why.

Because `cache_dir()` is called implicitly as part of importing `torch._dynamo` (triggered merely by using `@torch.compile`, before any actual compilation happens), the resulting traceback surfaces deep inside PyTorch's own import machinery, nowhere near anything that looks disk-related. For a caller several layers up the stack (e.g. an inference server initializing `torch.compile` as part of its own startup), this produces a deeply confusing, seemingly unrelated crash.

**Repro:**

```python
import os
os.environ["TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR"] = "/some/dir/with/no/write/permission"

import torch

@torch.compile
def f(x):
    return x @ x

f(torch.randn(8, 8))
```

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../torch/_dynamo/package.py", line 1267, in <module>
    DynamoCache = DiskDynamoCache(os.path.join(cache_dir(), "dynamo"))
  File ".../torch/_inductor/runtime/cache_dir_utils.py", line 20, in cache_dir
    os.makedirs(cache_dir, exist_ok=True)
  File "<frozen os>", line 225, in makedirs
PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/some/dir/with/no/write/permission'
```

(If the directory already exists but a deeper write inside it fails, the error is instead wrapped as `torch._dynamo.exc.InductorError: PermissionError: ...`, slightly better, still uncaught, still doesn't mention disk space/permissions explicitly.)

**Expected behavior:** a clear, actionable error naming the directory and the likely cause (disk full / permission denied / read-only filesystem), not a bare stdlib `PermissionError`/`OSError` with no context.

### Why this matters beyond one project

Any project that invokes `torch.compile` directly, with its own `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR`, or torch's own default cache location, will hit this same confusing crash the moment that cache directory is unwritable, with nothing in the traceback pointing at disk or permissions. This is especially easy to hit in CI, containers, or any environment where `$HOME`/the default cache location is read-only or quota-limited, since it fires at import time rather than only when compilation is actually invoked.

### Suggested fix

Wrap the `os.makedirs` call in `cache_dir()` to catch `OSError` and re-raise with an explicit message naming the directory and the likely cause:

```python
def cache_dir() -> str:
    cache_dir = os.environ.get("TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR")
    if cache_dir is None:
        cache_dir = default_cache_dir()
    cache_dir = os.path.abspath(cache_dir)
    os.environ["TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR"] = cache_dir
    try:
        os.makedirs(cache_dir, exist_ok=True)
    except OSError as e:
        raise OSError(
            f"Failed to create or access torch.compile cache directory "
            f"'{cache_dir}' (TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR). This usually means "
            f"the disk is full, the directory is not writable, or the "
            f"filesystem is read-only. Original error: {e}"
        ) from e
    return cache_dir
```

Scoping this to just `cache_dir()` for now. Other cache-write paths deeper in Inductor/Triton may hit the same class of unguarded `OSError`, but that's a separate, follow-up investigation, happy to open a tracking issue for that separately rather than widen this one.

Happy to submit a PR for the change above.

items.title: [Inductor] Config patches are applied after SIMD tiling selection
items.author: krymaciag
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

SIMDScheduling.codegen_node_schedule() calls get_tiling_and_scores() and creates kernel choices before collecting the config_patches. It applies those patches only while calling kernel.codegen_kernel(). As a result, a patch for a tiling setting for example triton.prefer_nd_tiling cannot affect tiling selection.

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/d2f3a9d2e41e2fb201224ec61f74aa000a37e513/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L4329

Expected behavior: If patches are intended to control the generated kernel’s tiling, apply them while selecting tiling and creating kernel choices as well as during code generation.

Actual behavior: Tiling uses the surrounding config. Patches take effect only during kernel code generation.

Could you confirm whether patches are intended to not affect tiling?


### Error logs

None.

### Versions

Versions Observed in PyTorch main on 12 October 2026 at commit d2f3a9d2e41e2fb201224ec61f74aa000a37e513.

items.title: [Data][LLM][SGLang] Multimodal support for the SGLang engine
items.author: August0830
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Add multimodal support to the SGLang engine path of ray.data.llm, so that a batch job mixing text with media can be declared once and run on either engine. Concretely, SGLangEngineProcessorConfig should accept rows carrying images, video or audio, use the same column conventions and produce the same output columns as the vLLM path, and behave the same way when something cannot be honored — raise, rather than degrade. All three media types are in scope.

### Use case

We run offline scoring and labeling pipelines: a table in, a table out, one row per item to process, where the row carries both the prompt text and the thing to look at (product or content images, sometimes short video or audio clips). The jobs are batch — table-in / table-out scoring runs over a heterogeneous fleet with GPUs from both NVIDIA and AMD — and the model is a vision-language (or omni) model served by SGLang.

We want these jobs to run through ray.data.llm the same way text-only jobs — and jobs on vLLM — already do: declare a processor, point it at the input and output tables, and get Ray Data's scheduling, retries, rate limiting and metrics, instead of maintaining a bespoke batch script per pipeline.

Today that is not possible: multimodal support exists only on the vLLM path — on the SGLang side the request model carries only prompt / prompt_token_ids and the call never passes SGLang's native image_data, so a media-carrying row is processed as text only. A team whose model is deployed on SGLang either writes its own inference loop and loses everything the template provides, or configures the SGLang processor with media columns and gets plausible-looking results that ignored the media, with no error — the case we hit ourselves, and the reason we are filing this.

items.title: [RFC]: Support Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) Disaggregation in AIBrix Gateway
items.author: varungup90
items.body_excerpt: ### Summary This RFC proposes adding Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) disaggregation support to AIBrix Gateway. Today, AIBrix supports Prefill/Decode (PD) disaggregation. With growing multimodal workloads, the encoding stage can also become a significant and independently scalable part of inference. EPD disaggregation separates inference into three stages: * Encode (E): Process multimodal inputs such as image, video, or audio and generate intermediate representations. * Prefill (P): Process prompt tokens and encoder outputs and generate KV cache. * Decode (D): Perform autoregressive token generation. The Gateway should become aware of these worker roles and route requests to the appropriate Encode, Prefill, and Decode worker pools. ### Motivation Encode, Prefill, and Decode have different compute and memory characteristics. Running all stages on the same workers can lead to resource contention and makes it difficult to scale each stage independently. EPD disaggregation enables: * Independent scaling of Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. * Better resource utilization for multimodal workloads. * Different hardware or parallelism configurations for each stage. * Isolation of expensive multimodal encoding from Prefill/Decode workloads. * Reuse of the existing AIBrix PD routing architecture for multimodal serving. vLLM has started supporting disaggregated encoder architectures, including EPD-style deployments: * https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/ascend/en/latest/user_guide/feature_guide/epd_disaggregation.html * https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/disagg_encoder/ ### Proposed Change Extend AIBrix Gateway’s existing PD disaggregation support to understand an additional Encode worker role. Conceptually: For multimodal requests, the Gateway should: 1. Identify compatible Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. 2. Select workers using the existing AIBrix load-balancing framework. 3. Pass the required routing/transfer metadata to the inference engine. 4. Allow the inference engine and its connectors to handle encoder-output and KV-cache transfers. For text-only requests, the Encode stage can be bypassed and existing PD routing can continue to be used. The implementation should reuse the existing PD routing infrastructure as much as possible rather than introducing a separate routing architecture. Initial Scope * Add encode as a supported worker role alongside prefill and decode. * Discover and maintain Encode/Prefill/Decode worker pools. * Extend PD routing to select a compatible E/P/D execution path. * Support multimodal requests requiring an Encode stage. * Keep encoder-output and KV-cache transfer outside of the Gateway. * Add basic stage-level routing metrics and failure handling. Future work can explore encoder-cache-aware routing, heterogeneous hardware selection, and independent autoscaling of E/P/D worker pools. Open Questions * Should Encode workers be shared across multiple Prefill/Decode pools? * What metadata should the Gateway provide to coordinate encoder-output transfer? * Should worker selection happen in E → P → D order, or should Decode/Prefill capacity drive the selection first? * How much of the existing PD router can be generalized into an EPD stage-aware router? ### Alternatives Considered _No response_ ### Area Not sure

items.title: [Bug] Streamed /v1/messages responses are never charged against TPM
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When `/v1/messages` is called with `"stream": true`, the gateway never counts the tokens against the user's TPM limit, and no `request_end` line or token usage metrics are emitted for the request.

vLLM's Anthropic-compatible stream reports usage in the final `message_delta` event as `input_tokens` and `output_tokens`, without `total_tokens`. `processStreamingResponse` takes the total from `total_tokens` alone, so it stays 0, and `HandleResponseBody` skips metering when the total is 0.

The non-streaming path already handles this: `processLanguageResponse` derives the total from prompt and completion when `total_tokens` is missing. The streaming path never got the same fallback. Since #2997 routes Messages requests through the gateway, they all hit this path.

`validateRequestBody` only enforces `stream_options.include_usage` for chat completions, so a user with a TPM limit can stream through `/v1/messages` without the limit ever moving.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Set a TPM limit for a user.
2. Send `POST /v1/messages` with `"stream": true` to a vLLM backend through the gateway.
3. The user's `_TPM_CURRENT` counter doesn't change and no `request_end` is logged.

I reproduced this with a unit test that feeds a vLLM-shaped Messages stream to `HandleResponseBody`: usage comes back as `{PromptTokens:25 CompletionTokens:15 TotalTokens:0}` and the rate limiter's `Incr` is never called. I haven't run it against a live cluster.

### Expected behavior

Same as the non-streaming path: when `total_tokens` is absent, the total is input + output and the request is metered.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: main (9190b145)
- LLM(s) being used: vLLM `/v1/messages`

Area: Gateway

items.title: [Bug] /v1/messages/count_tokens returns 501 through the gateway
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` can't be used through the gateway. vLLM and SGLang both serve it next to `/v1/messages`, and it's what the Anthropic SDK calls for `client.messages.count_tokens()`.

The request does reach the gateway plugin, because it matches the `/v1/messages` PathPrefix on both the reserved route and the per-model routes. But `validateRequestBody` matches paths exactly and has no case for it, so the plugin answers `501 unknown request path`.

Adding the case alone isn't enough. The response is just `{"input_tokens": N}`, with no `model` or `usage`, so `processLanguageResponse` treats it as an unknown response and replaces it with a 500. `/tokenize` ran into the same thing and is excluded in `isLanguageRequest` for that reason (#2732).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy a vLLM model behind the gateway.
2. Send `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` with `{"model": "<model>", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]}`.
3. The gateway returns 501 `unknown request path`.

I hit both the 501 and the 500 in unit tests against main (9190b145). I haven't run it on a live cluster.

### Expected behavior

The request is routed by `model` like `/v1/messages`, and the engine's response is passed back unchanged. There's nothing to meter, since the endpoint only counts tokens.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: main (9190b145)
- LLM(s) being used: vLLM, SGLang

Area: Gateway

items.title: [Bug] ModelRouter never updates an existing HTTPRoute
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

ModelRouter creates a model's HTTPRoute once and never touches it again. `createHTTPRoute` ignores `AlreadyExists`, and the resync added in #2873 only recreates routes that are missing.

This bites on a default install. With no routing strategy set, the plugin just adds the `model` header and Envoy sends the request through that model's HTTPRoute, so the paths the route was created with are the only ones that work.

It shows up in two ways:

- After an upgrade, models that were already deployed don't get the paths added since v0.7.0 (`/tokenize`, `/pooling`, `/v1/score` and so on). Those requests 404 until someone deletes the route and lets it get recreated.
- Changing the port label, the service-name annotation or `model-router-custom-paths` on a running workload has no effect. `updateRouteFromWorkload` sees the change, but it only calls `createHTTPRoute`, which hits `AlreadyExists`. A new `AIBRIX_GATEWAY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` never gets applied either.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy a model on v0.7.0 with no routing strategy.
2. Upgrade to main.
3. `POST /tokenize` for that model returns 404, and `<model>-router` still has the old paths.

I reproduced this and the port change in unit tests and with envtest on main (c60f1d91). I haven't tried the actual upgrade on a cluster.

### Expected behavior

The resync should also update an existing route when it's out of date, not just recreate missing ones.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: main (c60f1d91), default install

Area: Gateway

items.title: [Bug] Streamed /v1/completions without stream_options.include_usage is never charged against TPM
items.author: ptimizeroracle
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

same family as #3008 / #3009, the other streamed path that never reaches the tpm counter

for a user with a tpm limit, `validateRequestBody` rejects a streamed chat completion that does not set `stream_options.include_usage`, because without it the engine sends no usage chunk and there is nothing to meter. the check is tied to `requestPath == PathChatCompletions` (`pkg/plugins/gateway/util.go`), so the same request on `/v1/completions` is accepted. the engine then streams no usage, `processStreamingResponse` ends with a zero total, and `HandleResponseBody` skips the tpm increment

measured on main @ d0500b0, user with `Tpm: 1000`:

| request | accepted | tokens metered |
|---|---|---|
| `/v1/chat/completions`, `stream: true`, no `stream_options` | no, 400 `include usage for stream options not set` | n/a |
| `/v1/chat/completions`, `stream: true`, `include_usage: true` | yes | from the usage chunk |
| `/v1/completions`, `stream: true`, no `stream_options` | **yes** | **0** |
| `/v1/completions`, `stream: true`, `include_usage: true` | yes | from the usage chunk |

so a tpm limited user who streams legacy completions without `stream_options` is never counted. rpm is still enforced

### Steps to Reproduce

drop this in `pkg/plugins/gateway/` and run `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway -run TestStreamedCompletionsWithoutIncludeUsage -v`

```go
package gateway

import (
	"fmt"
	"testing"

	"github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pkg/utils"
)

func TestStreamedCompletionsWithoutIncludeUsage(t *testing.T) {
	user := utils.User{Name: "u", Rpm: 10, Tpm: 1000}
	reqs := []struct{ name, path, body string }{
		{"chat, no stream_options", PathChatCompletions, `{"model":"m","stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}`},
		{"chat, include_usage", PathChatCompletions, `{"model":"m","stream":true,"stream_options":{"include_usage":true},"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}`},
		{"completions, no stream_options", PathCompletions, `{"model":"m","stream":true,"prompt":"hi"}`},
		{"completions, include_usage", PathCompletions, `{"model":"m","stream":true,"stream_options":{"include_usage":true},"prompt":"hi"}`},
	}
	for _, r := range reqs {
		_, _, _, stream, errRes := validateRequestBody("r", r.path, []byte(r.body), user)
		fmt.Printf("%-32s stream=%v rejected=%v\n", r.name, stream, errRes != nil)
	}
	noUsage := "data: {\"id\":\"cmpl-1\",\"choices\":[{\"text\":\"hello\",\"finish_reason\":\"stop\"}]}\n\ndata: [DONE]\n\n"
	usage, _ := processStreamingResponse("r1", []byte(noUsage), true)
	fmt.Printf("completions stream, no usage chunk    total=%d\n", usage.TotalTokens)
	withUsage := "data: {\"id\":\"cmpl-1\",\"choices\":[{\"text\":\"hello\",\"finish_reason\":\"stop\"}]}\n\ndata: {\"id\":\"cmpl-1\",\"choices\":[],\"usage\":{\"prompt_tokens\":2,\"completion_tokens\":1,\"total_tokens\":3}}\n\ndata: [DONE]\n\n"
	usage, _ = processStreamingResponse("r2", []byte(withUsage), true)
	fmt.Printf("completions stream, with usage chunk  total=%d\n", usage.TotalTokens)
}
```

output

```
chat, no stream_options          stream=true rejected=true
chat, include_usage              stream=true rejected=false
completions, no stream_options   stream=true rejected=false
completions, include_usage       stream=true rejected=false
completions stream, no usage chunk    total=0
completions stream, with usage chunk  total=3
```

### Expected behavior

`/v1/completions` gets the same treatment as chat for a tpm limited user. two ways, your call: reject with the same 400 when `stream_options.include_usage` is missing, or set it on the way to the engine so the client does not have to. the first is a few lines in `validateCompletionRequest`, the second changes the body and needs the content length update

### Environment

- AIBrix version: main @ d0500b0
- Deployment environment: none, unit level reproduction with `go test`
- Cloud provider: n/a
- LLM(s) being used: n/a, the no usage stream shape is what an openai compatible engine sends when `include_usage` is not set, not captured from a live vllm here
- Client library version: n/a

### Area

Gateway

found with ai assistance, i reran the reproduction myself on current main. i sent this together with the `/v1/messages` case to maintainers@aibrix.ai on the 11th, opening it here now that #3008 covered the other half in public

items.title: [Bug] Evicting one branch of the Preble prefix tree drops pods from its parent prefix
items.author: hmdsefi
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

`LPRadixCache.evictNode` in `pkg/utils/prefixcacheindexer/tree.go` removes the evicted node's pods from every parent node. It does not check whether another child of that parent still has the pod.

prefix-cache-preble records the target pod on every node of the request's path (`PostRouteUpdate`), so a parent prefix lists every pod that cached any of its branches. When one branch expires, the parent and the root lose those pods, even if another branch on the same pod is still cached. Requests that share the parent prefix then no longer match that pod, and the router falls back to cost-based routing.

## Steps to Reproduce

Unit level, with `NewLPRadixCache(2)`:

1. `AddPrefix([1 2 3], "m1", "default/p1")`, `AddPrefix([1 2 4], "m1", "default/p1")` and `AddPrefix([1 2 4], "m1", "default/p2")`. The tree is `[1 2]` with the children `[3]` and `[4]`.
2. Make only the `[4]` node older than the 5 minute TTL and call `Evict(time.Now())`.
3. Call `MatchPrefix([1 2 9], "m1", [p1, p2])`.

At d0500b03 it returns the matched tokens `[1 2]` and no pods.

## Expected behavior

`[1 2]` should still match p1, which still caches `[1 2 3]`. p2 only had `[1 2]` through the evicted branch, so it is right to drop p2.

## Environment

- AIBrix version: main at d0500b03
- Deployment environment: unit test of pkg/utils/prefixcacheindexer
- Cloud provider (if applicable): n/a
- LLM(s) being used: not model specific
- Client library version (if applicable): n/a

## Area

Gateway

I'd like to fix this. I have a change with tests ready and will open a PR.

items.title: [Feature] Add non-preemptive placement priority for ModelClaim
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
## 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

ModelClaim placement currently uses FIFO ordering when multiple unplaced claims compete for newly available warm-pool capacity. FIFO cannot express that some serving declarations should receive the next placement opportunity before less urgent ones.

Add an explicit, non-preemptive placement priority so operators can control admission order without changing the lifecycle of models that already have an instance.

## Use Case

An operator runs several ModelClaims in a constrained shared GPU pool. When capacity becomes available, an important production model should be considered before ordinary claims, while an infeasible high-priority claim must not leave usable capacity idle.

Claims that omit priority should retain today's behavior with priority `0`.

## Proposed Solution

Add `spec.priority` to ModelClaim with the following contract:

- non-negative `int32` with default `0`;
- immutable after creation;
- higher values receive earlier placement consideration;
- equal priorities retain FIFO ordering by creation time, then name;
- priority applies only to claims without a recorded instance;
- ordering is non-preemptive and does not change wake, sleep, replacement, or existing-instance behavior;
- BestEffortFIFO skips invalid or currently infeasible claims;
- an acquired make-room reservation keeps its turn;
- a denied claim reports `Scheduled=False` with reason `WaitingForPlacementTurn` without increasing placement-refusal backoff.

Queue ordering should be an optimization. An authoritative admission check must enforce correctness across controller restarts, independent backoff timers, and interleaved watch events.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The API server defaults omitted priority to `0` and rejects negative values.
- [ ] Higher-priority feasible claims are placed before lower-priority competitors.
- [ ] Equal-priority claims retain deterministic FIFO ordering.
- [ ] Invalid, disjoint, or infeasible claims do not block feasible claims.
- [ ] Existing instances, wake ordering, failed-instance replacement, and reservations preserve current behavior.
- [ ] Priority denial is observable and does not increase refusal backoff.
- [ ] Generated CRDs/API clients, unit tests, controller integration tests, ModelClaim E2E tests, and bilingual documentation are updated.

## Area

Orchestration (controllers and CRDs) / scheduling

## Implementation

Tracked by #3036.

items.title: [Bug] RayClusterFleet never requeues for its progress deadline, so stalled rollouts are not marked failed on time
items.author: Jackmeson1
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

A RayClusterFleet whose rollout stalls is not marked `ProgressDeadlineExceeded` when its `progressDeadlineSeconds`
runs out, unless something else happens to trigger a reconcile.

`syncRolloutStatus` (`pkg/controller/rayclusterfleet/progress.go`, around line 109 at `bdcb544`) discards the duration
returned by `requeueStuckDeployment`, the time left until the deadline. The changed-status path of `syncRolloutStatus` returns only an error,
and both rollout strategies return an empty `reconcile.Result`. So no requeue is scheduled for the deadline check.
`progressDeadlineSeconds` is documented as the time after which a stalled rollout is reported as failed
(`api/orchestration/v1alpha1/rayclusterfleet_types.go`, around line 65; `multi-node-inference.rst`).

Pause and resume are handled by #3033, which persists the paused/resumed condition so the deadline baseline is right
after a resume.

## Steps to Reproduce

Unit level, with controller-runtime's fake client: a fleet with `progressDeadlineSeconds: 600` whose Progressing
baseline is 60 seconds old and whose rolling update makes no further progress. Reconciling it at `bdcb544` returns
`{Requeue: false, RequeueAfter: 0}`; the expected result is `RequeueAfter: 540s`. The same holds for each of the six
rollout exits (three RollingUpdate, three Recreate) when rollout-status evaluation leaves an eligible Progressing
baseline.

The linked PR's `TestDeadlineScheduling` encodes these cases. To see them fail on `bdcb544`, run the PR's test file
against `bdcb544`'s `progress.go`, `rayclusterfleet_controller.go`, `recreate.go` and `rolling.go` (for example with
`go test -overlay`), leaving out `TestRecreateOperationErrors`, which needs the new helper signature:

```bash
GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly GOPROXY=off go test -count=1 ./pkg/controller/rayclusterfleet/...   -run '^TestDeadlineScheduling$' -overlay=<overlay.json>
```

35 `TestDeadlineScheduling` subtests fail that way, for example `RequeueAfter: 0` where 540s is expected.

## Expected behavior

After rollout-status evaluation, an eligible Progressing condition schedules the remaining deadline as
`RequeueAfter`, with a one-second minimum, so timeout detection no longer depends on an unrelated event. Disabled
deadlines (nil or `MaxInt32`), paused or deleting fleets, missing baselines, and conditions that end up completed or
timed out request no new timer; completion or real progress can still clear an earlier timeout.

Recreate can still remain unscheduled while it waits for old clusters, if no new ReplicaSet exists and Progressing
is missing or still `NewReplicaSetAvailable`; establishing that baseline is a separate change.

Exact deadline equality is not timed out. The returned delay does not guarantee an exact wall-clock reporting time,
and an empty result does not cancel work already queued.

## Environment

- AIBrix version: `bdcb544`
- Deployment environment: unit tests of `pkg/controller/rayclusterfleet` (controller-runtime fake client)
- LLM(s) being used: not model specific

## Area

Orchestration (controllers, CRDs)

I'd like to fix this. I have the change and tests ready and will open a PR.

items.title: [Bug]: FlashInfer CUTLASS MoE selected on fp4-less builds (CUDA toolkit < 12.8); gpt-oss dies at engine start
items.author: RyanClark2k
items.body_excerpt:
## Environment

- H100 SXM (SM90), driver 550.163.01 (host CUDA toolkit 12.4 at `/usr/local/cuda`)
- torch 2.11.0+cu129, Python 3.12; vLLM built from source at 34ad15827 (the #48438 branch — its diff doesn't touch FlashInfer or MoE backend selection, and the code cited below is identical on current main)
- `flashinfer-python==0.6.13` and `flashinfer-cubin==0.6.13` (both from `requirements/cuda.txt`); `flashinfer-jit-cache` NOT installed (it is only installed in `docker/Dockerfile`, not pinned in requirements)

The instance is torn down so I can't attach `collect_env.py` output, but the relevant coordinates are above and the failure is fully explained by source below.

## Repro

```python
from vllm import LLM
llm = LLM(
    model="openai/gpt-oss-20b",
    max_model_len=2048,
    kernel_config={"moe_backend": "flashinfer_cutlass"},
)
```

FlashInfer JIT-compiles `fused_moe_90` for several minutes (successfully), the model loads, then engine init fails:

```
RuntimeError: Check failed: (false) is false: Could not construct fused moe op with the
requested input combination Activation: bfloat16, Weight: uint8, Output: bfloat16
```

There is no workaround via dtype: `gpt_oss_mxfp4` rejects anything but bfloat16 at config validation.

## Root cause

1. vLLM selects the backend: `FlashInferExperts._supports_quant_scheme` allows `(kMxfp4Static, None)` on `is_device_capability(90)` (`fused_moe/experts/flashinfer_cutlass_moe.py`), and the availability check is `has_flashinfer_cutlass_fused_moe()`, an import check.
2. vLLM's call contract is correct: packed fp4 weights as `torch.uint8` with `use_w4_group_scaling=True`, which matches flashinfer's `isWFP4A16Quant()` predicate (`use_w4_group_scaling && weight == uint8 && !use_packed_weights`).
3. flashinfer gates fp4 out of the build on old toolkits: `flashinfer/jit/fused_moe.py:120` — `"-DENABLE_FP4" if is_cuda_version_at_least("12.8") else ""`. With system nvcc 12.4, the JIT build succeeds but the entire `isWFP4A16Quant()` construction branch in `flashinfer_cutlass_fused_moe_binding.cu` (which instantiates `CutlassMoeFCRunner<..., __nv_fp4_e2m1>`, a CUDA 12.8+ type) is compiled out, so runner construction falls through to the ICHECK above.

So "supported" is a property of the flashinfer *build*, and vLLM's gates only look at the GPU arch and importability. Confirmed empirically: installing `flashinfer-jit-cache==0.6.13+cu129` (prebuilt with a modern toolkit, exactly what the Dockerfile does) and rerunning the identical command works; I used the resulting engine for reload validation on #48312-related work the same day.

## Who hits this

Anyone installing vLLM from source or pip (not the Docker image) on a host whose CUDA toolkit is older than 12.8 while using any fp4-dependent FlashInfer path (gpt-oss MXFP4, NVFP4 CUTLASS MoE). Docker users are immune because the image installs `flashinfer-jit-cache`, which is also why CI doesn't see it. Old toolkits on new-enough drivers are common on rented GPUs.

## Proposed fix

Either or both, in order of preference:

1. A build-capability probe in `vllm/utils/flashinfer.py` (prebuilt modules present, or flashinfer's own `is_cuda_version_at_least("12.8")` predicate passes), threaded into the fp4-dependent scheme gates so selection falls back to Marlin/Triton with a log line instead of crashing after minutes of JIT compilation.
2. Pin `flashinfer-jit-cache` in `requirements/cuda.txt` alongside `flashinfer-python`/`flashinfer-cubin` so non-Docker installs get toolkit-independent kernels. (It needs the CUDA-specific index URL, which may be why it's Docker-only today.)

The cleanest long-term shape is a capability query exposed by flashinfer itself rather than vLLM probing its jit internals; I've filed flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3951 asking for that, and either way I'm happy to implement the vLLM side.

AI assistance was used to root-cause and validate this; I reviewed the analysis and can defend it end to end.


### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: Fully-masked softmax rows exponentiate to 1 in the FMHA no-loop kernel
items.author: StephenLReed
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM: 1.3.0rc23 (built from `f20ea652`); behaviour re-checked against `main` @ `fbda11f5`
- GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 (sm_120), driver 595.71.05
- PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12.13
- Ubuntu 25.10, kernel 6.17.0-41-generic
- Backend: PyTorch; single GPU, no TP/PP
- Model where observed: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 with FP8 KV cache (where model-specific)

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Reproduction

In `cpp/kernels/fmha_v2/src/fused_multihead_flash_attention_kernel_noloop.h`, `CHECK_NEG_INF` is
enabled only for bidirectional sliding-window, sliding-window, and custom masks. When it is compiled
out, a row whose running maximum is still `-FLT_MAX` — every score in the row masked — evaluates
`expf(-FLT_MAX - (-FLT_MAX))`, which is `expf(0) == 1`. Each masked score therefore contributes
weight 1 instead of 0.

The requirement belongs to the softmax input state, not to a mask type: any instantiation that can
present an entirely masked row is affected, including ordinary causal and padding masks.

### Expected behavior

A fully-masked softmax row contributes zero weight to the attention output.

### actual behavior

The row's running max is still -FLT_MAX, so every masked element evaluates expf(0) == 1 and the row attends masked positions with weight 1. Silent: no error, no NaN. Presents as sequence-length-banded output corruption.

### additional notes

We can demonstrate the arithmetic directly by inspection of `apply_exp_with_mask`. We do **not** have
an isolated regression test attributing our production symptom to this line alone: the fix was
deployed alongside an unrelated kernel-enumeration change, and the evidence is a multi-day production
soak rather than a controlled A/B.

A maintainer with the fmha_v2 test harness can construct the direct case far more cheaply than we
can: any causal-mask configuration whose final Q tile is partial should show masked positions
receiving weight 1 before the change and 0 after.

**Questions for maintainers**

1. Is enabling the guard unconditionally the fix you would want, or would you prefer it gated on the
   configurations that can actually produce a fully-masked row?
2. Is there a known-good harness in `cpp/kernels/fmha_v2` you would want a regression test added to?
3. Has the performance impact of the guard on previously-unguarded instantiations been characterised
   anywhere? We have not measured it.

Per CONTRIBUTING.md this Issue Request precedes the patch, which is ready and applies cleanly to `main` @ `fbda11f5`.

items.title: Add MXFP8 support for DeepEP-style MoE dispatch/combine kernels
items.author: dishamehra
items.body_excerpt:
The current DeepEP dispatch/combine paths used by vLLM are compatible with block-FP8 quantization, but do not yet support MXFP8. They would like to use MXFP8, specifically for decode nodes.

DeepEP currently has two dispatch/combine collective implementations for MoE models in vLLM:
- prefill / high_throughput: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/prepare_finalize/deepep_ht.py
- decode / low_latency: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/prepare_finalize/deepep_ll.py

Support ask:
- Add MXFP8 quantization format support to the dispatch/combine kernels
- Add support for a batched-format MXFP8 MoE kernel.
- Integrate the MXFP8 MoE kernel support into vLLM so that it is compatible with the low_latency DeepEP communication path.
 
The highest-priority path is: MXFP8 + decode / low_latency. It would also be useful to support: MXFP8 + prefill / high_throughput but low_latency decode support is the more important use case.
