items.title: docs: track API, prose, HTML rendering, and broken-link findings
items.author: kangbintNV
items.body_excerpt:
## Scope

Documentation findings span API behavior, technical accuracy, prose, HTML rendering, and links. The examples below show one case for each issue type; all four identified broken links are listed. Source corrections are in PR #5494. After the docs are published, verify the rendered pages and link destinations.

## One example per issue type

- **API Contract (P0):** The [cascade API](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/api/cascade.html) labels the `BatchPrefillWithSharedPrefixPagedKVCacheWrapper` constructor as `BatchDecodeWithSharedPrefixPagedKVCacheWrapper`.
- **Technical Accuracy (P1):** The [JAX FFI tutorial](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/tutorials/generated/jax_tvm_ffi/flashinfer_jax_tvm_ffi.html) says three additional packages are required but lists only two.
- **Grammar (P1):** The [attention API](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/api/attention.html) says `for batch of requests`; it needs `for a batch of requests`.
- **Clarity (P1):** The [sampling API](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/api/sampling.html) repeats `the sampling` in one sentence about deterministic sampling.
- **Punctuation (P1):** The [sampling API](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/api/sampling.html) joins two independent sentences with a comma after `probabilities`.
- **Spelling (P1):** The [communication API](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/api/comm.html) says `Initialization referece`.
- **Terminology (P2):** The [KV layout tutorial](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/tutorials/kv_layout.html) says `kV-Cache` instead of `KV-Cache`.
- **Formatting / HTML rendering (P0):** The [sampling API](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/api/sampling.html) displays literal `:param logits:` and `:type logits:` inside the `sampling_from_logits` description instead of structured parameter fields.

## Broken Link (P0): all four cases

1. **CUDA Programmatic Dependent Launch, published API:** The [attention API](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/api/attention.html) uses an [old URL](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/#programmatic-dependent-launch-and-synchronization) that returns 404. Use the [current CUDA section](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/04-special-topics/programmatic-dependent-launch.html).
2. **FlashInfer MLA article, published API:** The [attention API](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/api/attention.html) links to a [missing article](http://flashinfer.ai/2025/02/10/flashinfer-deepseek-mla.html). Use the [FlashInfer 0.2 MLA section](https://flashinfer.ai/2024/12/16/flashinfer-v02-release.html#fused-multi-head-latent-attention-mla-decoding-kernel).
3. **KDA repository, source documentation:** [`docs/api/kda.rst`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/b18a18247a831ddefa5a8308463c1113ac4b508a/docs/api/kda.rst#L650) links to an [unavailable upstream repository](https://github.com/humanfia/kda-for-kda-release). Link to the [vendored KDA implementation](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/tree/main/flashinfer/kda_kernels/persistent).
4. **CUDA Binary Compatibility, source documentation:** [`docs/design_docs/jit_cache_provider_wheels.md`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/b18a18247a831ddefa5a8308463c1113ac4b508a/docs/design_docs/jit_cache_provider_wheels.md#L250) uses an [old section URL](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#binary-compatibility) that redirects to the guide index without the intended anchor. Use the [current Binary Compatibility section](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/01-introduction/cuda-platform.html#binary-compatibility).

items.title: [Bug]Nightly Release fails across cu129, cu130, and cu134 because pytest cannot import `scripts` plugin
items.author: cindyzxq
items.body_excerpt:
## Description
Nightly Release run [#410](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/actions/runs/38357605641) failed on `main` at `86da418ad500351e10612d1ea1b1ae0316e3585a`. All 14 observed parameterized jobs failed during pytest startup while importing a plugin, before the evidence identifies any collected test case.

### Name and Version version: b1-571d0d5 (571d0d540df04f25298d0e159e520d9fc62ed121, 2026-07-18) built with CUDA 13.0.88, CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 (-> 120a) GGML_CUDA_FA=ON GGML_CUDA_GRAPHS=ON GGML_CUDA_FORCE_CUBLAS=OFF ### Operating systems Linux ### GGML backends CUDA ### Hardware 2x NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16GB (GB206, sm_120), driver 580.105.08 PCIe Gen5 x8 each, no NVLink nvidia-smi topo -p2p r -> CNS (Chipset not supported) AMD Ryzen 7 9700X, 32GB RAM, kernel 6.14.11 ### Models Qwen3.6-27B Q6_K (MTP head included) 21.30 GiB ### Problem description & steps to reproduce With --split-mode tensor, one of the two GPUs intermittently deadlocks and never recovers. Requests are minimal (19 input tokens / 2 generated tokens), sent at 61-second intervals. The deadlock occurs at a rate of roughly 1 in 1000 requests, i.e. about once every 13–17 hours of wall-clock time. It always hangs in launch_slot_, on the first request after an idle period of 40+ seconds. Neither print_timing nor release is ever printed after that point. /health keeps returning {"status":"ok"}, while /slots becomes unresponsive. No Xid errors are logged during the hang. Running with a single GPU only, the issue does not occur.

I isolated this further by testing different GGML_CUDA_ALLREDUCE backends:

GGML_CUDA_ALLREDUCE | Result -- | -- internal | Hangs. ~1 in 970 requests (≈16.4 hours) nccl (NCCL 2.30.7, -DGGML_CUDA_NCCL=ON) | Hangs. Occurred after 13.8 hours none (butterfly) | Testing in progress

The issue has never occurred with --split-mode layer.

What I've ruled out:

  • Not a hardware fault — Running test-backend-ops on the suspect GPU alone (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<uuid>, no AllReduce path involved) passes 13163/13163. llama-bench run continuously for 25 minutes stays stable at ±0.04 t/s with zero errors.
  • Not PCIe/power management — ASPM disabled (pcie_aspm.policy=performance), persistence mode enabled, PCIe runtime PM control=on, zero AER/correctable errors.
  • Not P2P/IOMMU — GGML_CUDA_P2P is unset, and the chipset does not support P2P.
  • Not request cancellation — The client's cancel arrives 46 seconds after the hang begins. SERVER_TASK_TYPE_CANCEL is handled at the task-queue level; an in-flight llama_decode() cannot be interrupted.
  • Not an environment change — Driver, kernel, and llama.cpp binary have all been unchanged for the weeks preceding onset.
### First Bad Commit Not yet identified (no bisect has been performed). However, ggml/src/ggml-cuda/allreduce.cu is identical between master and my local build. The last commit touching this file is 7f3f843 (2026-05-13). ### Relevant log output During the hang (no Xid; the following repeats indefinitely) slot launch_slot_: id 0 | task 10130 | processing task, is_child = 0 （以降 print_timing も release も出ない） srv stop: cancel task, id_task = 10130 srv stop: cancel task, id_task = 10133 srv stop: cancel task, id_task = 10136 ... (No print_timing or release is printed after this point.) items.title: torch.fx.Tracer.record_stack_traces is broken in torch 2.4.0
items.author: gilfree
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.fx.Tracer` has a `record_stack_traces` member. It does not give the correct stack trace, starting with torch  2.4 RC.

I am not sure it is part of the external API, but it was nice to have. The following is working in 2.3, but broken in 2.4RC


```python
import torch.fx
class M1(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1)
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.linear(x)
class M2(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.m1 = M1()
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.m1(x)
m = M2()
tracer = torch.fx.Tracer()
tracer.record_stack_traces=True
graph = tracer.trace(m)
sym=torch.fx.GraphModule(m,graph)
print(sym.print_readable())
assert 'code: return x + self.linear(x)' in sym.print_readable()
assert 'code: return x + self.m1(x)' in sym.print_readable()
```

It was broken in this PR: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/121449/ where you stopped using the find_user_frame (or an equivalent function) to filter non user stack traces.

Something along these lines can be probably used as a fix:

```python
    def create_proxy(self, kind, target,args, kwargs, name, type_expr = None, proxy_factory_fn = None):
....
     if self.record_stack_traces and not proxy.node.stack_trace:
            proxy.node.stack_trace = _find_user_frame2_4(''.join(CapturedTraceback.extract().format()))


    def _find_user_frame2_4(self, stack_trace):
        stack_trace=stack_trace.split('\n')
        if 'torch/fx/proxy.py' in stack_trace[-3]:
            stack_trace=stack_trace[:-1]
            while len(stack_trace)>2 and '/fx/' in stack_trace[-2]:
                stack_trace=stack_trace[:-2]
        return '\n'.join(stack_trace)
```

Notes:
- I am not sure why you don't see the effect in `torch.export.export`.
- `torch.export.unflatten` looses stack trace for collapsed modules.

items.title: [AMD] CoalesceAsyncCopy produces a layout the direct-to-LDS lowering cannot coalesce when a warp spans more than the fastest shared dimension
items.author: bogdan-petkovic
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

### Describe the bug

`TritonAMDGPUCoalesceAsyncCopy` can rewrite an async copy into a src layout that the direct-to-LDS lowering then rejects on GFX9. It happens when the blocked order and the shared order differ and a warp has more lanes than the fastest shared dimension has elements.

For a swizzled shared encoding the pass distributes the lanes and warps along the shared order and then rebuilds the blocked encoding with the original blocked order (added in #10928). The order of a blocked encoding also decides how the lanes are linearized, so once the lanes span more than one dimension, the first lanes walk along the dimension that is strided in LDS and the writes are no longer coalesced. This only works while all lanes of a warp fall in the fastest shared dimension, like the 64x2 tile in the tests of #10928.

The existing test `async_copy_different_order` in `test/TritonGPU/amd/amd-coalesce-async-copy.mlir` already shows it. Its expected layout, `threadsPerWarp = [32, 2], warpsPerCTA = [1, 4], order = [1, 0]` for an `order = [0, 1]` shared layout, fails the same way when it is lowered.

### Reproducer

Triton main at 20d9d98fead78c2f65e1b3ba5a7881d86a836dad. No GPU needed, this is a compile failure.

`repro.mlir`, a 16x4 f32 copy with 2 warps on gfx950:

```mlir
#blocked = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [16, 4], warpsPerCTA = [2, 1], order = [1, 0]}>
#shared = #ttg.swizzled_shared<{vec = 1, perPhase = 1, maxPhase = 1, order = [0, 1]}>
#smem = #ttg.shared_memory
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas" = 1 : i32, "ttg.num-warps" = 2 : i32, "ttg.target" = "hip:gfx950", "ttg.threads-per-warp" = 64 : i32} {
  tt.func @copy(%input: tensor<16x4x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked> {tt.contiguity = dense<[1, 4]> : tensor<2xi32>, tt.divisibility = dense<[16, 16]> : tensor<2xi32>, tt.constancy = dense<[1, 1]> : tensor<2xi32>},
                %view: !ttg.memdesc<16x4xf32, #shared, #smem, mutable>) {
    %token = ttg.async_copy_global_to_local %input, %view : tensor<16x4x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked> -> <16x4xf32, #shared, #smem, mutable>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

```
triton-opt repro.mlir --tritonamdgpu-coalesce-async-copy=gfx-arch=gfx950 --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx950
```

```
repro.mlir:7:14: error: cannot lower 'ttg.async_copy_global_to_local' to a direct-to-LDS copy: the resulting writes into shared memory are not coalesced for a vectorization of 1 element(s). Adjust the blocked or shared encoding so each warp writes a contiguous range.
```

CoalesceAsyncCopy rewrites the src to `#ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [16, 4], warpsPerCTA = [1, 2], order = [1, 0]}>`. Lanes 1 to 3 then take the next columns, 16 elements apart in LDS. The same tile with `order = [0, 1]` lowers to a single buffer load to LDS:

```
sed 's/warpsPerCTA = \[2, 1\], order = \[1, 0\]/warpsPerCTA = [1, 2], order = [0, 1]/' repro.mlir > shared-order.mlir
triton-opt shared-order.mlir --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx950
```

And the existing test case:

```
awk 'BEGIN{RS="// -----\n"} /async_copy_different_order/' test/TritonGPU/amd/amd-coalesce-async-copy.mlir > different-order.mlir
triton-opt different-order.mlir --tritonamdgpu-coalesce-async-copy=gfx-arch=gfx942 --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx942
```

fails with the same error.

### How we hit it

In rocmlirTriton (https://github.com/ROCm/rocmlirTriton) a non-power-of-two K tile is split into power-of-two segments, so a K tile of 36 has a last segment of 4. For f32 convolutions on gfx950 with an M tile of 16 or 32 the copy of that segment is a 16x4, 32x2 or 16x8 tile, which is exactly this case. Our weekly tuning ran into it on 677 configs. We disabled those tile sizes on gfx950 for now.

In our tree, falling back to the shared order when the rebuilt encoding cannot be lowered fixed all of them and left the code of every config that already compiled unchanged. We did not send that as a PR because it calls `canLoadDirectToLDS` from the pass, and a fix that builds the right layout up front seems preferable. Happy to test any fix.


### Environment details

Triton main at 20d9d98fead78c2f65e1b3ba5a7881d86a836dad, built from source with CMake (TritonRelBuildWithAsserts, nvidia and amd backends, only the triton-opt target) against the prebuilt LLVM from cmake/llvm-info.json (b010a18d2b648cab83c83967ff26b8fde11acdc6). Ubuntu 22.04.5 on x86_64, GCC 11.4.

No GPU is needed, this is a compile failure in triton-opt and the target comes from gfx-arch (gfx950 for the reproducer, gfx942 for the existing test case). We first hit it compiling f32 convolutions for gfx950 in rocmlirTriton, whose vendored Triton has the same CoalesceAsyncCopy code.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Picking this up. I read the pass and the mechanism checks out: the swizzled branch distributes lanes along the shared order and then stamps the original blocked order back on, which re-linearizes the lanes. Once a warp spans more than the fastest shared dimension, consecutive lanes walk a dim that is strided in LDS, and the rewritten copy is exactly what the direct-to-LDS lowering rejects.

Fix I am testing: after building the blocked-order candidate, check it with canLoadDirectToLDS (the same predicate the lowering uses, already called from this pass) and keep the shared-order distribution when the candidate would not lower. That matches what you validated in rocmlirTriton, and leaves every config whose rewritten layout already lowers byte-identical. Will add lit coverage for both the pass output and the end-to-end lowering of your 16x4 repro.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body: PR up: #12159. The pass now checks the re-stamped encoding with `canLoadDirectToLDS` and keeps the shared-order distribution when the src order cannot lower. Your 16x4 reproducer lowers cleanly with it, and `async_copy_different_order` turned out to have the same latent problem, its expected layout changes to the shared order as well.

items.title: [Performance]: Beam search re-materializes Result.output_token_ids from pybind once per beam
items.author: yifanQi98
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

#### Background

For beam-search requests, `GenerationResultBase._handle_response` iterates over beams and calls `_handle_sequence` once per beam:

```python
finish_reasons = response_result.finish_reasons
# output_token_ids = (beams, tokens)
if self.sampling_params.use_beam_search:
    for beam_idx, _ in enumerate(response_result.output_token_ids):   # result.py:692
        self._handle_sequence(finish_reasons, response_result,
                              beam_idx, logprobs_result,
                              req_perf_metrics_dict)
```

`_handle_sequence` then reads the same property again, once per call:

```python
if self.sampling_params.use_beam_search:
    output.token_ids = [
        *decoder_output_prefix,
        *response_tensors.output_token_ids[src_idx],      # result.py:402
    ]
else:
    ...
    output.token_ids.extend(response_tensors.output_token_ids[src_idx])   # result.py:407
```

`LlmResult.output_token_ids` is not in `LlmResult.py_result_properties`, so `LlmResult.__getattr__` falls through to `getattr(self._result, item)` on the **pybind** `bindings.executor.Result`. That property returns a freshly built nested Python list on every access — it is not cached on either side:

```python
>>> a, b = llm_result.output_token_ids, llm_result.output_token_ids
>>> a is b
False
>>> a[0] is b[0]
False
>>> a == b
True
```

So for a request with `N` beams, one response converts the full `(N, tokens)` structure from C++ **N + 1 times** when once is sufficient. Because the per-conversion cost is itself O(N · tokens), the redundant work is **quadratic in beam width**.

This is the dominant host-side cost for the "short decode length, very wide beams" pattern (e.g. SID / generative-recommendation serving with `n = best_of = 500`, `max_tokens = 3`), where `_handle_sequence` does almost no work per beam other than these reads.

#### Measurement

Offline, no GPU, no model, no executor. A real `bindings.executor.Result` is constructed and populated (`output_token_ids` is settable), wrapped in a real `LlmResult`, and the **real** `GenerationResultBase._handle_sequence` is driven once per beam exactly as `_handle_response` does.

Three arms, interleaved, `gc.collect()` before every sample, median of 25:

- **A stock** — real `_handle_sequence` against the real `LlmResult`
- **C patched** — the same real source, textually rewritten so `response_tensors.output_token_ids` resolves to a binding materialized **once per response** (i.e. exactly the suggested fix below); every other attribute still reads the real `LlmResult` per beam, so this arm does not overstate the win
- **B snapshot** — every attribute pre-materialized; an upper bound

Access counts were obtained by running the real code path against a counting forwarder, not by reading the source by hand. For one 500-beam response:

| attribute | reads | served by |
|---|---|---|
| `time_breakdown_metrics` | 1000 | instance attr (cheap) |
| `output_token_ids` | **500** | **pybind** |
| `request_perf_metrics` | **500** | **pybind** |
| `cum_log_probs` / `log_probs` / `generation_logits` / `additional_*_outputs` | 500 each | `py_result` (Python-side) |
| `finish_reasons` | 1 | pybind |

Total 4501 attribute reads per response, 1001 of them pybind-served.

##### Results (ms per response, `tokens = 3`)

| beams | one pybind read | A stock | C patched | C saving | B upper bound | B saving |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 0.53 µs | 0.122 | 0.120 | −0.002 (1.6%) | 0.097 | −0.025 (20.5%) |
| 20 | 1.25 µs | 0.195 | 0.187 | −0.008 (4.1%) | 0.127 | −0.068 (34.9%) |
| 100 | 6.25 µs | 1.016 | 0.458 | −0.558 (54.9%) | 0.303 | −0.713 (70.2%) |
| 300 | 16.20 µs | 5.848 | 1.047 | −4.801 (82.1%) | 0.682 | −5.166 (88.3%) |
| **500** | **25.94 µs** | **14.428** | **1.543** | **−12.885 (89.3%)** | 0.985 | −13.443 (93.2%) |

At 500 beams, **89% of the per-response beam loop is redundant pybind re-conversion of one property.** 100 → 500 beams is 5× the width and 23× the waste, confirming the quadratic behaviour.

Below ~20 beams the effect is inside measurement noise (arm C's delta at beam=20 is 0.008 ms against a per-sample sd of 0.03–0.04 ms), so this is specifically a wide-beam problem.

##### Cross-check

Two independent estimates of the same quantity agree:

- micro: 500 reads × 25.94 µs = **12.97 ms**
- macro: arm A − arm C = **12.89 ms**
- ratio **0.99**

The residual between arm C and arm B (0.558 ms at 500 beams) is accounted for by the other 501 pybind reads (`request_perf_metrics` ×500 at ≈1.1 µs, `finish_reasons` ×1).

##### Correctness

Arms A, B and C produce **identical** `token_ids`, `cumulative_logprob`, `finish_reason` and `logprobs` for all 500 outputs, verified at every beam width in the sweep.

##### Version note

Measured against **1.3.0rc29**; the full environment is in the last section below. The
structure on `main` is identical for these reads (`_handle_sequence` at `result.py:369`,
the two `output_token_ids` reads at `:402`/`:407`, the beam loop at `:692`), so the
analysis and the suggested fix carry over unchanged. `main` does add three further per-beam
`getattr` calls; quantified under *Misc discussion* below.

#### Suggested fix

Materialize once per response and pass it down. Backward compatible: the parameter defaults to `None`, which preserves the current behaviour for every other call site.

```diff
--- a/tensorrt_llm/executor/result.py
+++ b/tensorrt_llm/executor/result.py
@@ -372,10 +372,19 @@
                          sequence_index,
                          logprobs_result=None,
                          req_perf_metrics_dict: Optional[dict[str,
-                                                              float]] = None):
-        """Handle a single sequence in the response."""
+                                                              float]] = None,
+                         output_token_ids=None):
+        """Handle a single sequence in the response.
+
+        ``output_to

items.title: numeric_limits constants wrong for float_ue8m0_t::lowest, tfloat32_t::epsilon and half_t::epsilon
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Three `numeric_limits` members return values inconsistent with the types' own encodings. Each was checked by compiling against include/ only and printing the results.

#### 1. `float_ue8m0_t::lowest()` returns the maximum magnitude

`include/cutlass/float8.h` lines ~1482 and ~1638 (std and platform specializations):

```cpp
static cutlass::float_ue8m0_t lowest() { return cutlass::float_ue8m0_t::bitcast(0xfe); }
```

`0xfe` is exponent 254, i.e. +2^127 - the same value as `max()`. For this unsigned format the smallest finite value is `bitcast(0x00)` = 2^-127 (`BitRepresentation::MIN_VALUE == 0`). This looks like a copy of the signed e4m3 constant into a signless type.

```
ue8m0 lowest=1.70141e+38 min=1.17549e-38 max=1.70141e+38 ; lowest<=min -> VIOLATED
```

Any code seeding a min-reduction or clamping with `lowest()` starts from +2^127 instead of 2^-127; `ue8m0` is the MX block-scale type, so scale-selection code is exposed.

Fix: `bitcast(0x00)` in both specializations (or derive from `BitRepresentation::MIN_VALUE`). Related but distinct from the FP6 `lowest()` report (#3493), which covers `float_subbyte.h`.

#### 2. `tfloat32_t::epsilon()` is a subnormal garbage constant

`include/cutlass/tfloat32.h` line ~312:

```cpp
static cutlass::tfloat32_t epsilon() { return cutlass::tfloat32_t::bitcast(0x1000); }
```

`0x00001000` decodes to a denormal (~1.4e-41). TF32 has 10 mantissa bits, so machine epsilon is 2^-10 (fp32 bits `0x3A800000`). The comment above it even says "smallest finite value", which suggests the member's intent drifted.

```
tf32 epsilon=0 bits=00001000 ; expected 2^-10 ~ 0.000976562
```

Fix: `bitcast(0x3A800000)`.

#### 3. `half_t::epsilon()` is off by 2x

`include/cutlass/half.h` lines ~618 and ~686 (both specializations):

```cpp
static cutlass::half_t epsilon() { return cutlass::half_t::bitcast(0x1800); }
```

`0x1800` = 2^-9. fp16 declares `digits == 10`, so machine epsilon should be 2^-10 = `0x1400`. The sibling `bfloat16_t` is internally consistent (digits 7, eps 2^-7):

```
half epsilon=0.00195312 (expected 2^-10 = 0.0009765625) ; bf16 epsilon=0.0078125 (correct)
```

Fix: `bitcast(0x1400)` in both places.
score_reasons: 匹配 Kernel 与正确性

items.title: zipped/tiled divide with a dynamic tiler skips divisibility checks on static layouts and returns a non-size-preserving layout
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

When a zipped/tiled divide receives a *dynamic* tiler against a *fully static* layout, the divisibility requirement is checked nowhere, and the result is a silently non-size-preserving layout.

```cpp
#include "cute/layout.hpp"
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    using namespace cute;
    auto L = make_layout(make_shape(_12{}, make_shape(_4{}, _8{})),
                         make_stride(_7{}, make_stride(_1{}, C<30>{})));
    auto d = zipped_divide(L, 128);   // 128 does not divide size(L) == 384
    print(d);
    print(" size="); print(size(d));   // 288
}
```

Actual output:

```
((12,4,2),(1,1,3)):((_7,_1,_30),(896,11,90))
 size=288
```

`size(d) == 288 != size(L) == 384`, strides run past the layout's cosize (896), and no diagnostic of any kind fires. Each individual configuration is handled correctly on its own:

- fully static tiler: compile-time `static_assert` fires ("Shape Divisibility Condition"),
- fully dynamic operands: the runtime assert catches it,
- mixed static layout / dynamic tiler: the static path's runtime check is compiled out (the shapes are static, so the dynamic assert sees nothing to test) and the static check cannot see the dynamic tiler, so every guard is skipped.

The Python port asserts on the same input, which highlights the gap when cross-checking.

### Suggested fix

In the mixed case, emit a runtime divisibility check (or a `CUTE_GCC_UNREACHABLE`-style guarded assert) comparing the dynamic tiler size against the known static layout size before performing the division, so misuses fail loudly instead of producing layouts whose size differs from the input.

items.title: EllGemm ColumnMajor-output workspace sizing uses the unswapped problem shape and undersizes split-K semaphores
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`device::EllGemm` computes its split-K semaphore workspace size from an unswapped problem shape, while `initialize()` builds the launch grid from the swapped one, so for rectangular problems on ColumnMajor outputs the workspace is sized for a different grid than the one that runs.

```cpp
// include/cutlass/gemm/device/ell_gemm.h:747-753  (get_workspace_size)
cutlass::gemm::GemmCoord tiled_shape = threadblock_swizzle.get_tiled_shape(
  args.problem_size,                       // (m, n, k)
  {ThreadblockShape::kM, args.ell_blocksize, ThreadblockShape::kK},
  args.split_k_slices);
...
bytes += sizeof(int) * size_t(tiled_shape.m()) * size_t(tiled_shape.n());

// include/cutlass/gemm/device/ell_gemm.h:768-773  (initialize)
cutlass::gemm::GemmCoord grid_shape = threadblock_swizzle.get_tiled_shape(
  {args.problem_size.n(), args.problem_size.m(), args.problem_size.k()},   // transposed
  {ThreadblockShape::kM, args.ell_blocksize, ThreadblockShape::kK},
  args.split_k_slices);
```

The transpose is intentional at the launch site (the kernel consumes the swapped convention), but the sizing call must match it. Arithmetic example with `ThreadblockShape = 128x128x32`, `split_k_slices = 4`, `m = 264`, `n = 136`: sizing yields `tiled_shape.m() * n() = 15 * 2 = 30` semaphores (120 bytes after the ell-block N scaling), while the launched grid is built from `(136, 264)` and needs `18` tiles along one axis instead of `15`, i.e. more semaphore slots than were allocated and zeroed. The reverse aspect ratio over-allocates harmlessly; the bad direction gives an undersized, partially uninitialized semaphore buffer feeding split-K accumulation.

The RowMajor-output specialization does not swap and is consistent.

### Suggested fix

Pass the same swapped problem shape to `get_tiled_shape` inside `get_workspace_size`:

```cpp
threadblock_swizzle.get_tiled_shape(
  {args.problem_size.n(), args.problem_size.m(), args.problem_size.k()}, ...)
```

items.title: [BUG] Constexpr missing in dynamic control-flow regions
items.author: nodeeeeee
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

## Motivation

I encountered this while implementing FlashAttention. The implementation naturally groups the load and MMA paths into JIT methods on a compile-time configuration object, and selects between them using the runtime warp index. A reduced version looks like this:

```python
class FlashAttention:
    @cute.jit
    def load(self, tensor, pipeline):
        ...

    @cute.jit
    def mma(self, tensor, pipeline):
        ...


@cute.jit
def fa4_device_body(
    fa: cutlass.Constexpr[FlashAttention],
    tensor: cute.Tensor,
    storage,
):
    warp_idx = cute.arch.make_warp_uniform(cute.arch.warp_idx())

    pipeline = make_pipeline(
        storage=storage,
        num_stages=fa.num_stages,
    )

    if warp_idx < 4:
        cute.arch.setmaxregister_decrease(fa.num_producer_regs)
        fa.load(tensor, pipeline)
    else:
        cute.arch.setmaxregister_increase(fa.num_mma_regs)
        fa.mma(tensor, pipeline)
```

Here, `self` in `FlashAttention.load()` and `FlashAttention.mma()` is a compile-time method receiver. The `fa` parameter in `fa4_device_body()` refers to the same kind of compile-time object, made explicit by its `Constexpr` annotation.

Writing the device body as an actual instance method makes this code compile, but only because the compiler has a special case that excludes a receiver whose name is literally `self`. Passing the same object as a named `Constexpr[FlashAttention]` parameter should have equivalent staging semantics, but currently does not.

## Problem

CuTe DSL treats `Constexpr[T]` parameters as compile-time Python meta values. They do not have an MLIR representation and must not become arguments or results of runtime control-flow regions.

However, when a method is called through a `Constexpr` receiver inside a dynamic `if`, the receiver is incorrectly captured as a region argument:

```python
class Receiver:
    @cute.jit
    def store(self, output):
        ...


@cute.kernel
def kernel(receiver: cutlass.Constexpr[Receiver], output: cute.Tensor):
    tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()

    if tidx == Int32(0):
        receiver.store(output)
```

The region analyzer currently treats the base object of every method call as a mutable runtime value, except when its name is literally `self`.

Consequently, `receiver` is added to the values carried through the dynamic `if`. Lowering then attempts to flatten the plain Python `Receiver` instance into MLIR values and fails with:

```text
error[TYPE_DYNAMIC_EXPR_UNSUPPORTED]:
A value carried through this `if` is a plain Python value (Meta value)
(a `Receiver`) that cannot be turned into a Runtime value (Staged value)
```

This means `self.method()` works because of the existing `self` special case, while an explicitly annotated `receiver: Constexpr[Receiver]` does not, despite having the same staging semantics.

## Root cause

`Constexpr` is a property of the original function parameter binding. The AST preprocessor removes parameter annotations while transforming the function, so the later control-flow region analysis no longer knows which names refer to `Constexpr` parameters.

`RegionAnalyzer.visit_Call()` therefore sees only a method call on a Python object and adds its receiver to `invoked_args`.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL 4.7/4.8 regression: FlashAttention-4 SM100 forward kernel spills registers (0 -> 176 B) vs 4.5.1, ~3% slower on B300
items.author: zpcore
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

With identical kernel source, CuTe DSL 4.7.x/4.8.0 generates PTX for the FlashAttention-4 SM100 forward kernel (`flash_attn.cute.flash_fwd_sm100.FlashAttentionForwardSm100`) that spills registers, where CuTe DSL 4.5.1 generated PTX that does not. The kernel is at the 128-register cap in both cases (512 threads per CTA), so the extra pressure becomes local-memory spills. The varlen causal fwd+bwd step is about 2–3% slower on B300.

The regression is in the generated PTX, not in ptxas: the 4.8.0 PTX still spills when assembled with the older ptxas 13.2, while the 4.5.1 PTX assembled with that same ptxas does not.

**Resource usage, same FA4 source (`fa4-v4.0.0.beta16`), same quack-kernels 0.4.1, sm_103a**

| Kernel | CuTe DSL 4.5.1 | CuTe DSL 4.8.0 |
|---|---|---|
| `FlashAttentionForwardSm100` | 128 regs, 0 B stack, 0 spill stores/loads, 5272 SASS instr | 128 regs, **112 B stack, 176 B spill stores / 176 B spill loads** (44 STL / 33 LDL), 5768 SASS instr |
| `FlashAttentionBackwardSm100` | 128 regs, 8 B stack, 1 STL / 5 LDL | 128 regs, 24 B stack, 24 B spill stores / 60 B spill loads (4 STL / 13 LDL) |

MMA (`UTCHMMA`/`UTCQMMA`), `MUFU`, and packed FP32 (`FFMA2`/`FMUL2`/`FADD2`) instruction counts in the forward kernel are identical between the two versions, so the difference is spill traffic rather than different math.

**PTX vs ptxas cross-check (forward kernel PTX from `CUTE_DSL_KEEP=ptx`)**

| PTX from | assembled with | Result |
|---|---|---|
| CuTe DSL 4.5.1 (PTX ISA 9.1) | ptxas 13.1 and 13.2 | 0 B stack, 0 B spills |
| CuTe DSL 4.8.0 (PTX ISA 9.4, `.version` lowered to 9.2) | ptxas 13.2 | 112 B stack, 176 B spill stores / 176 B spill loads |

Neither PTX contains `.local` declarations, so the spills are introduced by ptxas from register pressure in the 4.8.0 PTX.

`CUTE_DSL_COMPILER_OPT="remarks{ptx}"` with `CUTE_DSL_LINEINFO=1` on 4.8.0 reports the spills for both forward and backward, and marks `flash_attn/cute/tile_scheduler.py:923` (the varlen scheduler's `_get_num_m_blocks`, loading `cu_seqlens`) as the likely pressure region.

**Timing (B300, varlen causal, bf16, head_dim 128, fwd+bwd, median of 20 steps after 3 warmups, runs interleaved on one GPU)**

| Shape | CuTe DSL 4.5.1 | CuTe DSL 4.8.0 |
|---|---|---|
| 8192 tokens × 32 heads, 4 docs | 1.206–1.245 ms | 1.222–1.234 ms |
| 32768 tokens × 32 heads, 8 docs | 5.300–5.329 ms | 5.486–5.488 ms (+3%) |
| 32768 tokens × 16 heads, 1 doc | 12.35–12.38 ms | 12.71–12.84 ms (+3%) |

CuTe DSL 4.7.0 and 4.7.1 (measured with quack-kernels 0.6.5) show the same slowdown as 4.8.0. The current FA4 release (`fa4-v4.0.0.beta32`) with quack-kernels 0.6.5 on CuTe DSL 4.8.0 is within noise of beta16 on 4.8.0, so the difference tracks the DSL version, not the FA4 or quack version. I could not test 4.5.3 or 4.6.x with this FA4 source (import errors unrelated to the kernel), so the regression landed after 4.5.1 and by 4.7.0.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

1. Environment: NVIDIA B300 SXM6 (sm_103a), driver 590.48.01, PyTorch 2.11 (CUDA 13.0), Python 3.12.
2. FA4 source: `Dao-AILab/flash-attention` at tag `fa4-v4.0.0.beta16`, installed with `pip install --no-deps --no-build-isolation flash_attn/cute`.
3. Install `quack-kernels==0.4.1` (`--no-deps`) and one of:
   - `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.5.1` with `nvidia-cutlass-dsl-libs-cu13==4.5.1` (apache-tvm-ffi 0.1.6)
   - `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.8.0` with `nvidia-cutlass-dsl-libs-cu13==4.8.0` (apache-tvm-ffi 0.1.11)
4. Run the script below with `CUTE_DSL_KEEP=ptx,cubin CUTE_DSL_DUMP_DIR=<dir>`, then `cuobjdump --dump-resource-usage <dir>/*flash_fwd_sm100*.cubin`.

quack-kernels 0.4.1 annotates with `cute.core.ThrMma`/`ThrCopy`, which 4.8.0 exposes only on `cute`; the script aliases them so the same quack source imports on both DSL versions.

```python
import importlib.metadata as md
import json
import sys

import torch
import cutlass.cute as cute

for _name in ("ThrMma", "ThrCopy", "TiledMma", "TiledCopy"):
    if not hasattr(cute.core, _name) and hasattr(cute, _name):
        setattr(cute.core, _name, getattr(cute, _name))

from flash_attn.cute.interface import flash_attn_varlen_func


def bench(total, heads, head_dim, docs):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    q, k, v = (
        torch.randn(total, heads, head_dim, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16, requires_grad=True) for _ in range(3)
    )
    cu = torch.linspace(0, total, docs + 1, device="cuda").round().to(torch.int32)
    max_seqlen = int((cu[1:] - cu[:-1]).max())

    def step():
        out = flash_attn_varlen_func(
            q, k, v, cu_seqlens_q=cu, cu_seqlens_k=cu, max_seqlen_q=max_seqlen, max_seqlen_k=max_seqlen, causal=True
        )
        out = out[0] if isinstance(out, tuple) else out
        out.float().square().mean().backward()

    for _ in range(3):
        step()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    times = []
    for _ in range(20):
        start, end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        start.record()
        step()
        end.record()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        times.append(start.elapsed_time(end))
    return round(sorted(times)[10], 3)


shapes = [(8192, 32, 128, 4), (32768, 32, 128, 8), (32768, 16, 128, 1)]
print(json.dumps({
    "cutlass_dsl": md.version("nvidia-cutlass-dsl"),
    "gpu": torch.cuda.get_device_name(),
    "median_ms": {f"{t}x{h}h_d{d}_{n}docs": bench(t, h, d, n) for t, h, d, n in shapes},
}))
```

**Expected behavior**

CuTe DSL 4.8.0 generates PTX for this unchanged kernel source with register pressure comparable to 4.5.1, so the forward kernel does not spill and runs at 4.5.1 speed. If this is a deliberate lowering change, guidance on a compile option or kernel-side change that avoids the spill would help.

**Environment details**

- GPU: NVIDIA B300 SXM6 (sm_103a), driver 590.48.01
- CuTe DSL: 4.5.1 (good), 4.7.0 / 4.7.1 / 4.8.0 (spills), CUDA 13 libs
- ptxas used in the cross-check: 13.1, 13.2
- PyTorch 2.11, CUDA 13.0, Python 3.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL from_dlpack rejects float8_e4m3fn tensors (dtype_map lists Float8E5M2 only)
items.author: Vinnie6167
items.body_excerpt:
## Describe the bug

`cutlass.cute.runtime.from_dlpack` rejects `torch.float8_e4m3fn` tensors:

```
KeyError: Unsupported element type in dlpack: 'Float8E4M3FN'. Supported types are:
['Bool', 'Int64', 'Int32', 'Int16', 'Int8', 'UInt64', 'UInt32', 'UInt16', 'UInt8',
 'Float64', 'Float32', 'Float16', 'BFloat16', 'Float8E5M2']
```

The runtime already decodes the DLPack type code and reports the element type as
`Float8E4M3FN` (the string comes out of `libcute_dsl_runtime.so`, which also knows
`Float8E4M3`, `Float8E4M3FNUZ`, `Float8E8M0FNU`, `Float4E2M1FN`, ...). Only the Python
lookup table in `TensorDescriptor.element_type` /
`python/CuTeDSL/cutlass/base_dsl/runtime/tensor_descriptor.py` stops at `Float8E5M2`, so
every other 8-bit float that the runtime recognizes is rejected at import time even though
`cutlass.Float8E4M3FN` is a fully supported kernel element type.

PyTorch is not the limiting side: `torch.empty(8, dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn).__dlpack__()`
succeeds on torch 2.11 and the capsule round-trips through `torch.from_dlpack`.

## Steps/Code to reproduce bug

```python
import torch
from cutlass.cute.runtime import from_dlpack

x = torch.empty(8, dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, device="cuda")
t = from_dlpack(x, assumed_align=16)   # KeyError: Unsupported element type in dlpack: 'Float8E4M3FN'
```

## Expected behavior

`from_dlpack` returns a `cute.Tensor` with `element_type == cutlass.Float8E4M3FN`, the same
way it does for `torch.float8_e5m2`.

## Workaround in use

Callers currently export the storage as `uint8`/`int8` and overwrite `element_type`
afterwards, e.g. FlashInfer does this in `flashinfer/gemm/kernels/bmm_fp8_blackwell.py`,
`flashinfer/attention/cute_dsl/fmha.py`, and pending PR flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5533:

```python
t = from_dlpack(x.view(torch.uint8), assumed_align=16)
t.element_type = cutlass.Float8E4M3FN
```

Adding the missing names to the `dtype_map` (at least `Float8E4M3FN`; ideally the other
strings the runtime emits) would let these call sites drop the reinterpretation.

## Environment details

- nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0 (`nvidia_cutlass_dsl_libs_cu13-4.8.0`), and `main` as of 2026-10-07
- torch 2.11.0+cu130
- Linux x86_64, CUDA 13.0

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL: SIGSEGV compiling integer ** (int32/int64), including 2 ** 3
items.author: JayceSu98
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

Compiling a CUDA kernel containing `x ** y`, where both operands are loaded
from integer CUDA Tensors, terminates the Python process with SIGSEGV (exit
status 139) inside `cute.compile()`.

The reproducer uses only small positive inputs: `x = 2`, `y = 3`, with expected
output `8`. It does not involve zero bases, negative exponents, overflow, or
Python-valued constant evaluation. Compilation does not return, and the kernel
is not launched.

This reproduces for both `int32` and `int64` with native NVIDIA CuTeDSL wheels:

- **4.5.2**;
- **4.8.0 (final release, cu12)**;
- **4.8.0.dev0 (cu12)**, tested separately before checking the final release.

For 4.8.0 final, the frontend and compiler were freshly installed into an
isolated target from matching 4.8.0 wheels. No source changes or custom compiler
forks were used.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

Save this as `minimal_integer_pow.py` in an environment with native NVIDIA
CuTeDSL and CUDA-enabled PyTorch:

```python
import argparse

import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute
import torch
from cutlass.cute.runtime import from_dlpack


@cute.kernel
def pow_kernel(a: cute.Tensor, b: cute.Tensor, out: cute.Tensor):
    i, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
    x = a[i]
    y = b[i]
    out[i] = x ** y


@cute.jit
def launch(a: cute.Tensor, b: cute.Tensor, out: cute.Tensor):
    pow_kernel(a, b, out).launch(grid=(1, 1, 1), block=(128, 1, 1))


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--dtype", choices=("int32", "int64"), default="int32")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    print("CuTeDSL", cutlass.__version__, flush=True)
    print("PyTorch", torch.__version__, "CUDA runtime", torch.version.cuda,
          flush=True)
    print("GPU", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0), flush=True)
    print("dtype", args.dtype, "runtime inputs: a=2, b=3", flush=True)
    dtype = getattr(torch, args.dtype)
    a = torch.full((128,), 2, dtype=dtype, device="cuda")
    b = torch.full((128,), 3, dtype=dtype, device="cuda")
    out = torch.full_like(a, -123)
    handles = [from_dlpack(t, assumed_align=16) for t in (a, b, out)]
    print("COMPILE_BEGIN", flush=True)
    compiled = cute.compile(launch, *handles)
    print("COMPILE_OK", flush=True)
    compiled(*handles)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    result = out.cpu()
    assert torch.equal(result, torch.full_like(result, 8)), result
    print("PASS: synchronized output = 8", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Run each dtype in a separate process:

```bash
python minimal_integer_pow.py --dtype int32
echo "exit=$?"
python minimal_integer_pow.py --dtype int64
echo "exit=$?"
```

Observed with 4.8.0 final:

```text
CuTeDSL 4.8.0
PyTorch 2.7.0+cu128 CUDA runtime 12.8
GPU NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB
dtype int32 runtime inputs: a=2, b=3
COMPILE_BEGIN
PROCESS_EXIT_STATUS 139
```

`COMPILE_OK` is never reached. The shell reports `Segmentation fault`.
The int64 case also exits with status 139 during compilation.
4.5.2 additionally prints `!!!!!!! Segfault encountered !!!!!!!`.

**Expected behavior**

The kernel should compile and produce `8` for all elements. If runtime integer
exponentiation is not supported by this compilation path, an explicit compiler
diagnostic would be preferable to a process-level crash.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**

- Environment location: Docker, Linux x86_64.
- GPU: NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB (SM80).
- Python: 3.10.
- PyTorch: 2.7.0+cu128; PyTorch CUDA runtime: 12.8.
- CUDA Toolkit: 12.9.
- NVIDIA driver: 610.43.02.
- CuTeDSL: 4.5.2; 4.8.0 final with `nvidia-cutlass-dsl`, `libs-base`,
  `libs-core`, and `libs-cu12` all at 4.8.0; separately 4.8.0.dev0 cu12.
- Reproduced with file caching disabled (`CUTE_DSL_ENABLE_FILE_CACHING=0`).
- The reproducer compiles an `@cute.jit` launcher, not a bare `@cute.kernel`.

The container originally had older user-space driver libraries. Matching host
driver libraries were selected for these test processes without replacing the
system installation. The CUDA execution controls below successfully compiled,
launched, synchronized, and checked device output with that same setup.

**Additional context**

Control cases use the same Tensor-loaded inputs `2` and `3`, the same
128-thread block, and the same DLPack/compilation bridge. Successful cases
synchronize the device and check every output, rather than only compiling.

| Expression | 4.5.2 int32 / int64 | 4.8.0 final cu12 int32 / int64 |
|---|---|---|
| `x ** y` | Both SIGSEGV during compilation | Both SIGSEGV during compilation |
| `x + y`, `x * y`, `x // y`, `x % y` | Both pass | Both pass |
| `x - y`, `x / y`, `-x`, `abs(x)` | Both pass | Not tested |
| `cutlass.min`, `cutlass.max`, `==`, `<` | Both pass | Not tested |
| `&`, `\|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>` | Both pass | Not tested |
| float32 `x ** y` | Pass, output 8 | Pass, output 8 |

Integer true division controls use float32 output. These are bounded controls,
not exhaustive coverage of all scalar operations or input domains.

The 4.5.2 pre-lowering IR contains `math.ipowi` on the loaded integer values.
An earlier GDB run stops inside the native NVIDIA `_cutlass_ir.so`, but does
not provide useful symbols. We have not identified a specific internal pass
root cause or established that every affected version has the same root cause.

We found the older floating-point power discussion #2296, but it concerns
`v ** 1.3`, increased compilation time, and a suspected runtime hang, rather
than this positive-integer compilation SIGSEGV. We could not find a matching
public issue or a documented fix for this integer-power reproducer.

Could you help clarify whether Tensor-loaded integer `**` is intended to be
supported, and whether this crash matches a known issue or existing fix?

items.title: [Feature request] `torch.export` .save/.load could support `safetensors` and/or `weights_only=True`
items.author: stu-twelvelabs
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Today, torch.export will load tensors via
```
def deserialize_torch_artifact(serialized: Union[Dict[str, Any], Tuple[Any, ...], bytes]):
    if isinstance(serialized, (dict, tuple)):
        return serialized
    if len(serialized) == 0:
        return {}
    buffer = io.BytesIO(serialized)
    buffer.seek(0)
    # weights_only=False as we want to load custom objects here (e.g. ScriptObject)
    artifact = torch.load(buffer, weights_only=False)
    assert isinstance(artifact, (tuple, dict))
    return artifact
```
Security teams really don't like this I have learned 🙂. In the interest of leveraging the awesome benefits of export more safely, it would be amazing to add optional support for any or all of `safetensors` and/or `weights_only=True`!

Thank you for all the work on `torch.export`, it has a very promising future!

### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

cc @chauhang @penguinwu @avikchaudhuri @gmagogsfm @zhxchen17 @tugsbayasgalan @angelayi @suo @ydwu4

comments.author: unbiasedcodex
comments.body:
I've opened PR #171653 that hardens the existing implementation from #158247.

The problem: The current code falls back to weights_only=False for any exception, which still allows arbitrary code execution.

The fix: My PR restricts the fallback to only known safe PyTorch internal types (ScriptObject), rejecting unknown classes instead of loading them.

Changes:
  - Added whitelist of safe fallback patterns
  - Modified deserialize_torch_artifact() and related functions in _package.py
  - Added test to verify unknown classes are rejected

Known limitation: The current approach uses string matching on error messages to identify safe types. If error message formats change in the future, this could break. I consider this a minor refinement rather than a critical flaw, but if the team prefers a more robust approach (e.g., catching specific exception types or inspecting the class directly), I'm happy to improve it.

This builds on the existing work rather than replacing it. Would appreciate a review!

comments.author: AbhijatSaxena
comments.body:
Hi, a question about how this relates to [CVE-2026-4538](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-4538) ("deserialization in the pt2 Loading Handler", listed against 2.10.0). Scanners now flag torch 2.14.1 for it with no fixed version. The only PyTorch reference on the NVD record is #176791, which added a `weights_only` flag to `torch.export.load` and was closed by its author a week before the CVE was published, so this issue seems to be the closest place to ask.

On current main, `deserialize_torch_artifact` tries `weights_only=True` and falls back to `weights_only=False` ([serialize.py#L446-L458](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e342e9a9d7123c2b78940da0ea3fdb0dfa9beeb0/torch/_export/serde/serialize.py#L446-L458)). Pickled weights/constants are loaded with `weights_only=False` ([_package.py#L889-L895](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e342e9a9d7123c2b78940da0ea3fdb0dfa9beeb0/torch/export/pt2_archive/_package.py#L889-L895), [L947-L953](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e342e9a9d7123c2b78940da0ea3fdb0dfa9beeb0/torch/export/pt2_archive/_package.py#L947-L953)), and custom/opaque objects go through `_pickle_load_obj` / `pickle.loads` ([L970-L980](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e342e9a9d7123c2b78940da0ea3fdb0dfa9beeb0/torch/export/pt2_archive/_package.py#L970-L980)). The `torch.export.load` docstring already says "uses pickle under the hood ... Never load data from an untrusted source" ([__init__.py#L350-L351](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e342e9a9d7123c2b78940da0ea3fdb0dfa9beeb0/torch/export/__init__.py#L350-L351)), and that warning is in 2.14.1 too.

So two questions, mainly so advisory databases can be told something definite:

1. Is that docstring warning the official position, i.e. loading `.pt2` from untrusted sources isn't supported and CVE-2026-4538 is expected behaviour rather than a bug?
2. Or is the plan to provide an opt-in safe path, along the lines of #199042 (currently open, superseding #191149), with the default flipped later as was done for `torch.load`?

Either answer would help. Thanks!

items.title: [v.2.15.0] Release Tracker
items.author: atalman
items.body_excerpt:
We cut a [release branch](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/release/2.15) for the 2.15.0 release.

Our plan from this point is roughly:

* Phase 1 (until 19/10/26): work on finalizing the release branch
* Phase 2 (after 19/10/26): perform extended integration/stability/performance testing based on Release Candidate builds.

This issue is for tracking cherry-picks to the release branch.

## Release dates

* M3: Release branch cut (week of 5/10/26)
* M4: Release branch finalized, Announce final launch date, Feature classifications published (week of 19/10/26) - Final RC is produced.
* M4.1: Tutorial drafts submission deadline (23/10/26)
* M5: External-Facing Content Finalized (27/10/26)
* M6: Release Day (28/10/26)

## Cherry-Pick Criteria

**Phase 1 (until 19/10/26):**

Only low-risk changes may be cherry-picked from main:

1. Fixes to regressions against the most recent minor release (e.g. 2.14.x for this release; see [module: regression issue list](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22module%3A+regression%22+))
2. Critical fixes for: [silent correctness](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+correctness+%28silent%29%22), [backwards compatibility](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+bc-breaking%22+), [crashes](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+crash%22+), [deadlocks](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+deadlock%22+), (large) [memory leaks](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+memory+usage%22+)
3. Critical fixes to new features introduced in the most recent minor release (e.g. 2.14.x for this release)
4. Test/CI fixes
5. Documentation improvements
6. Compilation fixes or ifdefs required for different versions of the compilers or third-party libraries
7. Release branch specific changes (e.g. change version identifiers)

Any other change requires special dispensation from the release managers (currently @atalman, @huydhn, @albanD). If this applies to your change please write "Special Dispensation" in the "Criteria Category:" template below and explain.

**Phase 2 (after 19/10/26):**

Note that changes here require us to rebuild a Release Candidate and restart extended testing (likely delaying the release). Therefore, the only accepted changes are **Release-blocking** critical fixes for: [silent correctness](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+correctness+%28silent%29%22), [backwards compatibility](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+bc-breaking%22+), [crashes](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+crash%22+), [deadlocks](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+deadlock%22+), (large) [memory leaks](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+memory+usage%22+)

Changes will likely require a discussion with the larger release team over VC or Slack.

## Cherry-Pick Process

1. Ensure your PR has landed in master. This does not apply for release-branch specific changes (see Phase 1 criteria).
2. Create (but do not land) a PR against the [release branch](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/release/2.15).
   <details>

    ```bash
    # Find the hash of the commit you want to cherry pick
    # (for example, abcdef12345)
    git log

    git fetch origin release/2.15
    git checkout release/2.15
    git cherry-pick -x abcdef12345

    # Submit a PR based against 'release/2.15' either:
    # via the GitHub UI
    git push my-fork

    # via the GitHub CLI
    gh pr create --base release/2.15
    ```

    You can also use the `@pytorchbot cherry-pick` command to cherry-pick your PR. To do this, just add a comment in your merged PR. For example:

    ```
    @pytorchbot cherry-pick --onto release/2.15 -c critical
    ```
    (`-c docs` - is the category of your changes - adjust accordingly):

    For more information, see [pytorchbot cherry-pick docs](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/wiki/Bot-commands#cherry-pick).

    </details>

3. Make a request below with the following format:

```
Link to landed trunk PR (if applicable):
*

Link to release branch PR:
*

Criteria Category:
*
```

1. Someone from the release team will reply with approved / denied or ask for more information.
2. If approved, someone from the release team will merge your PR once the tests pass. **Do not land the release branch PR yourself.**

**NOTE: Our normal tools (ghstack / ghimport, etc.) do not work on the release branch.**

Please note HUD Link with branch CI status and link to the HUD to be provided here.
[HUD](https://hud.pytorch.org/hud/pytorch/pytorch/release%2F2.15)

items.title: [ROCm] Batched linalg.svd and linalg.eigh fail with hipErrorInvalidConfiguration above 65536 matrices on RDNA (rocSOLVER gesvdjBatched / syevd_strided_batched)
items.author: jeffdaily
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

My agent came up with this analysis, but I've read and approved it.

> #196745 covers the hipBLAS batched calls (getrf, getrs, geqrf, trsm, gels) and the hipSOLVER potrf/potrs batched calls, which launch nothing above 65536 matrices on RDNA; #192612 chunks those at 65535. Two rocSOLVER paths in `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/linalg/BatchLinearAlgebraLib.cpp` are still unchunked and hit the same limit on gfx1201 (ROCm 10.1, rocSOLVER 3.37):
>
> - `torch.linalg.svd` / `svdvals` for matrices up to 32x32, which ROCm's default gesvdj driver routes to `gesvdjBatched` (`apply_svd_cusolver_gesvdjBatched`);
> - `torch.linalg.eigh` / `eigvalsh`, which ROCm routes to `rocsolver_*syevd_strided_batched` (`apply_syevd_batched_rocsolver`).
>
> Both succeed at batch 65536 and raise `RuntimeError: HIP error: invalid configuration argument` at 65537 and above, for n = 3, 5 and 32. The limit is exactly 65536 batches. gfx942 is not affected.
>
> One visible consequence: `test_lu_solve_batched_many_batches` (a `@slowTest` in test/test_linalg.py) fails on gfx1201 at its (262144, 5, 5) case inside `make_fullrank_matrices_with_distinct_singular_values`, which calls `torch.linalg.svd` on the whole batch, before it reaches the lu_solve code under test. On a slow-test run this would look like a regression of #192612 when it is this limit.
>
> The fix on the PyTorch side is the same 65535-element chunking #192612 applies, in `apply_svd_cusolver_gesvdjBatched` and `apply_syevd_batched_rocsolver` (and `apply_syevj_batched` / `xsyevBatched` if they are reachable on ROCm). The library limit itself is being reported to the rocSOLVER team with #196745.

Reproducer:

```python
import torch
for n in (65536, 65537):
    a = torch.randn(n, 3, 3, device="cuda")
    s = torch.linalg.svdvals(a)                    # gesvdjBatched for m, n <= 32
    w = torch.linalg.eigvalsh(a @ a.mT)            # rocsolver syevd strided batched
    print(n, "ok")
```

```
65536 ok
RuntimeError: HIP error: invalid configuration argument
```

### Versions

torch 2.16.0a0+git1a989ff (viable/strict of 2026-10-13, built for gfx1201), ROCm 10.1 / HIP 7.16.26385, rocSOLVER 3.37, AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201), Linux.


cc @sunway513 @jithunnair-amd @pruthvistony @ROCmSupport @jataylo @hongxiayang @naromero77amd @pragupta @jerrymannil @xinyazhang @jianyuh @nikitaved @mruberry @walterddr @Lezcano

items.title: [Serve][LLM] Export `SGLangServer` from a public module
items.author: dstrodtman
items.body_excerpt:
## Description

`SGLangServer` is only importable from a private module, but it's a documented value for a public API field. Ray's own SGLang user guide therefore renders a `_internal` import as the first line readers copy.

### Current state

The class is defined at `python/ray/llm/_internal/serve/engines/sglang/sglang_engine.py:91` and re-exported by that package's `__init__.py`. It carries no `@PublicAPI` annotation and has no public import path.

### It's already named in a public API

`LLMConfig` is `@PublicAPI(stability="stable")`, and its `server_cls` field description names this class explicitly (`python/ray/llm/_internal/serve/core/configs/llm_config.py:225`):

```python
server_cls: Optional[Union[str, Any]] = Field(
    default=None,
    description="The serve class to use.(e.g., LLMServer, SGLangServer or other Server backends).",
)
```

So the public config documents `SGLangServer` as a supported value while giving users no public way to import it.

### The documentation shows the private import

Both SGLang examples on the [SGLang user guide](https://docs.ray.io/en/master/serve/llm/user-guides/sglang.html) open with it, and both lines are inside the rendered `literalinclude` region:

```python
# doc/source/llm/doc_code/serve/sglang/sglang_serving_example.py:2
# doc/source/llm/doc_code/serve/sglang/sglang_multinode_example.py:2
from ray.llm._internal.serve.engines.sglang import SGLangServer
...
    server_cls=SGLangServer,
```

## Suggested fix

There's already an established pattern for exactly this in `python/ray/serve/llm/deployment.py`, which wraps internal server classes as thin annotated subclasses and exports them:

```python
@PublicAPI(stability="stable")
class LLMServer(InternalLLMServer):
    pass

__all__ = ["LLMServer", "PDDecodeServer", "PDPrefillServer", "DPServer"]
```

Adding `SGLangServer` alongside those four would make the import public without moving or restructuring the implementation.

One caveat worth a maintainer's judgment: unlike the four classes already there, `SGLangServer` doesn't subclass `LLMServer` — it's a standalone, duck-typed server class — so the wrapper isn't a literal copy of the existing pattern. And SGLang support is still evolving (#62480, #63901, #63020), so `stability="alpha"` may fit better than `"stable"`. Either is a large improvement over `_internal` for a value the public config already advertises.

## Checklist

- [ ] Decide the stability level (`alpha` seems right given ongoing SGLang work)
- [ ] Export `SGLangServer` from a public module, following the `ray/serve/llm/deployment.py` pattern
- [ ] Update the two doc examples to the public path
- [ ] Add to the API reference

## Related

Same class of problem as #58624 (`DeploymentID`), which is open with the `usability` label.

I'm on the Anyscale docs team and found this while auditing private-module imports in `doc/source`. Happy to send the documentation-side PR once there's a public path to point at; I'd rather not paper over it by leaving the private import in place.

items.title: [Data] Support projection, filter, and limit pushdown for read_hive table reads
items.author: jiangxt2
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Track table-read pushdown as a follow-up to [PR #66573](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66573), as discussed in [the review](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66573#discussion_r4201555292).

The HiveServer2 reader proposed in #66573 supports `table=` reads and a source-level `limit` argument. It does not incorporate downstream Dataset projections, filters, or `Dataset.limit()` into the submitted HiveSQL. Columns and rows that Ray later discards can therefore still be transferred from HiveServer2.

The requested behavior is:

- Push required columns into the SQL projection while preserving output column names, order, and types.
- Push supported filter expressions into SQL only when their type and NULL semantics match Ray's evaluation. Keep unsupported conditions as residual filters in Ray.
- Push downstream limits into SQL when this preserves the original operation order. Do not move a limit ahead of residual filtering or move filtering ahead of an existing source-level limit.

These capabilities should compose correctly. Each Dataset execution should issue at most one HS2 data query, and failed reads should not be replayed.

This request is limited to HS2 `table=` reads. Rewriting caller-supplied `query=` SQL, direct storage reads, and optional query-schema inference ([#66840](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/66840)) are outside its scope.

### Use case

Users reading large Hive tables often need only a few columns, a subset of rows, or a small number of results. They should be able to express these requirements through Dataset operations and let Hive execute supported reductions, reducing data transfer and Ray-side processing.

Users can currently express these operations manually through `query=`, but the reader proposed in #66573 then requires an explicit Arrow schema. Table-read pushdown would retain the convenience of table metadata-based schema inference without requiring users to write SQL for each supported operation.

items.title: [Core] Memory monitor and worker killing are disabled on macOS; tasks exceeding available RAM make the machine unresponsive.
items.author: ctagard
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

### What happened
On macOS, when the combined memory of running tasks exceeds available RAM, Ray doesn't kill a worker or log a warning. The system compresses and swaps until it becomes unresponsive. On an M1 Ultra (128 GB) this required a hard reboot.

### Mechanism
OOM protection is compiled out on non-Linux platforms:
- [`src/ray/common/monitors/BUILD.bazel`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/68174559b27a4eba8db6b3c7ef7aaa2678ec20c8/src/ray/common/monitors/BUILD.bazel#L159-L167) selects `noop_memory_monitor_factory.cc` unless `//bazel:is_linux` ([`memory_monitor_factory.h`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/68174559b27a4eba8db6b3c7ef7aaa2678ec20c8/src/ray/common/monitors/memory_monitor_factory.h#L32): "On non-Linux platforms, returns a vector with a single NoopMemoryMonitor").
- [`src/ray/raylet/BUILD.bazel`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/68174559b27a4eba8db6b3c7ef7aaa2678ec20c8/src/ray/raylet/BUILD.bazel#L229-L237) selects `noop_worker_killing_policy_factory.cc` the same way.

### Expected behavior
The same behavior as on Linux: the memory monitor kills a worker according to the worker killing policy and the task fails with `OutOfMemoryError`. At minimum, Ray should warn.

### Measurements
I ran the script below on a macOS 26.6.2 VM (4 CPUs, 8 GB), sampled once per second, and stopped Ray when the memory pressure level reached 2:

| time | pressure level | free | compressor | file-backed | worker RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T+0 s | 1 | 986 MB | 375 MB | 2698 MB | 0 |
| T+2 s | 1 | 29 MB | 1008 MB | 2278 MB | 1103 MB |
| T+4 s | 1 | 33 MB | 2919 MB | 1806 MB | 955 MB |
| T+6 s | 2 | | | | |

Swap had started (202 MB) when Ray was stopped. With smaller tasks (80 × 100 MB, 200 × 1 MB), concurrency is limited by `num_cpus` and memory pressure stayed normal.

Worker RSS decreases while actual usage increases because RSS on macOS excludes compressed pages. `proc_pid_rusage(pid, RUSAGE_INFO_V4)` → `ri_phys_footprint` includes them and doesn't require root.

Setting `RLIMIT_AS` in `worker_process_setup_hook` works only partially. Darwin rejects limits below a process's current virtual size (about 415 GB for Python), so only "current + N" can be set. With N = 1 GB, the tasks above fail with `MemoryError` and memory pressure stays normal. However, the limit applies to virtual memory and to each process separately, so it doesn't replace a node-level monitor.

### Suggested fix
- Add a Darwin `MemoryMonitorInterface` implementation and a `MemoryMonitorUtils` backend. System usage would come from `host_statistics64` (anonymous + wired + compressor pages) and per-process usage from `ri_phys_footprint`. It would use the existing `memory_usage_threshold`, `min_memory_free_bytes`, and `memory_monitor_refresh_ms`.
- Enable the existing worker killing policies on macOS. They depend on Linux only through `MemoryMonitorUtils`.
- Add a macOS `config_setting` next to `//bazel:is_linux`.

I'd like to implement this if it's acceptable. A smaller alternative is a startup warning on macOS.

Related: #66729 (Ray Data task memory metrics are Linux-only).

I used AI assistance (Claude Code) for the investigation tooling.


### Versions / Dependencies

Ray master @ 1309798 (nightly wheel), Python 3.12, macOS 26.6.2, arm64.


### Reproduction script

Warning: this exhausts memory and can make the machine unresponsive. Run it in a VM or monitor memory pressure in Activity Monitor.

```python
import os
import time

import ray

NUM_TASKS = 4  # 4 x 2 GB exceeds an 8 GB machine; scale so NUM_TASKS * TASK_GB > available RAM
TASK_GB = 2


@ray.remote
def hold(nbytes: int) -> int:
    buf = os.urandom(nbytes)  # incompressible
    time.sleep(30)
    return len(buf)


ray.init(num_cpus=NUM_TASKS)
print(ray.get([hold.remote(TASK_GB << 30) for _ in range(NUM_TASKS)]))
```

On the 8 GB VM, the memory pressure level reached 2 about 10 seconds after `ray.init()`. Ray logged nothing.


### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it. However, it is a very inconvenient and unexpected footgun when doing development on Ray applications on MacOS.

items.title: [Core] Add versioning to the GCS resource load pull to avoid re-fetching unchanged data
items.author: dancingactor
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

## Description 
GCS periodically pulls cluster resource data (resource availability and demand) for autoscaler usage. However, even for idle nodes whose resource data remains unchanged, GCS currently pulls this data redundantly.

In contrast, Ray Syncer avoids redundant resource view reports using a versioning system: Raylet returns nothing when a node's `version_ <= after_version`. In other words, Ray Syncer reports only when a node's resource state changes.

**I want to implement the same versioning system for GCS periodic pulls. On an idle cluster, this will significantly reduce the workload on both the GCS main thread and the pull thread.**
### Benchmark

Test configuration:
- Resources per node: 6
- Pending demand shapes per node: 10
- Cluster idle, which means no resources or demand change

| Nodes | Thread | Current | Versioned pull (proposed) | Reduction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100 | main | 1.82 | 0.006 | ~300× |
|  | pull | 0.78 | 0.25 | 3.1× |
| 1,000 | main | 15.90 | 0.006 | ~2,600× |
|  | pull | 7.15 | 2.43 | 2.9× |
| 5,000 | main | 79.03 | 0.007 | ~11,000× |
|  | pull | 35.73 | 12.94 | 2.8× |

items.title: [Bug] Console-created deployments are not discoverable by the AIBrix data plane
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
A deployment created from the Console can reach `Ready`, and its generated Service can handle requests directly, but the AIBrix Gateway does not discover it.

The generated Pod template currently has only the Console/application labels ([code](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/apps/console/api/deployment/provider/kubernetes.go#L633-L642)). It is missing the AIBrix model labels defined in [`pkg/constants/model.go`](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/pkg/constants/model.go#L23-L37), such as `model.aibrix.ai/name` and `model.aibrix.ai/port`. The [mocked app manifest](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/development/app/config/templates/deployment/deployment.yaml#L6-L23) shows the expected shape.

To reproduce:

1. Create a deployment in Console with the dev [`mock-vllm` template](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/apps/console/api/store/demo.go#L569-L590).
2. Wait for it to become ready.
3. Inspect the Pod labels with `kubectl get pods --show-labels`.
4. Port-forward the generated Service: `/v1/chat/completions` works.
5. Send the same request through the AIBrix Gateway: the model has no discovered backend.

A Console deployment reported as ready should also be callable through the AIBrix data plane.

The fix will likely need to map the Console Model's `serving_name`, the effective container port, and the template engine to the canonical AIBrix labels. Please reuse the existing label constants. If a different model-name mapping is intended, it should be documented as part of the change.

This is complete when the mock model can be deployed from Console and reached through the Gateway, with a small rendering test plus an end-to-end check.

items.title: [Bug] vLLM classification models can't be reached through the gateway
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

vLLM serves its classification API at `POST /classify` (`vllm/entrypoints/pooling/classify/api_router.py`), and has done so since at least v0.9. The gateway only knows `/v1/classify`, which is SGLang's OpenAI-style route. #1905 added that path as the vLLM endpoint, but vLLM doesn't serve it.

So a vLLM classification model can't be reached through the gateway on either path:

- `POST /classify` matches no HTTPRoute, so Envoy returns 404 before the plugin ever sees it. Even with a route, `validateRequestBody` has no case for it and would answer 501.
- `POST /v1/classify` is routed, but the vLLM pod answers 404.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy a vLLM sequence-classification model behind the gateway.
2. Send `POST /classify` with `{"model": "<model>", "input": "some text"}`. Envoy returns 404.
3. Send the same body to `/v1/classify`. The request reaches the pod, which returns 404.

I found this by reading the routes and code on main (9190b145) and confirmed the 501 with a unit test. I haven't run it on a live cluster.

### Expected behavior

`POST /classify` is routed by `model` to that model's pods, the same way `/tokenize` and `/pooling` are.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: main (9190b145)
- LLM(s) being used: vLLM

Area: Gateway

items.title: [Bug] A served model loses its pending count and output predictor when its only pod or its adapter is updated
items.author: Jackmeson1
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

When the only pod serving a model gets an ordinary informer update (for example a status heartbeat), or a
ModelAdapter is updated with the same instance list, the cache deletes the model and builds a new one. The model's
in-flight accounting and learned output predictor are lost while the model is still being served.

- `updatePod` is a delete plus a re-add (`pkg/cache/informers.go`, lines 185–212 at `453ab36`).
  `deletePodAndModelMappingLocked` deletes the model when its last pod mapping goes (lines 599–601), and the re-add
  creates a new `Model` with a new `OutputPredictor` (lines 486–491).
- `updateModelAdapter` removes every old instance before adding the new list (lines 314–321), so an unchanged
  instance list does the same thing.
- `DoneRequestCount` then decrements the new object (`pkg/cache/cache_impl.go`, lines 397–399), so the model-level
  `pendingRequests` goes to `-1`. The balanced-accounting test (`pkg/cache/cache_test.go`, around line 698) expects
  exactly one increment and one decrement.
- `GetOutputPredictor` returns the fresh predictor, which has no history and returns the cold value.

The comment at `addPodLocked` (around line 390) already says a same-IP re-add must resume counters because the pod
never stopped serving. That resume covers the pod snapshot only, not the model.

## Steps to Reproduce

Unit level, using the cache's own `addPod`/`updatePod`/`AddRequestCount`/`DoneRequestCount` paths:
1. Add one pod serving model `m`. Call `AddRequestCount` for `m` and record a few outputs into its predictor.
2. Deliver an `updatePod` for the same pod (same IP, model label unchanged).
3. Check the model state, then call `DoneRequestCount`.

At `453ab36`:

```text
only-replica status update rebuilt the model: pending=0 want 1, samePredictor=false, predict=1 want not cold 1, afterDone=-1 want 0
unchanged adapter update rebuilt the model: pending=0 want 1, samePredictor=false, predict=1 want not cold 1, afterDone=-1 want 0
```

The same steps with a second replica of `m` keep the counter and the predictor, because the model never reaches
zero pods.

## Expected behavior

A model that is served before and after an update keeps its `*Model`: pending counters, output predictor and its
history, and router. A real delete of the last pod, or a model-name change, still ends the model's lifetime.

What this reproduction shows is the counter going to `-1` and the predictor resetting. Effects on queueing, latency
or routing were not measured.

## Proposed fix, and two questions before I write it

Reconcile membership in place in `informers.go`, under `Store.mu`: compute the incoming eligibility and edges before
removing the departing ones, keep the published `*Model` while it is still served, and diff adapter instance lists
instead of replacing them. The fix is about 300 production lines plus tests, so I'd split it into two PRs: pod
updates first, then adapter updates.

Two behaviours change on purpose, and I'd like your view on both before writing the code:
1. **Router construction retry.** Today a model whose queue router failed to construct gets another attempt only
   because updates recreate the model. Once the model is kept, the retry has to be explicit. The proposal is one
   construction attempt per membership event while the router is nil, keeping any non-nil router.
2. **Adapter edge ownership.** To keep a model across adapter updates, the cache needs to record which ModelAdapter
   (by `namespace/name`) installed each adapter edge, with a deterministic order, so that removing one source does
   not drop edges another still provides. That record is discarded when its last edge goes.

Does this direction work for you? I have the reproduction ready and can open the first PR.

## Environment

- AIBrix version: `453ab36`
- Deployment environment: unit tests of `pkg/cache` (Go 1.27)
- LLM(s) being used: not model specific

## Area

Gateway / cache

items.title: [Bug] Request trace never uses some log2 token buckets because the index is truncated
items.author: hmdsefi
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

`RequestTrace.getTraceKey` in `pkg/cache/trace.go` builds the `input:output` trace key from the log2 token buckets:

```go
inputIndex := int64(inputBucket / RequestTracePrecision) // Convert to int without precision loss.
```

`getTokenBucket` rounds log2(tokens) to a multiple of 0.1, but `bucket / 0.1` is not always an exact integer in floating point, and `int64(...)` truncates. For the 4.3 bucket the quotient is `42.999999999999993`, so the index is 42. Of the indexes 0 to 200, ten are never produced (43, 81, 86, 91, 162, 167, 172, 177, 182 and 187), and their requests are counted under the index below.

This affects the trace the gateway writes for the GPU optimizer when `AIBRIX_GPU_OPTIMIZER_TRACING_FLAG` is on. The optimizer reads the index back as log2(tokens) times 10, so a 20-token request is read as about 18 tokens and a 270-token request as 256.

## Steps to Reproduce

```go
trace := cache.NewRequestTrace(0)
key, _ := trace.AddRequestTrace("req", 20, 270, "")
```

At d0500b03 `key` is `42:80`. log2(20) is 4.32 and log2(270) is 8.08, so it should be `43:81`.

## Expected behavior

The index should be the rounded bucket times 10, so every bucket can appear in the trace.

## Environment

- AIBrix version: main at d0500b03
- Deployment environment: unit test of pkg/cache
- Cloud provider (if applicable): n/a
- LLM(s) being used: not model specific
- Client library version (if applicable): n/a

items.title: [Bug] VTC token tracker keeps a user under totals it no longer has after a partial prune
items.author: hmdsefi
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

In `UpdateTokenCount` (`pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/vtc/token_tracker.go`):

```go
oldTotal := t.userTotals[user]
t.pruneExpiredBucketsAndUpdateState(user, cutoff)
totalAfterPruning := t.userTotals[user]
...
newTotal := totalAfterPruning + newTokens
t.updateUserTotalAndMinMax(user, oldTotal, newTotal)
```

When pruning removes some but not all of the user's buckets, `pruneExpiredBucketsAndUpdateState` already moves the user in `totalsToUsers` from `oldTotal` to `totalAfterPruning`. The last call then removes the user from `oldTotal`, where it no longer is, and adds it under `newTotal`. The user stays listed under `totalAfterPruning` as well.

`GetMinTokenCount` then reports a total that no user has, and the VTC router computes its bucket size, `(min + max) / 2`, from it. With steady traffic most updates prune part of the window, so `totalsToUsers` gets a new stale entry on almost every update.

## Steps to Reproduce

Tracker with a 100 ms window (`WithWindowSize(100), WithTimeUnit(Milliseconds)`):

1. `UpdateTokenCount(ctx, "user1", 100, 0)`, and a few milliseconds later `UpdateTokenCount(ctx, "user1", 30, 0)`.
2. Once the first bucket has left the window and the second has not, call `UpdateTokenCount(ctx, "user1", 50, 0)`.
3. `GetTokenCount` for user1 and `GetMaxTokenCount` are 80, but `GetMinTokenCount` is 30, and `totalsToUsers` lists user1 under both 30 and 80.

In a loop of 50 updates with 5 buckets in the window, one user ended up with 45 entries in `totalsToUsers`, and the min was 65 while the user's total was 285.

## Expected behavior

After an update the user is listed only under its current total, and the min and max come from current totals.

## Environment
