items.title: [QST] SM120 FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate, plain form against block-scaled form with unit scales
items.author: emre570
items.body_excerpt:
**What is your question?**

On an RTX 5080, the plain FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate runs at half the rate of the block-scaled FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate. When all scale bytes are `0x7F` (UE8M0 1.0), the two forms give equal bits.

My FP8 attention kernel in CuTe DSL used `MmaFP8Op`. I changed it to `MmaMXF8Op` with constant unit scales and no other change. The kernel time went from 123.6 ms to 83.6 ms and the output is byte-equal (sgl-project/sglang#43390). So a user can do this today. My question is about the default.

1. Is there a reason to keep the plain form for E4M3 x E4M3 with FP32 accumulate on SM120?
2. If there is no reason, do you want `MmaFP8Op` and `rr_op_selector_sm120` to emit the block-scaled form with unit scales for this case? I can send a PR.

### Related report

The same behavior is reported in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5963 for the FlashInfer SM120 FP8 attention kernel, with RTX 5090 numbers and a bit-identity check. That issue also points to the MXFP8 attention work in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3628 and flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4149. The numbers below add an RTX 5080 and a CUTLASS GEMM measurement to that report.

### Scope

E4M3 x E4M3, FP32 accumulate, one RTX 5080 (driver 595.99.02, CUDA 13.3, CUTLASS `ffa119a12`). I did not measure other types or other cards.

### Raw MMA rate

Independent MMA chains, no memory access, 84 SMs. The rate is the same from 4 to 32 warps per SM.

| instruction | TFLOP/s |
|---|---:|
| `kind::f8f6f4.m16n8k32 ... f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32` | 246 |
| `kind::mxf8f6f4.block_scale.scale_vec::1X.m16n8k32 ... f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32.ue8m0` | 489 |

### Bit equality

- Random finite inputs. 0 of 704,643,072 accumulator registers differ.
- Negative control with scale 2.0. 704,643,071 registers differ.
- Edge cases (subnormal, ±448, NaN bytes, accumulator start at zero, FLT_MAX, subnormal, infinity, NaN). 30 classes, 176,160,768 registers each, 0 bits differ.

### CUTLASS GEMM

I used the SM120 `CollectiveBuilder` with `OpClassTensorOp`, pingpong schedule, tile 128x128x128, FP32 output. Then I changed only the instruction in `SM120_16x8x32_TN<float_e4m3_t, float_e4m3_t, float>` to the block-scaled form. The scale `0x7F7F7F7F` stays in a register. There is no scale factor tensor and no additional load. The patch is 34 lines.

I measured 30 shapes from real models. All 30 give 0 different output words. Five examples:

| shape source | M x N x K | plain | patched | speedup |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Wan 2.2 14B, `to_q` | 32760 x 5120 x 5120 | 236.1 | 398.6 | 1.69x |
| Llama 3.3 70B, MLP up | 4096 x 28672 x 8192 | 234.7 | 398.1 | 1.70x |
| FLUX.1-dev, FFN up | 4608 x 12288 x 3072 | 231.8 | 393.3 | 1.70x |
| MiniMax-H3, FFN up | 30272 x 14336 x 5376 | 234.6 | 363.5 | 1.55x |
| Gemma 3 27B, MLP up | 128 x 21504 x 5376 | 195.8 | 203.4 | 1.04x |

TFLOP/s. The speedup is 1.55x to 1.72x for the 22 shapes with M of 4096 or more. It is 1.04x to 1.82x for the 8 shapes with M = 128, where the low end is DRAM-bound.

Nsight Compute on the stock plain kernel shows the tensor pipe 96% busy. The MMA instruction rate is 47.9% of the peak.

One caution. These numbers use `max_swizzle_size = 8`. With the default of 1, three large shapes become DRAM-bound and the patched kernel is slower than the plain kernel (0.88x). I can open a different issue for that with the data.

### Where the plain form is used

- CuTe DSL `MmaFP8Op`
- `rr_op_selector_sm120` in `sm120_mma_builder.inl`, `sm120_array_mma_builder.inl` and `sm120_blockwise_mma_builder.inl`

cuBLASLt on the same card uses `QMMA.SF.16832.F32.E4M3.E4M3.E8` in its FP8 GEMM kernel and no plain `QMMA`.

I can share the benchmark source, the patch and the raw results if they are useful.

items.title: [BUG] sm120 GEMM hangs when K = 0 (grouped and non-grouped) after can_implement(), initialize() and run() return success
items.author: vera-rubin
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

On sm120, a CUTLASS 3.x GEMM with K = 0 passes `can_implement()`, and `initialize()` and `run()` return `kSuccess` in the tested release builds. The records show zero-K kernels not completing within 10, 15 or 60 seconds.

- **Grouped GEMM, where K = 0 is documented as supported.** With the sm120 ptr-array kernel, the recorded K = {128, 0, 256, 0} and {0, 0, 0, 0} groups do not complete within the recorded timeouts, while {128, 128, 128, 128} and {256, 512} pass. The mainloop source indicates that one K = 0 group is sufficient. CHANGELOG 4.3.0 says ([CHANGELOG.md L715](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/CHANGELOG.md?plain=1#L715)):

  > Enable GEMM_K = 0 in grouped gemm.

  The same case was fixed for Hopper in #2547 and for sm100 grouped GEMM in #2746.
- **Non-grouped GEMM, a validation gap.** The docs don't say whether K = 0 is supported, and a debug build stops at `assert(gmem_prob_shape[0] >= 1)` in `make_tma_copy_desc` ([copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp L957](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cute/atom/copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp#L957)). A release build (`-DNDEBUG`, as the examples use) prints `Error: Failed to initialize the TMA descriptor 1` to stderr, `initialize()` still returns `kSuccess`, and the launched kernel does not complete before the recorded timeout. With M = 0 or N = 0, the same kernel's `run()` returns `Error Internal` instead. Upstream examples 79a (NVFP4) and 79c (MXFP8 x MXFP6) time out at `--k=0`. Our own tests time out the same way with FP8 (cooperative and pingpong) and NVFP4 cooperative kernels at 128x128, and with FP8 at 300x392 with L = 2 and with beta = 0. They use real (non-null) A/B buffers.

A caller whose K can be 0 at run time (for example a weight-gradient GEMM for an MoE expert that received no tokens) is an illustrative scenario. This makes reachability plausible, not demonstrated for a deployed SM120 framework, product, or protected workload.

The submitted computation does not complete within the recorded timeout. Software waiting for it can lose availability; recovery and impact on other GPU users were not assessed. No confidentiality or integrity failure was demonstrated.

**Cause (our reading):**

1. The producer issues TMA loads only inside `for ( ; k_tile_count > 0; --k_tile_count)` ([sm120_mma_tma.hpp L400](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_tma.hpp#L400), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp L665](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp#L665)), so at K = 0 it loads nothing.
2. The consumer `mma()` clears the accumulators and then calls `pipeline.consumer_wait(smem_pipe_read)` unconditionally ([sm120_mma_tma.hpp L526](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_tma.hpp#L526), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp L848](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp#L848)). No TMA transaction ever completes that barrier. The array mainloops have the same first wait ([sm120_mma_array_tma.hpp L516](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_array_tma.hpp#L516), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_array_tma.hpp L934](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_array_tma.hpp#L934)).
3. The collectives' `can_implement()` checks only TMA alignment ([sm120_mma_tma.hpp L278](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_tma.hpp#L278), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp L399](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp#L399)). When the descriptor encode fails, [copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp L1066-L1080](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cute/atom/copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp#L1066-L1080) prints the error and calls `assert(false)`, which `NDEBUG` compiles out, so `initialize()` still reports success.

Other architectures, read, not run (we have no sm90 or sm100 GPU):

- Hopper's ptr-array mainloop guards the first wait with `if (k_tile_count > 0)` ([sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp L533](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp#L533)). Hopper's non-grouped mainloop has only a debug `assert(k_tile_count >= 1)` before an unconditional `consumer_wait` ([sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp L481-L487](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp#L481-L487)).
- The sm100 mainloops skip the first wait when `k_tile_count <= 0` ([sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp L670](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp#L670), [sm100_blockscaled_mma_warpspecialized.hpp L991](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm100_blockscaled_mma_warpspecialized.hpp#L991)).

**What a one-line guard did.** We added `if (k_tile_count <= 0) { return; }` right after `clear(accum)` in `mma()` and rebuilt on the RTX 5090:

- In `sm120_mma_tma.hpp` and `sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp`: the non-grouped K = 0 cases we re-ran completed with D = beta*C, bit-exact against a double-precision host reference (FP8 cooperative at 128x128 and at 300x392 w

items.title: Expert Parallelism (EP) roadmap for SM12x b12x MoE kernel (b12x_fused_moe / B12xMoEWrapper)
items.author: ItamarTerem
items.body_excerpt:
Hi flashinfer team,
We're deploying a large MoE model (384 experts, top_k=8) on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120/Blackwell workstation) using the b12x_fused_moe CuteDSL kernel via TensorRT-LLM's pytorch backend, and have hit the Expert Parallelism restriction:

b12x_fused_moe does not yet support Expert Parallelism
(num_local_experts={X} != num_experts={Y}).
Use a different MoE backend for EP configurations.

This comes from the explicit guard in flashinfer/fused_moe/cute_dsl/b12x_moe.py (both in the free function b12x_fused_moe and in B12xMoEWrapper.__init__), confirmed in flashinfer version 0.6.12.
Context on why this matters for us specifically: without EP, every GPU must retain workspace/routing capacity sized for the full state_E (all 384 experts), even though tensor parallelism already shards each expert's weights across GPUs. This is a meaningful, measured memory cost — in our case, the dynamic workspace's packed_input buffer alone accounts for roughly 7–11GB/GPU across a 60-MoE-layer model, purely from having to size for the worst-case "all experts active" scenario rather than a num_experts/ep_size subset.

What we're asking:

1. Is EP support for the SM12x b12x kernel family (static/dynamic/micro backends) on the roadmap, even at a preliminary stage?
2. Is there a rough timeline or tracking issue we could follow?
3. Are there known architectural blockers specific to SM120 (vs. SM100/SM103, where other kernels like MegaMoE already support EP) that make this a harder problem here?

We also note that vLLM's FlashInferB12xExperts (_supports_parallel_config) explicitly declines to use this backend when EP is requested, for the same underlying reason — so this appears to be a shared, cross-framework limitation rather than something specific to our integration.
Happy to provide more detail on our exact shapes/config if useful. Thanks for your work on this — the b12x kernel has otherwise been the only correctness-verified MoE path we've found for SM120 (CUTLASS produces silently incorrect output on this architecture in our testing).

items.title: [RFC]: [Store] Heat-Aware Object Tracking and DRAM Eviction
items.author: buyongxi
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

# [RFC] [Store] Heat-Aware Object Tracking and DRAM Eviction

## Summary

This RFC proposes a reusable per-object heat signal in Mooncake Store and uses
DRAM eviction as its first consumer.

Each object keeps a compact exponentially decayed access count. During an
existing eviction scan, the Master builds a heat distribution over eligible
ordinary DRAM candidates and derives a dynamic quantile cutoff. Cold ordinary
objects are evicted before hot ordinary objects, while existing lease, pin,
group, tenant and replica safety rules remain unchanged.

The same heat signal may later be reused by DFS/SSD promotion, dynamic
replication or other placement policies. Those consumers are outside the scope
of this RFC.

## Motivation

Mooncake Store currently uses approximate LRU for ordinary objects. Recency is
a useful default, but it cannot distinguish a frequently reused object with a
longer reuse distance from a recently accessed one-off object.

This matters when limited DRAM is used in front of SSD, DFS or another remote
tier. Evicting frequently reused objects increases lower-tier reads, network
traffic and promotion work. Adding frequency awareness can improve DRAM
retention decisions in these deployments.

Several Store policies also need a notion of popularity. Implementing an
independent counter or sketch for eviction, promotion and replication would
create inconsistent semantics and duplicate access-path work. A compact heat
value attached to object metadata provides one reusable signal while allowing
each consumer to define its own policy.

## Goals

1. Add frequency awareness to ordinary DRAM eviction.
2. Provide a reusable Master-side heat signal for future tiering policies.
3. Avoid global synchronization or online quantile updates on every Get.
4. Preserve existing eviction targets, safety checks and pin priorities.
5. Keep the feature bounded in memory and disabled by default.

## Non-Goals

1. Heat does not replace hard pin or soft pin.
2. Hot objects are not guaranteed to remain in DRAM under severe pressure.
3. This RFC does not implement DFS promotion, replication or prefetch policy.
4. Heat is not persisted in snapshots or the HA operation log.
5. No client-visible API for setting heat is introduced.

## Proposed Design

### Per-object heat

Each object stores a compact heat value and its last update time:

```cpp
struct KeyHeatState {
    float value;
    uint32_t updated_at_seconds;
};
```

At time `t`, stored heat `H0` from time `t0` is evaluated as:

```text
H(t) = H0 * 2 ^ (-(t - t0) / half_life)
```

A successful access records:

```text
H_new = min(maximum_heat, H(t) + 1)
```

Decay is lazy, so inactive objects require no timer or background update. The
timestamp uses monotonic seconds. Calculations use `double`; the bounded stored
value uses `float` because heat is a ranking signal rather than accounting
state.

Heat belongs to the logical object, not to one replica. Adding, moving or
removing replicas therefore does not reset popularity. Removing the object
removes its heat together with metadata.

### Access path

Heat is updated when a successful lookup grants the normal read lease. The
lease and heat update use the object's existing metadata lock.

The Get path does not update a global histogram or sketch. It only reads time,
decays one object's value and increments it. Failed lookups do not add heat.
When the feature is disabled, the existing lease-only path remains unchanged.

### Eviction census and cutoff

`BatchEvict()` already scans metadata shards. When heat-aware eviction is
enabled, each scan worker also builds a fixed-size thread-local logarithmic
histogram from eligible ordinary DRAM candidates. Histograms are merged after
the scan, without holding shard locks.

The cutoff is derived from the configured quantile:

```text
cutoff = max(minimum_heat,
             upper_bound(quantile_bucket(protection_quantile)))
```

An object is hot only when `current_heat > cutoff`.

`minimum_candidates` disables heat tiering for a census that is too small, and
`minimum_heat` prevents a zero-heavy startup distribution from treating unused
objects as hot. The census is a view of the current eviction candidates, not an
exact continuously updated cluster snapshot.

### Eviction order

Heat adds one ordering level inside the existing ordinary candidate class:

```text
ordinary cold objects
    -> ordinary hot objects, if required
    -> existing soft-pin fallback, if allowed and still required
```

Within each heat tier, Mooncake continues to use the existing lease-deadline
ordering. Every selected object is looked up again and revalidated before any
metadata or replica is changed.

Heat changes victim order only. It does not change the eviction target or
weaken lease, hard-pin, soft-pin, group, tenant, replica, offload or OpLog
correctness checks. If cold candidates cannot satisfy the target, hot objects
remain evictable.

## Reuse by Other Policies

The implementation separates:

1. per-object heat state and decay operations;
2. mergeable heat-distribution observation;
3. consumer-specific decisions such as an eviction cutoff.

Future policies should reuse the current per-object heat through a shared
internal accessor, but may use different thresholds and populations.

For example, DFS promotion could combine object heat with replica location,
object size, available DRAM and promotion rate limits. Its admission threshold
does not need to equal the DRAM eviction cutoff.

The existing Count-Min Sketch remains useful for high-cardinality admission
before an object has stable Master metadata. Per-object heat instead provides a
collision-free value for objects already represented by metadata, with lazy
continuous decay and natural object lifecycle. The two mechanisms are
complementary rather than interchangeable.

## Configuration

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `heat_aware_eviction_enabled` | `false` | Enable heat tracking and heat

items.title: [Core] RESCHEDULING placement group busy-spins the GCS main thread when it can't be scheduled
items.author: dancingactor
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

If scheduling a placement group in the `RESCHEDULING` state fails, `GcsPlacementGroupManager` keeps retrying scheduling it(~90k retry/s), which busy-spins the GCS main thread. Every retry is guaranteed to fail the same way until the next resource sync update arrives, so retrying before then is unnecessary and only blocks the GCS main thread.

Here is the issue in detail:

- Placement group P is already scheduled successfully on nodes A and B, with one bundle on each node.
- Node A dies, so P needs to be rescheduled elsewhere, and P enters the `RESCHEDULING` state.
- `GcsPlacementGroupManager` treats a `RESCHEDULING` placement group as top priority, so it inserts P at the front of the queue.
- The cluster doesn't currently have available resources for P, so `GcsPlacementGroupManager` fails to schedule P.
- `GcsPlacementGroupManager` immediately reinserts P at the front of the queue and retries scheduling it. The cluster resources haven't been updated yet, so it fails again.
- This retry loop keeps running and busy-spins the GCS main thread, starving other tasks. It only stops when a resource sync update finally provides enough available resources for P.

In this case, every retry between two resource sync updates is completely redundant, because it is guaranteed to produce the same result.

### Proposed Change

I think Solution 1 is better because it solves busy-loop and keeps the `RESCHEDULING` PG at top priority.
|            | Solves busy-loop | Keeps `RESCHEDULING` PG top priority |
| ---------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| master     | No               | Yes                                  |
| Solution 1 | Yes              | Yes                                  |
| Solution 2 | Yes              | No                                   |
#### Solution 1
Only retry scheduling a `RESCHEDULING` PG when a resource sync update arrives

#### Solution 2
Back off the `RESCHEDULING` PG the same way as a normal PG when retrying (the first attempt still gets top priority). This also solves the busy-loop problem, but it removes the top priority of the `RESCHEDULING` PG.

These PRs already proposed this change:
- https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65007
- https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65970


### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray: 3.0.0.dev0, built from source at commit a1a2cc64ee

### Reproduction script

``` python
import time

import psutil

import ray
from ray.cluster_utils import Cluster
from ray.util.placement_group import placement_group, placement_group_table

# Head node with 0 CPUs and two 1-CPU workers, both filled by a placement group.
cluster = Cluster(initialize_head=True, head_node_args={"num_cpus": 0})
workers = [cluster.add_node(num_cpus=1) for _ in range(2)]
ray.init(address=cluster.address)
pg_a = placement_group([{"CPU": 1}])
pg_b = placement_group([{"CPU": 1}])
ray.get([pg_a.ready(), pg_b.ready()])

# Remove pg_a's node. pg_a becomes RESCHEDULING: it's feasible, but pg_b holds the
# only remaining CPU.
node_id = placement_group_table(pg_a)["bundles_to_node_id"][0]
cluster.remove_node(next(w for w in workers if w.node_id == node_id))
while placement_group_table(pg_a)["state"] != "RESCHEDULING":
    time.sleep(0.1)
time.sleep(1)

# Nothing in the cluster changes from here on.
gcs = psutil.Process(cluster.head_node.all_processes["gcs_server"][0].process.pid)
start = placement_group_table(pg_a)["stats"]["scheduling_attempt"]
gcs.cpu_percent()
time.sleep(5)
end = placement_group_table(pg_a)["stats"]["scheduling_attempt"]
print(f"pg_a scheduling attempts in 5s: {end - start}, GCS CPU: {gcs.cpu_percent():.0f}%")
```

items.title: [Bug]: multi-node trtllm-serve with the MPI orchestrator (trtllm-llmapi-launch) hangs during executor startup; cause under investigation
items.author: dmvevents
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- CPU architecture: x86_64
- GPU: 2× node, 8× NVIDIA H200 each (16 GPUs total), AWS `p5en.48xlarge`
- Networking: AWS EFA (32 NICs/node), EFA 1.50 userspace + aws-ofi-nccl (GIN); Kubernetes StatefulSet with `hostNetwork: true` (pod IP == node IP on a `10.x.0.0/16` primary CIDR), sshd on :2222 for the `mpirun` bootstrap.
- Libraries:
  - Container: `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc9`
  - TensorRT-LLM: v1.3.0rc9 line (source paths below verified against this line)
  - NCCL 2.30.4, PyTorch as shipped in the container
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (container)
- Orchestrator: MPI (`trtllm-llmapi-launch` → `mpirun`), i.e. the `MpiCommSession`/IPC-executor path (not Ray).

### Who can help?

Leaving blank for a core maintainer to route (executor / IPC / multi-node serving).

### The bug

On a **multi-node** `trtllm-serve` launched with the **MPI orchestrator** (ranks spanning two hosts),
startup **hangs at IPC-executor init**. Rank-0's orchestrator creates its ZMQ IPC queues bound to
**loopback** and advertises that `tcp://127.0.0.1:PORT` endpoint to all workers. The 8 worker ranks on
the *second* host try to connect to `127.0.0.1:PORT`, which resolves to *their own* loopback, never
reach rank-0, and exit — so `MpiSession`/IPC init blocks forever waiting for them to connect.

This is specifically an **IPC-executor** problem, not an MPI / NCCL / EFA problem: the `mpirun`
cross-node bootstrap is clean (all 16 ranks start; `orted` launches on the worker node over ssh), and
the hang is **before** NCCL init.

### The hang (reproduced, frozen 8+ minutes, GPUs idle)

`trtllm-serve` freezes right after these lines and never proceeds:

```
[TRT-LLM] [W] Orchestrator is creating IPC executor
rank 0 using MpiCommSession to bind to external MPI processes
[TRT-LLM] [I] Generating a new HMAC key for server proxy_request_queue
[TRT-LLM] [I] Generating a new HMAC key for server worker_init_status_queue
[TRT-LLM] [I] Generating a new HMAC key for server proxy_result_queue
```

Rank-0 waits for the 16 workers to connect to `worker_init_status_queue`; the 8 worker-node ranks
never connect (they start, fail to reach rank-0, exit → `orted` defunct), so init hangs.

### Root cause (source, v1.3.0rc line)

1. `tensorrt_llm/executor/ipc.py:58` — the queue bind address defaults to a hardcoded loopback:
   ```python
   self.address_endpoint = address[
       0] if address is not None else "tcp://127.0.0.1:*"
   ```
2. `tensorrt_llm/executor/proxy.py:494` — `worker_init_status_queue = IpcQueue(is_server=True,
   name="worker_init_status_queue")` is constructed with **no `address`**, so it uses that loopback
   default; `proxy.py:520` then advertises that `tcp://127.0.0.1:PORT` endpoint to the workers.
   Cross-host workers connecting to `127.0.0.1:PORT` hit their **own** loopback → fail.
3. **No routable-IP override exists.** A whole-tree grep of `tensorrt_llm/executor/` for
   `TLLM_*ADDR|*IP|*HOST`, `0.0.0.0`, `get_local_ip`, `use_hostname` finds nothing that sets the
   orchestrator IPC bind address. (`TLLM_SPAWN_PROXY_PROCESS_IPC_ADDR` is an `ipc://` unix socket for
   the RPC-proxy path — even more node-local — and `MASTER_ADDR` is for the Ray backend, not the MPI
   IPC executor.)

So on a single node everything binds and connects on loopback and works; the moment ranks span hosts,
the loopback-bound orchestrator queues are unreachable by the remote workers.

### Expected behavior

A multi-node MPI-orchestrated `trtllm-serve` should let the orchestrator IPC queues bind to a
**routable** address (or `0.0.0.0`) and advertise rank-0's **routable IP** (not `127.0.0.1`) to the
workers, so cross-host workers can connect and `/health` comes up.

### Reproduction

```bash
mpirun -np 16 -H <node0>:8,<node1>:8 \
  --mca plm_rsh_args "-p 2222 -o GSSAPIAuthentication=no" \
  -x TRTLLM_FORCE_COMM_METHOD=... \
  trtllm-llmapi-launch trtllm-serve <a-MoE-model> \
  --tp_size 16 --ep_size 16 --pp_size 1 ...
# hangs at "Orchestrator is creating IPC executor" (see log above); GPUs idle.
```
(`GSSAPIAuthentication=no` is only needed so ssh doesn't stall on GSSAPI KEX against a no-KDC node —
unrelated to the IPC bug.)

### A candidate direction — and why this is filed as an issue, not a "fix" PR

An env-overridable bind address gets *past* the freeze once, but is **not a reliable fix**, so I am
filing this as a defensive-note issue rather than presenting a patch as done:

```diff
--- a/tensorrt_llm/executor/ipc.py
+++ b/tensorrt_llm/executor/ipc.py
-        self.address_endpoint = address[
-            0] if address is not None else "tcp://127.0.0.1:*"
+        self.address_endpoint = address[
+            0] if address is not None else ("tcp://%s:*" % os.environ.get("TLLM_IPC_BIND_IP", "127.0.0.1"))
```
Run with `-x TLLM_IPC_BIND_IP=<rank-0 routable node IP>`.

**Caveat (measured):** with this change + `TLLM_IPC_BIND_IP=<node0 IP>`, **one** attempt advanced all
the way to `launch_server` (past the IPC freeze); a subsequent clean relaunch (stale procs + port
reaped) **re-hung at the same IPC freeze**. So a routable-IP bind is *necessary but not sufficient*.
Unconfirmed which of: (a) the env did not thread to rank-0 on the relaunch (env propagation), (b) a
second worker-connected queue still binds loopback, or (c) an ephemeral-port node↔node reachability
issue. A complete fix should (i) bind the orchestrator IPC to a routable/`0.0.0.0` address, (ii)
advertise the routable IP (not `0.0.0.0`/`127.0.0.1`) to workers, and (iii) ensure **every**
worker-connected queue (not just `worker_init_status_queue`) uses it — then prove a clean multi-host
`trtllm-serve` reaches `/health`.

### Proven workaround

Switching the orchestrator from MPI to **Ray** (`--orchestrator_type ray` / the Ray-backed launch
path, which uses `MASTER_ADDR` for a routable rendezvous) brings multi-node `trtllm-serve` up cleanly
on the same 2-node substrate. So the defect is specific to the **MPI IPC-executor** bind path, and
there is a working alternative

items.title: [Bug]: Block-scaled FP8 model fails during NVRTC warmup in a pip-less uv environment
items.author: dtemraz
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM: `1.3.0rc29` (PyTorch backend)
- Python: 3.12
- Environment: virtual environment created with `uv venv` (no `pip` installed in the venv)
- GPU: H100 SXM 80 GB
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` (block-scaled FP8)

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [ ] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction


On a machine with a supported NVIDIA GPU and working CUDA dependencies:

```bash
uv venv /tmp/trtllm-uv-repro --python 3.12
uv pip install --python /tmp/trtllm-uv-repro/bin/python \
  --index-strategy unsafe-best-match \
  --prerelease=allow \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.nvidia.com \
  'tensorrt_llm==1.3.0rc29' 'mpmath==1.3.0'

export PATH=/tmp/trtllm-uv-repro/bin:$PATH

/tmp/trtllm-uv-repro/bin/trtllm-serve Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8 --backend pytorch
```

The environment has no venv-local `pip` executable unless it is installed separately. 
The failure is observed during engine warmup, at the first block-scaled FP8 GEMM JIT compilation.


### Expected behavior

TensorRT-LLM should locate the JIT include headers using the installed package's location without requiring the `pip` command to exist in the environment. If the headers cannot be located, the error should identify the missing include path or package-location lookup failure.


### actual behavior

On the tested setup, serving fails during warmup with:

```text
RuntimeError: NVRTC compilation failed
```

The failure originates in JIT include-directory discovery: getJitIncludeDirs() locates the required headers by invoking pip show tensorrt_llm and parsing the Location: field.

In a uv-created virtual environment without pip, this command may resolve to a system-level pip that cannot locate the package installed in the virtual environment. As a result, the required include paths are missing, and compilation of fp8_block_scaling_gemm fails.

The error surfaces as RuntimeError: NVRTC compilation failed, without identifying the missing include paths.

BF16 inference works in the same environment.

## Workaround

Installing `pip` into the same virtual environment and ensuring its executable is first on `PATH` resolves the issue in the tested setup.

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: [BUG] SM90 blockwise FP8 GEMM reuses modified B scales across M waves
items.author: 1sgtpepper
items.body_excerpt:
## Which component has the problem?

CUTLASS C++

## Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

SM90 cooperative blockwise FP8 GEMM applies the preceding M wave's A scale again when processing the next M wave. With CTA tile 256×128×128 and scale granularity 128×64×128, `D[128,0]` is **1024 instead of 512**.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

In a checkout of `59e3a3338d516ca6ce0e073af8da65289678a35c`:

```sh
curl -fL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/1sgtpepper/cutlass/75e7b4a8a2859c317209d81c91c5ab9158a573e7/test/regression/fp8_scale_wave.cu -o fp8_scale_wave.cu
nvcc -std=c++17 -O3 -lineinfo --expt-relaxed-constexpr \
  -gencode=arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a \
  -Iinclude -Itools/util/include fp8_scale_wave.cu -o fp8_scale_wave
./fp8_scale_wave
```

Inputs are FP8 E4M3 ones, with A scales 2 and 4 across the row bands and B scales 1 and 2 across the column bands.

```text
minimal l=0 m=128 n=0 actual=1024 expected=512
minimal tile=256x128x128 scale=128x64x128 stages=3 problem=256x128x128x1 mismatches=16384 FAIL
```

**Expected behavior**

Each M wave multiplies its own A scale by the original B scale for the current K tile.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**

- CUTLASS `59e3a3338d516ca6ce0e073af8da65289678a35c`, main as of September 8, 2026. The affected collective is byte-identical in `v4.8.0dev` and `v4.7.1`; these releases were not executed.
- H100 80GB HBM3, driver 580.95.05; CUDA 13.1.1.
- Modal cloud GPU, Ubuntu 24.04 container, Linux x86_64.

**Additional context**

The `ScaleMsPerWave == 1 && ScaleNsPerTile > 1` path modifies B-scale registers reused by successive M waves, in both the main loop and drain. Reloading B's original scales makes all ten `--all` cases pass; restoring the old code restores the same six failures.

items.title: [Serve] [RFC] Computed Retry-After for backpressure rejections
items.author: vinay7373
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

PR #65193 added `BackpressureConfig`. Deployments can now reject backpressured requests with a 429 and a static `Retry-After` header. Each caller (proxy or `DeploymentHandle`) has its own request queue, and at the time of a backpressure rejection a static `Retry-After` value can be incorrect in both directions. If the queue is deep and the static value is too short, clients retry into another rejection, adding load exactly when the system is trying to shed it. If the queue drains fast and the value is too long, capacity sits idle while clients wait.

This proposal computes the `Retry-After` value from observed load. This makes the header a reliable estimate of when capacity will be available, instead of a number the operator guessed. This was the original shape of the production request behind #65193 and it fits the discussion there about making 429 the default at some point.

No OSS inference server does this today (TGI, Triton, NVIDIA Dynamo and TorchServe all reject without a retry hint). The closest prior art is cloud-side (Azure OpenAI's `retry-after-ms`, AWS's `x-amz-retry-after`) and per-client rate limiters, where the value can be exact because a rate window is a clock. Capacity recovery is not a clock, so here the value is an estimate at any layer.

## Goals

- An opt-in `BackpressureConfig` policy that computes `Retry-After` from load signals the rejecting component already has.
- Keep the rejection path as cheap as it is today. No RPCs, locks or extra work on reject-and-respond.
- Degrade gracefully: computed, else static, else no header. Never fail or delay a rejection.

## Non-goals

- Changing when requests are rejected. Admission control is a separate discussion.
- Guaranteeing admission at the suggested time. The header is a hint, not a reservation.
- Changing the default rejection status code. Tracked separately.
- Implementing any further policy, such as the cluster-informed one (see "Future policies").

## Proposed API

```python
from ray.serve.config import BackpressureConfig

@serve.deployment(
    max_queued_requests=64,
    backpressure_config=BackpressureConfig(
        status_code=429,
        retry_after_policy="queue_drain_rate",   # NEW: "static" (default) | "queue_drain_rate"
        retry_after_s=5,                         # static value; also the fallback for computed policies
    ),
)
```

`retry_after_policy` is a named policy instead of a bare `"auto"` so future strategies can be added without changing what existing configs mean.

## Proposed design

This design adds a new field to `BackpressureConfig` called `retry_after_policy`, and one new policy named `queue_drain_rate` that computes `Retry-After` from the rejecting component's observed queue depth and drain rate.

The overall mechanism has 3 basic aspects: (i) how to compute the `Retry-After` value (what the `queue_drain_rate` policy implements), (ii) where to compute it, and (iii) who stamps the header and emits it to the client.

These boil down to emission and estimation. Emission answers (iii) and is fixed: the rejecting component stamps the header. Estimation covers (i) and (ii): one shared implementation, invoked at the two places Serve rejects today, each feeding its own local signals.

### The `queue_drain_rate` policy (this proposal)

```
retry_after = ceil(observed_queue_depth / drain_rate)
```

- **The numerator is the depth observed at rejection.** It is at least `max_queued_requests`, since a rejection only fires once the queue has reached the cap, and occasionally a little above it: the router's check is not atomic, and replica-rejected requests re-enter the queue behind new arrivals. The raise site already holds this number (it is in the `BackPressureError` message today), so using the observed value costs nothing and is exact.
- **`drain_rate` is the live signal**: how fast the queue empties, updated at the end of every interval as `drain_rate = 0.3 * rate_over_last_interval + 0.7 * previous_drain_rate`. `rate_over_last_interval` is the fresh measurement: requests drained during the interval that just ended. `previous_drain_rate` is this same formula's output from the previous update, so it carries the whole history with older intervals fading out. The 70% weight on the trend keeps lumpy traffic from whipping the value around (completions land in bursts, so a single interval can read 0 or 3x the true rate), and the 30% on the fresh measurement keeps the estimate chasing real load changes within a few intervals. The split, the interval length and the warmup threshold are implementation constants with environment-variable overrides, like Serve's other internal tunables, not new `BackpressureConfig` fields. The update runs on a lightweight background timer in the component's existing metrics machinery (default 1s). An interval with zero completions counts as a real observation when work is in flight, since that is what slow drain looks like, but idle intervals (nothing running or queued) skip the update instead of decaying the rate. The rate counts as warm after a configurable minimum number of counted intervals; until then the fallback applies.
- **Two call sites, one implementation.** On the proxy path the router rejects; its drain rate is its own assignment throughput, from a monotonic counter added at the existing send event (the current per-replica counter is an in-flight gauge, so it can't provide a rate). The rate is fleet-blended: faster replicas take more assignments, so mixed hardware is priced in. On direct ingress the replica rejects; its drain rate is its own completion rate, and its queue is drained only by itself. Same formula, different local inputs, different values, each describing its own queue. A replica's value is a conservative upper bound, since a retry may be re-balanced to a replica that frees up sooner.
- **Clamp to [1, 60] seconds.** Common client SDKs ignore `Retry-After` above 60s.
- **Jitter (for example +/-20%) is applied in the shared heade

comments.author: johntaylor-cell
comments.body:
My main concern is how this RFC and direct-ingress work together.  Serve is moving toward direct-ingress with HAProxy as the default, and on that path the router is no longer the module that rejects the request.  HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve, and it already has retry-after functionality (as does Envoy).  Both implement it very differently from what the RFC proposes.  Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction.  It is also per-client, and HAProxy exposes queue-based metrics so the limit can fire only under real back pressure.  I suggest we provide a way to enable that functionality in HAProxy, which Serve already generates config for but does not use today.

If we also want retry-after on the router path (when direct-ingress is disabled), I would try to duplicate HAProxy's time-based functionality, rather than use a forecast. That is a larger change than this RFC scopes, since admission control is listed as a non-goal, but I think it is worth deciding explicitly rather than estimating.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Thanks for the review. Breaking it down into where we agree and where we don't.

**Where we agree:**

1. The RFC did not cover the direct-ingress path. That was a real gap and I updated the RFC. Short version: on direct ingress the same policy runs at the replica, using its own queue depth divided by an EWMA of its own completion rate. Same formula, one shared estimator implementation, two call sites. A replica's queue is drained only by itself, so that vantage is even simpler than the router's.

2. Per-client rate limiting at the HAProxy layer is valuable. It answers "this client exceeded its quota", and its Retry-After can be exact because a rate window is a clock. That is complementary to this RFC, which answers "the deployment is out of capacity, here is when to come back". I would support that as a separate proposal and am happy to file it.

**Where we don't agree, and why:**

1. "HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve" as the rejector. Not for backpressure today. On the direct-ingress path the replica rejects the request (see the "Request dropped due to backpressure" emission sites in [replica.py on the ray-2.58.0 tag](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/python/ray/serve/_private/replica.py)). HAProxy passes the replica's response through, and its errorfiles only rewrite HAProxy-generated errors. #65193 shipped 429 + Retry-After on this path, tested with `RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_DIRECT_INGRESS=1`.

2. "Functionality Serve already generates config for but does not use". I checked `haproxy_templates.py`: no stick-tables, no track-sc, no deny rules, no Retry-After anywhere in the generated config. Enabling this would be new work, not switching on something dormant.

3. "Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction". I checked the [HAProxy docs](https://www.haproxy.com/documentation/haproxy-configuration-tutorials/security/traffic-policing/) on this. HAProxy's computed Retry-After is `http-after-response set-header Retry-After %[src,table_expire(...)]`: the time until the client's stick-table rate-limit record expires. That is per-client policing, and it is exact because a rate window is deterministic. For capacity overload (server maxconn queue full, `timeout queue` expiring) the docs show no Retry-After computation: that 503 ships without a hint. The queue timer measures elapsed wait, not time until capacity returns. When capacity frees depends on service completions and arrivals, and no layer can know that exactly, including HAProxy, which cannot see how long the inference ahead of a request will take. Any capacity Retry-After is an estimate at every layer. That is why the RFC ships an acceptance criterion and telemetry to measure the estimate, instead of claiming exactness.

Rate limiting and capacity backpressure are different problems. An exact time-based Retry-After exists for the first and cannot exist for the second. This RFC is scoped to the second, now explicitly works on both ingress paths, and leaves room for a HAProxy rate-limiting proposal alongside it.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@johntaylor-cell 

My thoughts on your a HA Proxy based admission control and what I see as limitations:

- As you mentioned the HAProxy queue resets on every reload and Serve reloads HAProxy on every replica-set change. So the primary queue evaporates exactly during autoscaling churn (your own finding).
- Composition traffic never passes HAProxy, so the Serve backstop must stay. That means 3 admission systems with 3 threshold vocabularies to keep coherent.
    - Users configuring three queueing layers instead of one: per-server `maxconn` plus timeout queue in HAProxy, `max_queued_requests` at handles, `max_ongoing_requests` at replicas. Three knobs at three levels in different units (connections vs requests, per instance vs per caller vs per replica) that all have to be sized against each other and re-sized as the cluster scales. Mis-size any pair and you get double queueing or shedding while replicas sit idle. That is more error prone, not simpler.
- The default proxy path gets nothing from it.
- Per-deployment BackpressureConfig granularity would have to be re-expressed in generated HAProxy config.
- Moving where queueing happens is an admission-control redesign, which this RFC explicitly scopes out as a non-goal.
- On jittered-static vs computed: 
    - jitter only spreads retries around a center, it cannot make the center reliable. With `retry_after_s` we already ship the option to set a fixed, guessed value at config time, so a jittered constant is not a new proposal, it is [#65193](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65193) plus jitter. Drain rate moves 10-100x across load regimes, so the constant is wrong exactly when it matters. A 5s center against a 60s real drain means every jittered retry comes back early and gets refused again. Guessing that constant is the problem this RFC exists to remove. So a computed value using drain rate is more reliable. And @suppagoddo 's suggestion for A/B against a jittered-static baseline will show it under real workloads and make this measurable.

One policy, `queue_drain_rate` which computes `retry_after` on rejection using below formula:

comments.body:
hello guys, some information and test for this RFC.

I tested the proposal on Ray 2.58.0 and found two implementation details worth checking before coding it.

First, num_requests_sent_to_replicas is an in-flight gauge: it increments on send and decrements on completion. It cannot directly provide assignment throughput, so the router likely needs a monotonic counter at the accepted-assignment event.

Second, router queue depth is not always equal to max_queued_requests at rejection. Internal replica rejection can cause requests to re-enter after new requests occupy temporarily freed slots. With a cap of 8, 1,418 of 17,270 router rejection events had an observed depth of 9–11. I did not observe this on the direct-replica path.

I also compared the computed policy with a tuned jittered-static baseline over 90 held-out distributed runs. Conditional local-drain header MAE was 1.865s for the computed policy and 1.141s for static 2s. The computed policy generated fewer attempts, so this looks like a precision versus retry-cost tradeoff rather than a clear winner.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@JerryChaox Thanks for testing the approach and for those valuable findings. Here are my thoughts on each of them:

1. Agree (and my earlier comment was wrong on this) that `num_requests_sent_to_replicas` is an in-flight gauge, increments on send (`router.py:404`) and decrements on completion (`router.py:412`). I will fix this by adding a new monotonic assignment counter at the same send event. So the raise site and the counters live on the same object and the drain rate is still a derivation over local state.

2. This is a great find. Agreed. This finding makes the formula better: use the observed depth at rejection as the numerator instead of the configured cap. The raise site already holds that number, it is in the BackPressureError message today.

3. On your third observation, the A/B test: I see how a static value wins on a homogeneous workload, where a good constant like your 2s can be guessed or tuned in advance. But the whole purpose of this RFC is the case where the constant cannot be guessed in advance, because load regimes vary and move the drain rate. I'd like to know: a) Did drain time vary across your 90 runs? b) Was the 2s tuned per workload or once overall?

Your fewer attempts observation is the most interesting part. MAE weighs a 1s early and a 1s late suggestion equally, but the costs are not equal: early means a wasted attempt plus more load on a system that is already shedding, late means idle wait. So I think we should use a asymmetric or composite metric that penalizes wasted attempts (penalize early more than late).

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Acceptance criteria spec:

1. Ground truth: Each rejection records the observed depth D and the drain counter value at that moment. Ground truth T is the wall time until the counter advances by D: assignments at the router, completions at the replica on direct ingress. This measures what the header claims, that the observed backlog clears. It does not measure whether a specific retry gets admitted, since that depends on other clients' arrivals. T stays measurable under continuous overload because the counter keeps advancing even when the queue never dips below the cap.
2. Metric: An asymmetric loss between the suggested delay `s` and `T`: `0.75 * max(T - s, 0) + 0.25 * max(s - T, 0)`. One second too early costs 3x one second too late, because an early retry wastes an attempt and adds load while the system is shedding and a late one only waits, bounded by the clamp. The minimizer of this loss is the 75th percentile of the drain time distribution, so the estimator gets a concrete target. MAE is reported as secondary for comparability. Scoring is offline over logged pairs, on the pre-jitter post-clamp value.
3. Baseline: The comparison arm is jittered static, with the constant tuned only on calibration runs disjoint from the evaluation set (rule: 75th percentile of calibration drain times, one global constant). A per-scenario tuned static is also reported. Runs are open loop (clients ignore the header) with autoscaling off and a pinned replica set.

@suppagoddo For me to run the above acceptance test I'll need one structured record per rejection with `policy id, fallback rung used, observed depth, drain rate estimate and warm flag, pre-jitter and post-jitter values, and the counter value at rejection`. Plus the counter itself readable by a test harness at sub-second granularity. Everything already exists at the raise site or in estimator state; the cost is one log line on a path that already logs a warning today. Please make sure this record emission is part of your implementation.

Pass bar (proposal): 
- Computed beats the static baseline on the primary loss by at least 20% in aggregate across the scenarios
- is never more than 10% worse in any single scenario
- the undershoot rate lands at 25 +/- 10 points
- and cold start falls back to the static value cleanly.

cc. @JerryChaox @abrarsheikh @johntaylor-cell

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
**AI serving regimes for the acceptance runs**

Now that the implementation is up for review (#66798), here are the regimes the acceptance runs will cover. The runs collect the metrics defined in my acceptance comment above. The scenarios its pass bar refers to are drawn from these regimes. I'm deriving the regimes from real-world AI serving, using two characteristics: load and completion.

What a regime is: An AI serving regime is a recurring pattern of load and completion at the component that rejects requests. Load is how requests arrive. Completion is how they finish: how long each one runs, how many run at once, and whether they finish one at a time or in batches.

**Why these two (load and completion)?**
Ground truth in the acceptance spec is the time for the drain counter to advance by the observed depth: assignments at the router, completions at the replica on direct ingress. Both count the completion process, seen from each vantage, since the router hands a queued request to a replica when one finishes. So completion sets the drain time directly. Load decides when the queue overflows and what the estimator sees between rejections, such as idle gaps. Latency is an outcome of both, not an input.

Completion is the important half in AI serving, because processing time is not known when a request arrives. A generative model decides its output length while it generates, and in production "the remaining output length of an LLM request is not conditioned on the generated length so far" [1]. Drain speed cannot be computed from what is in the queue. It has to be measured from completions.


**Completion regimes:** 
The estimator samples once per second, so what matters is how far apart completions arrive at that scale.

| Regime | Examples | Completions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| W1 Real-time predictive | vision, ranking, LLM code completion | Dense: many per second | Latency bounds of 15 to 250 ms [2]. Code completion has a median output of 13 tokens [3] |
| W2 Batched execution | `@serve.batch`, dynamic batching | Grouped: a batch finishes together | Each response returns once its whole batch is evaluated [4] |
| W3 Interactive LLM | chat on continuous batching | Dense to moderate: seconds each, many at once | A median of 129 output tokens [3] at 20 to 50 tokens/s [5] |
| W4 Long-running LLM | reasoning, long context, agent steps | Sparse: minutes each, few at once | A mean of 3,880 output tokens [6]. Long contexts limit how many run at once [7] |

**Load regimes:**

| Regime | Arrivals | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| L1 Steady | A constant rate. The runs use fixed-interval schedules so repeated runs are comparable | MLPerf's Server scenario models online load with Poisson arrivals [2] |
| L2 Bursts and idle gaps | High-rate bursts separated by silence | API traffic is "aperiodic... characterized by burstiness" [8]. Short-term arrivals are "often bursty (CV > 1)" [1] |
| L3 Mix shift | A steady rate, but the request mix changes, so completions speed up or slow down | Services have "widely different prompt and token distributions" [3]. In one 48-hour window, 29 of 2,412 clients sent 90% of requests [1] |

**Scenarios:** 
|# | Cell | Completions | Expected drain time | Load |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | W1, L1 | every 0.25 s | 2 s | 2x drain |
| S2 | W3, L1 | every 2.5 s | 20 s | 2.5x drain |
| S3 | W1 to W3, L3 | every 0.25 s, then every 1 s | 4 s, then 16 s | 2x drain |
| S4 | W1, L2 | every 0.25 s during bursts | 4 s | 3x drain for 20 s, then idle for 25 s |
| S5 | W3, L1, mixed fleet | every 0.4 s, from one fast and one 4x slower replica | 10 s | 2.4x drain |
| S6 | W4, L1, beyond cap | every 8 s | 240 s | 4x drain |
| S7 | W1, L1, cold start | every 0.25 s | 4 s | 3x drain from the first second |
| S8 | W3, L1, pipeline | every 1 s at the inner deployment | 8 s | 3x drain |
| S9 | W2, L1 | 8 at once every 4 s | about 8 s | 2x drain |
| S10 | W4, L1 | every 8 s | about 48 s | 2x drain |

[1] ServeGen, NSDI'26: https://

items.title: [Data] object-store SHUFFLE_V2 map/reduce tasks ignore label_selector
items.author: viiccwen
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

`ExecutionOptions.label_selector` promises to constrain every task and actor created by a Dataset, including shuffle and aggregation tasks. The object-store SHUFFLE_V2 map and reduce operators do not merge that selector into the remote options passed to their tasks.

Both V2 shuffle map and reduce tasks should carry the Dataset's `label_selector`. When a task has an operator-level selector, its entries take precedence for conflicting keys, matching the existing `merge_label_selector()`
contract and non-V2 shuffle behavior.

- `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/shuffle_operators/shuffle_map_operator.py`
- `python/ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/shuffle_operators/shuffle_reduce_operator.py`

### Versions / Dependencies

`master`

### Reproduction script

Start a two-node cluster where only the worker carries the `training` label.
For example, start the worker with:

```bash
ray start --address=<head-address> --labels='{"ray-subcluster":"training"}'
```

Then run the following against that cluster. With a currently nonexistent label selector, correct behavior is for the map/reduce tasks to remain pending; current behavior submits them without the selector and allows them to run on available nodes.

```python
import ray
from ray.data.context import DataContext, ShuffleStrategy

ray.init(address="auto")

ctx = DataContext.get_current()
ctx.shuffle_strategy = ShuffleStrategy.SHUFFLE_V2
ctx.execution_options.label_selector = {"ray-subcluster": "does-not-exist"}

result = ray.data.range(100, override_num_blocks=4).repartition(2, keys=["id"])
print(result.materialize().take_all())
```

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

items.title: [URICache] Size tracked by RAY_RUNTIME_ENV_WORKING_DIR_CACHE_SIZE_GB can become negative
items.author: Aleksei-Poliakov
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

When tasks starts ray keeps track of the initial size of the working dir, but if GC runs and deletes it - the amount subtracted from the running sum is the actual size. Consider the following scenario:
* RAY_RUNTIME_ENV_WORKING_DIR_CACHE_SIZE_GB = 1MB
* the very first task runs, it's initial working dir size is 2MB, but after it's done - there is 100MB of temporary files left in the working directory
* now GC runs (since 2MB > 1MB limit), it does 2MB - 100MB = -98MB (negative 98MB)
* the following task runs, it's initial size is also 2MB and it also leaves 100MB of data
* now GC does NOT run because (-98MB + 2MB < 1MB limit)
* as tasks keep piling up - chances run the node will run out of space before GC gets a chance to run again

### Versions / Dependencies

Tried running this on two versions: 2.59.0 and 2.40.0 - this is reproducible in both

### Reproduction script


```
"""Ray's working_dir cache stops evicting after the first working dir that grew in use.

End to end on one local node, no cluster::

    python uri_cache_e2e_repro.py

1. ``ray start --head`` with ``RAY_RUNTIME_ENV_WORKING_DIR_CACHE_SIZE_GB=0.001``
   (a 1 MiB cap) and a private ``--temp-dir``.
2. Three drivers in turn, each with its own 2 MiB ``working_dir``. A task in each
   writes 64 MiB into the working dir (the worker's cwd), reports the directory
   size, and the driver exits.
3. After each driver exits, wait for the runtime_env agent to report the URI
   unused and list ``<temp-dir>/session_latest/runtime_resources/working_dir_files``.

Expected: every working dir is deleted when its job ends; each is over the cap on
its own. Actual: job 1's is deleted, job 2's and job 3's stay. The cache credited
each URI with its unpacked size (setup log: "Added URI ... with size") but on
eviction subtracted the size measured at deletion, 33 times larger, so the total
Ray keeps went negative after job 1 and ``total > cap`` never held again.

The cap is compared against credited sizes only, which is why the working dir is
padded above the cap: a smaller one is never considered for eviction at all.

Runs ``ray stop`` at the end.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os
import re
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import time
from pathlib import Path

import ray

PORT = 6399
TEMP_DIR = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "ray_uri_cache_e2e_repro"
CACHE_CAP_GB = "0.001"
WORKING_DIR_MIB = 2  # above the cap, like a real code bundle
WRITE_MIB = 64
JOBS = 3
RAY_CLI = [sys.executable, "-m", "ray.scripts.scripts"]  # the ray CLI of this interpreter

DRIVER = f"""
import os, sys, ray
from ray._private.utils import get_directory_size_bytes

ray.init(address="127.0.0.1:{PORT}", runtime_env={{"working_dir": sys.argv[1]}}, log_to_driver=False)

@ray.remote
def write_into_working_dir(mib):
    with open("output.bin", "wb") as f:  # the worker's cwd is the unpacked working_dir
        f.write(b"\\0" * (mib * 1024 * 1024))
    return get_directory_size_bytes(os.getcwd())

print("SIZE_AT_JOB_END", ray.get(write_into_working_dir.remote({WRITE_MIB})))
ray.shutdown()
"""

ADDED = re.compile(r"Added URI (\S+) with size (\d+)")


def working_dir_files() -> list[str]:
    d = TEMP_DIR / "session_latest" / "runtime_resources" / "working_dir_files"
    return sorted(p.name for p in d.iterdir() if p.is_dir()) if d.exists() else []


def runtime_env_logs() -> str:
    # add() logs through the per-job logger (runtime_env_setup-<job>.log); the agent
    # reports the URIs it hands to mark_unused in runtime_env_agent.log.
    logs = TEMP_DIR / "session_latest" / "logs"
    if not logs.exists():
        return ""
    return "\n".join(p.read_text() for p in sorted(logs.glob("runtime_env*.log")))


def wait_for(pred, timeout: float = 60.0):
    deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        result = pred()
        if result:
            return result
        time.sleep(0.5)
    return None


def main() -> int:
    sys.stdout.reconfigure(line_buffering=True)  # keep prints in order with Ray's stderr log
    shutil.rmtree(TEMP_DIR, ignore_errors=True)
    TEMP_DIR.mkdir(parents=True)
    env = {**os.environ, "RAY_RUNTIME_ENV_WORKING_DIR_CACHE_SIZE_GB": CACHE_CAP_GB}
    subprocess.run(
        RAY_CLI + [
            "start", "--head", f"--port={PORT}", f"--temp-dir={TEMP_DIR}",
            "--num-cpus=2", "--object-store-memory=200000000",
            "--include-dashboard=false", "--disable-usage-stats",
        ],
        check=True, env=env, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL,
    )
    driver = TEMP_DIR / "driver.py"
    driver.write_text(DRIVER)
    print(f"ray {ray.__version__}, RAY_RUNTIME_ENV_WORKING_DIR_CACHE_SIZE_GB={CACHE_CAP_GB}, "
          f"{WORKING_DIR_MIB} MiB working dirs, each job writes {WRITE_MIB} MiB into its own")

    seen: set[str] = set()
    implied_total = 0  # the arithmetic URICache does: + credited size, - size at deletion
    left: list[str] = []
    try:
        for job in range(1, JOBS + 1):
            working_dir = TEMP_DIR / f"working_dir_{job}"
            working_dir.mkdir()
            (working_dir / "marker.txt").write_text(f"job {job}\n")  # distinct URI per job
            (working_dir / "code.bin").write_bytes(b"\0" * (WORKING_DIR_MIB * 1024**2))
            try:
                run = subprocess.run(
                    [sys.executable, str(driver), str(working_dir)],
                    check=True, capture_output=True, text=True,
                )
            except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
                print(f"job {job}: driver failed\n{e.stderr}")
                return 2
            size_at_job_end = int(run.stdout.split("SIZE_AT_JOB_END")[1].split()[0])

            def added():
                for m in ADDED.finditer(runtime_env_logs()):

items.title: Illegal memory access in triton kernel and non-determinism codegen
items.author: xw285cornell
items.body_excerpt:
Hi team, we seem to identified an issue that triton is generating non-deterministic codegen results, and in certain cases (small chances) it seems to have illegal memory access due to out of bound access in shared memory. 
The triton code is fairly simple (shown below). We run the code many times (disabled pytorch's codegen cache) and it seems it produced different shared memory: 
Most of times: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 2560, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}
Sometimes: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 544, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}

So sometimes it only asks for 544 bytes for shared memory space which might lead to out of bound access to shared mem. We checked and ttir is the same across the two runs, but llir is different. Wondering if you can shed some lights on this (and whether the codegen is deterministic. Also this is still on llvm IR - not sure if it repros in MLIR. 

```
from torch._inductor.triton_ops.autotune import pointwise

@pointwise(
    size_hints=[262144, 64],
    tile_hint=TileHint.DEFAULT,
    filename="notebook",
    meta={
        "signature": {0: "*bf16", 1: "*fp32", 2: "*bf16", 3: "i32", 4: "i32"},
        "device": 0,
        "constants": {},
        "mutated_arg_names": [],
        "configs": [instance_descriptor(divisible_by_16=(0, 1, 2, 3), equal_to_1=())],
    },
)
@triton.jit
def triton_(
    in_ptr0,
    in_ptr1,
    out_ptr0,
    xnumel,
    ynumel,
    XBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
    YBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
):
    xnumel = 262144
    ynumel = 62
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:, None]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    yoffset = tl.program_id(1) * YBLOCK
    yindex = yoffset + tl.arange(0, YBLOCK)[None, :]
    ymask = yindex < ynumel
    x0 = xindex % 512
    x1 = xindex // 512
    y2 = yindex
    x3 = xindex
    tmp0 = tl.load(
        in_ptr0
        + (
            512
            + x0
            + (1536 * x1)
            + (786432 * y2)
            + (786432 * (((x0 + (512 * x1)) // 262144)))
        ),
        xmask & ymask,
    ).to(tl.float32)
    tmp1 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (512 + x0), xmask)
    tmp2 = tmp1.to(tl.float32)
    tmp3 = tmp0 + tmp2
    tmp4 = 2.8284271247461903
    tmp5 = tmp3 / tmp4
    tl.store(
        out_ptr0 + (y2 + (62 * x3) + tl.zeros([XBLOCK, YBLOCK], tl.int32)),
        tmp5,
        xmask & ymask,
    )
```

items.title: [Bug] PodAutoscaler status is rewritten on every reconcile, alternating between two versions
items.author: AarnavNoble
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

For `scalingStrategy: KPA` or `APA`, the controller writes the PodAutoscaler status on every reconcile, even when nothing about the target or its metrics has changed. Two code paths set the same conditions with different text, and each one overwrites the other:

| Condition | `computeStatus` (start of `Reconcile`) | `reconcileCustomPA` |
|---|---|---|
| `AbleToScale` | reason `Configured`, empty message | reason `SucceededGetScale`, message `successfully retrieved target scale` |
| `ScalingActive` | message `desired=1, actual=1` | message `desired=1, actual=1; reason=stable` |

A reconcile that reads the first version writes the second, and the next one writes the first again.

The controller is set up with `For(&PodAutoscaler{})` and no event filter, and the comment on `hasObservedInvalidSpec` notes that "a status update also enqueues the object". So each of these writes should enqueue the next reconcile immediately, without waiting for the 10s resync. Every reconcile lists the target's pods and fetches metrics from each of them.

`scalingStrategy: HPA` has the same overlap between `computeStatus` and the conditions copied from the HPA in `reconcileHPA`. There the second write uses the object fetched before the first write, so I expect it to fail with a conflict on alternate reconciles; that error is logged and dropped. I have not written a test for the HPA path.

### Steps to Reproduce

The unit test below builds a reconciler on the fake client, reconciles one unchanged KPA PodAutoscaler ten times, and counts status writes. Save it as `pkg/controller/podautoscaler/status_stability_test.go` and run:

```
go test ./pkg/controller/podautoscaler/ -run TestReconcileSettlesWithoutRewritingStatus -v
```

Output on `main` at `6b9ce490`:

```
round  1: status writes=2 AbleToScale.reason="SucceededGetScale" ScalingActive.message="desired=1, actual=1; reason=stable"
round  2: status writes=1 AbleToScale.reason="Configured" ScalingActive.message="desired=1, actual=1"
round  3: status writes=1 AbleToScale.reason="SucceededGetScale" ScalingActive.message="desired=1, actual=1; reason=stable"
round  4: status writes=1 AbleToScale.reason="Configured" ScalingActive.message="desired=1, actual=1"
...
round 10: status writes=1 AbleToScale.reason="Configured" ScalingActive.message="desired=1, actual=1"
status was rewritten 8 times across 8 reconciles of an unchanged PodAutoscaler
```

<details>
<summary>status_stability_test.go</summary>

```go
package podautoscaler

import (
	"context"
	"testing"

	appsv1 "k8s.io/api/apps/v1"
	corev1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
	apimeta "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/meta"
	metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/schema"
	ktypes "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/types"
	"k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes/scheme"
	"k8s.io/client-go/tools/record"
	"k8s.io/utils/ptr"
	ctrl "sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime"
	"sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime/pkg/client"
	"sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime/pkg/client/fake"
	"sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime/pkg/client/interceptor"

	autoscalingv1alpha1 "github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/api/autoscaling/v1alpha1"
	"github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/monitor"

items.title: [Feature]: Thread the explicit NVFP4 4over6 recipe into the TRT-LLM gen, CUTLASS and Prims-TS fused-MoE backends (follow-up to #5152)
items.author: feih-nv
items.body_excerpt:
### Problem

#5152 (merged as 7bcf9183) made the NVFP4 4over6 recipe an explicit argument (`nvfp4_4over6=` / `QuantConfig.nvfp4_4over6`) on the quantization entry points and the CuTe-DSL MoE, but the other fused-MoE backends still resolve the recipe from the process-wide `FLASHINFER_NVFP4_4OVER6*` environment variables at dispatch time. Today only `CuteDslRunner` sets `supports_nvfp4_4over6 = True`; every other unified runner raises `NotImplementedError` on an explicit recipe, so a caller who pins a recipe cannot use those backends at all, and a caller who leaves it unset gets whatever the environment says.

Remaining environment-reading sites on `main` (72f88c79):

- TRT-LLM gen fused MoE: `csrc/trtllm_fused_moe_runner.cu` (per-token GEMM2 activation quant) calls `resolveNVFP4Recipe(kNVFP44Over6FromEnv)`; `TODO(aleozlx, #5141)`.
- CUTLASS fused MoE: `csrc/fused_moe/cutlass_backend/cutlass_fused_moe_kernels.cuh` `dispatchNVFP44Over6Config()` reads `getEnvNVFP4Use4Over6()` and friends; `TODO(aleozlx, #5141)`.
- Prims-TS: `flashinfer/prims_ts/moe/runner.py` `_nvfp4_per_token_global_scale_inv()` reads `FLASHINFER_NVFP4_4OVER6` / `_E4M3_USE_256`, but only from `_quantize_nvfp4_fc1_output_for_fc2`, which no NVFP4 tactic reaches (see below). Prims-TS is out of scope.
- Trace templates: the MoE traces carry no recipe axis, so a replayed trace depends on the environment.

Out of scope here: `moe_ep` (not part of the unified API).

### Requested outcome

Meet #5141 for TRT-LLM gen and CUTLASS: the public flat APIs accept an explicit recipe, and the backends consume it instead of reading process-global state at dispatch.

- Public flat APIs get `nvfp4_4over6=` (unset = environment, `None` = standard, `NVFP44Over6Config` = that recipe), as `cute_dsl_fused_moe` already does since #5152: `trtllm_fp4_block_scale_{,routed_}moe`, `cutlass_fused_moe`.
- Unified runners opt in through `QuantConfig.nvfp4_4over6` on the same shared layer.

Only the GEMM2-input quantization inside the MoE is affected (GEMM1 input is quantized by the caller):

- TRT-LLM gen quantizes it itself only in per-token mode, so it follows `CuteDslRunner`: a pinned recipe only with `per_token_scale=True` on NVFP4×NVFP4, `None` always allowed.
- CUTLASS has no per-token mode, but its `doActivation` quantizer has 4over6 variants, so the recipe applies on the standard path. The caller's `fc2_input_scale` must be built with the same `e4m3_max` (documented; a calibrated value cannot be checked).

The encoder/decoder pair already exists (`nvfp4_4over6_code()` in Python, `resolveNVFP4Recipe(int64_t)` in `nvfp4Recipe.h`):

1. **TRT-LLM gen** - `int64` recipe code in `MoERunnerArgs`, trailing FFI argument of `trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe`, decoded at the GEMM2 quant site in `trtllm_fused_moe_runner.cu` (`globalScaleInv()` keeps the per-token scale consistent, so no extra scale check). Python: `core.py` op and fake op, `TrtllmMoERunner` (`backends/trtllm/sm100_runner.py`), public flat kwarg; opt in `TrtllmFp4RoutedRunner`.
2. **CUTLASS** - recipe in `QuantParams::FP4`, trailing argument on `run_moe` / `run_moe_min_latency`, `dispatchNVFP44Over6Config()` dispatches on it (two call sites: `expandInputRowsKernelLauncher`, `doActivation`; all instantiations already exist). `cutlass_fused_moe` op, fake op and public kwarg (the unified CUTLASS runner calls it); opt in `CutlassNvfp4Runner`.
3. **Trace templates** - add the recipe to the FP4 MoE templates (TRT-LLM flat / routed / shared experts, CUTLASS), present only when non-default so existing definition names do not change.

**Not in scope: Prims-TS.** Its NVFP4 MoE path never requantizes the GEMM2 input: `map_trtllm_nvfp4_moe_tactic` fixes `fc1_dtype_c=E2M1` and `fc2_use_per_token_sf_b=False` for every tactic, so FC1's epilogue emits NVFP4 (no 4over6 variant) and `_quantize_nvfp4_fc1_output_for_fc2` is unreachable (confirmed on B200: environment on/off gives bit-identical output, the requantizer is never called). A recipe there would first need a selectable per-token FC2 config, which is a kernel-selection change rather than plumbing. `PrimsTsRunner` keeps rejecting explicit values through the base `MoERunner` check.

Each backend gets the config-equals-env bit-exactness test pattern from `tests/utils/test_fp4_quantize.py::test_nvfp4_quantize_config_equals_env` (explicit recipe with the environment off must equal unset recipe with the equivalent environment), plus CPU `check_support` rejection tests.

### Target hardware

SM100 / SM103 (Blackwell); hardware-independent API change.

### Inference engine

- TRT-LLM
- PyTorch native
- Custom / other

### Affected model or model family

Any NVFP4 model using the 4over6 recipe through the TRT-LLM gen or CUTLASS fused-MoE backends.

### Current workaround

Set the four `FLASHINFER_NVFP4_4OVER6*` variables process-wide and leave `QuantConfig.nvfp4_4over6` unset. Two recipes in one process, or one recipe per backend, are not possible.

### Impact

- API usability or integration complexity
- Correctness or numerical-quality risk (a pinned recipe silently differing from the environment would rescale activations by 448/256)

### Related work

- #5141 (parent request), #5152 (first half: quantization entry points, CuTe-DSL MoE, `QuantConfig` field), #3264 / #3448 (4over6 implementation and `NVFP44Over6Config`).

items.title: [Bug] TcpTransport connection pool: unbounded growth with threshold mass-GC; stale entries to restarted peers are never evicted
items.author: d3nb
items.body_excerpt:
## Environment

mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13 0.3.11.post1 (PyPI), used as SGLang PD-disaggregation KV transfer backend (`MC_FORCE_TCP=1`, `MC_TCP_ENABLE_CONNECTION_POOL=true`), same-host prefill(TP4) → decode(TP4), 8×B300, container network.

## Issue 1: pool grows unboundedly, then mass-closes tens of thousands of connections at once

Under sustained load (fixed 10-way concurrency, ~27K-token KV parcels, chunked), `/proc/net/tcp` on the sender side shows a sawtooth with ~8-minute period:

```text
03:15  ESTABLISHED 29024
03:17  ESTABLISHED 38952
03:18  ESTABLISHED 17724   TIME_WAIT 21089   <- ~21K connections closed within one minute
03:24  ESTABLISHED 44419
03:25  ESTABLISHED 45623   <- 83% of the ephemeral port range
03:26  ESTABLISHED 20738   TIME_WAIT 26831   <- ~27K closed at once
```

Two problems: (a) between flushes the pool keeps growing toward the ephemeral-port limit (we measured peaks at 83% of a widened 10240-65000 range — with the default ~28K-port range this would hit `EADDRNOTAVAIL` long before the flush); (b) the flush itself dumps 20K+ sockets into TIME_WAIT within seconds. A bounded pool with per-peer connection reuse would presumably hold this at a few hundred connections (we see ~566 ESTABLISHED steady when idle-ish).

## Issue 2: pooled connections to a dead/restarted peer are never evicted

If one side of the PD pair is restarted alone (its listen ports change), the surviving side's pool keeps the stale entries. Small transfers still succeed (presumably via new connections), but **large multi-slice transfers stall silently and permanently** — the sender reports no error, the receiver times out (`KVPoll.WaitingForInput` timeout after 300s). It also degrades progressively: after one single-sided peer restart we only measured throughput loss at high concurrency; after a second one, all large transfers hung. Restarting both sides together fully restores normal behavior.

## Ask

1. Bound the pool (per-peer cap + LRU reuse) instead of grow-then-mass-GC.
2. Evict/reconnect pool entries on connection failure or peer-identity change, so a peer restart doesn't silently poison large transfers.

Happy to provide more traces or test patches — this is reproducible on demand in our setup.

items.title: Five conv filter tile access iterators invert the byte scaling in add_pointer_offset (8/sizeof_bits instead of sizeof_bits/8)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Five conv filter tile access iterators invert the byte scaling in `add_pointer_offset`: they compute `pointer_offset * 8 / sizeof_bits<Element>::value` where every sibling iterator uses `pointer_offset * sizeof_bits<Element>::value / 8`.

Affected sites:

- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h:194
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_fixed_channels.h:165
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_few_channels.h:167
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv3d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h:160
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/depthwise_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_direct_conv_optimized.h:162

For fp32 (32 bits) the inverted form is a silent no-op multiplier of 8/32 vs the correct 4; for fp16 it scales offsets by 1/2 instead of 2. All 30+ sibling iterators (activation/dgrad/wgrad variants) use the correct form, e.g. conv2d_dgrad_filter_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h:187.

Currently latent: no in-tree caller passes nonzero element-granularity pointer offsets into these mainloop A/B iterators (kernels call `add_pointer_offset` on the epilogue D iterator only). The defect surfaces for any external user advancing these public iterators manually.

items.title: Sparse split-K kernels offset the E operand without the kElementsPerElementE division
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`SparseGemmSplitKParallel`-style serial split-K in `include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sparse_gemm.h` offsets the E (metadata) operand by the wrong amount for slices beyond the first:

```cpp
// sparse_gemm.h:237
cutlass::MatrixCoord tb_offset_E{
  threadblock_tile_offset.m() * Mma::Shape::kM,
  threadblock_tile_offset.k() * params.gemm_k_size / kSparse,   // missing / kElementsPerElementE
};
```

The E iterator's extent is expressed in packed element-E columns and divides twice (`sparse_gemm.h:269`, `problem_size_k / kSparse / kElementsPerElementE`), and the sibling kernel `gemm_sparse_universal.h:622` divides twice as well when offsetting:

```cpp
cutlass::MatrixCoord tb_offset_E{
  threadblock_tile_offset.m() * Mma::Shape::kM,
  offset_k / kSparse / kElementsPerElementE,
};
```

With the missing division, every K-slice `>= 1` of a split-K sparse GEMM starts its metadata reads far past the end of the packed E tensor; all accesses are predicated off and the slice runs on zero-filled (invalid) metadata.

Concrete numbers: fp16 (`kElementsPerElementE == 2`), K=128, `split_k_slices = 2`: slice 1 has an E extent of 4 columns while its offset column is 32. Zero valid accesses.

The same formula is duplicated in two more copies of this kernel body:
- `sparse_gemm_with_absmax.h:322`
- `sparse_gemm_with_visitor.h:153`

Reachability note: nothing in-tree exercises it (`device::SparseGemm` with `split_k_slices > 1`; example 15 uses one slice), so this is latent, but the wrapper accepts split-K (`device/sparse_gemm.h` passes `args.batch_count` through).

### Suggested fix

Divide by `kElementsPerElementE` in the offset at all three sites, matching `gemm_sparse_universal.h`:

```cpp
threadblock_tile_offset.k() * params.gemm_k_size / kSparse / kElementsPerElementE,
```
